#6833. My Most-Worn Winter Jacket Is $250

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Filson’s Insulated Canvas Outfitter is everything your vintage workwear isn’t.

Welcome to the Esquire Endorsement. Heavily researched. Thoroughly vetted. These picks are the best way to spend your hard-earned cash.

I was sitting at a dive bar in Brooklyn, looking past my wife and a friend during a lull in conversation at the two pool tables with two games going on. One guy—next team up, when I see him—was wearing the uniform: mesh-backed trucker hat, work pants with carabiner keys, and a vintage work jacket (you know the brand). But vintage gives that layer too much credit. It looked like its former owner was shot and left in a ditch—and our hero, like a member of the Joad family, needed a jacket, found the deceased, peeled this jacket off him, put it on, and kept on rolling toward the big city.

I focus back on the table. “Do y’all think we’ve run out of vintage?” I blurt out. “What?” My wife, with good reason, is confused; my buddy, silent, is equally so. “Like, vintage work jackets,” I say, pointing to this guy. “You know, America has been deindustrializing for half a century, and the whole 2020 resale boom has peaked. Maybe this guy is wearing that jacket because all the good vintage workwear is gone?” Neither of them cared enough to entertain me.

But I care to talk about it. The vintage-workwear ship has sailed, the bubble has popped—whatever. You do not need to pay $500 for some old guy’s work jacket in the name of “sustainability.” If you’re doing that at this point, you’re a victim. You’d be better off talking that $500 and splitting it in two. With the first $250, take someone out on a date. With the second $250, buy this Filson jacket—the unequivocally best barn coat, work jacket, or whatever you want to classify it as on the market. This is the only winter jacket a man needs.

The three-season version of this jacket, the regular Canvas Outfitter, is a perennial top seller for Filson. It is obviously a good barn jacket, classic in its hunting-inspired styling: flannel lining, corduroy collar, hand warmers, and big shell pockets. But if I were to get that style of old-school hunting jacket—and sorry to blaspheme against my beloved Filson—I would go to a few other brands.

Where Filson runs away with the barn-coat crown is in adding insulation; no one does it better. The original, though flannel lined, feels just a little too flimsy for me, and if it’s going to hit lower than my waist, I’d rather have full butt coverage. But with the insulation and the internal structure it provides, the jacket sits ever so slightly higher on the body. It’s not cropped, but the fit becomes more trucker or work jacket, less barn coat—hence my comparison to a Carhartt Detroit. Personally, it’s exactly what I want. Looks good no matter how you wear it; flatters any body type you can imagine.

That said, the actual benefit of that insulation is not aesthetic. It’s practical. This is one of the warmest jackets in my rotation, and it’s easily the most durable. The ten-and-a-half-ounce duck canvas never gets a nick—not on a hike, not on a day doing yard work. And while this is not at all a rain jacket, the polyester lining means it can put up with moisture infinitely better than something filled with down. If you get caught in a fall rainstorm, no worries. If you have a snow day, this is the ultimate outer layer. For that reason, it often ends up as one of my most-worn garments over the colder months.

To come back to my original point: Aren’t we all tired of the absurdity of vintage? I don’t mean to be anti-sustainability or anti–old clothes. But aren’t we tired of hype cycles around buying someone else’s clothing? Workwear is supposed to be bought cheap and worn hard. This jacket is the answer in my mind. It’s not trendy, nor is it especially expensive. You can buy one brand-new—novel, no?—for $250 (a steal these days) and know that every crease, every fade, every repaired armpit hole is yours and yours alone. Wear it for a few decades, then it’ll be your vintage. When you’re dead, some kid will sell it to a yuppie for a 200 percent markup. That’s the goal.

#6831. All the Photos of Princess Kate and Prince William on Their Overseas Tour of Mumbai

The royal pair will spend three days in India for the 2026 Earthshot Prize Awards

On Monday, November 16, Princess Kate and Prince William landed in Mumbai, India, for their first overseas royal tour in four years. The last time the pair made an international state visit was when they traveled to the Caribbean in the spring of 2022 to celebrate the late Queen Elizabeth II’s Platinum Jubilee.

Now, the Prince and Princess of Wales have hit the road again for the 2026 Earthshot Prize Awards, which are being hosted in Asia for the first time ever. The annual prize, founded by Prince William with an inaugural ceremony in 2021 and set to last until 2030, celebrates innovators who are breaking ground in the environmentalism space.

While it was announced back in February that William would be traveling for the ceremony, it was confirmed only this past weekend that Kate would be joining him. This marks her first major trip with William since her 2024 cancer diagnosis and eventual remission (she also took a solo trip to Italy this May).

The 2026 Earthshot ceremony takes place on November 17, but Kate and William are spending a total of three days in India. They began their trip with a visit to Ballard Estate, the business and shopping district of Mumbai. There, the Prince and Princess of Wales played a bit of gully cricket, took a ride on the metro, and visited local vendors and performers. Then, on day two, they stopped by the Bandra Worli Sea Link promenade and attended the Children’s Earthshot ceremony before dressing up for the official event.

For the rest of their time abroad, the royals will be “celebrating innovation, sustainability, youth leadership, and the enduring connections between the United Kingdom and India,” per their office at Kensington Palace.

#6829. The Property Brothers Reveal Why Lighting Tops Their Holiday Chore Checklist

The holidays are upon us, and while we busy our hands with turkeys, trees, and tinsel, the Property Brothers are gifting fans a few friendly tips for hosting across generations. Partnering with Home Instead, Drew and Jonathan Scott have developed a holiday chore checklist that every host should complete before guests arrive.

“The holidays are all about bringing family together. But when you're hosting aging loved ones, a little preparation can go a long way in making sure everyone feels comfortable and safe. As home renovation experts, we know that it's often the smallest changes that make the biggest difference,” the brothers explain.

Ahead, we’re sharing their top tips for a safe, festive, and inviting home this holiday season.

While string lights and extension cords are all holiday decor staples, they can be a major tripping hazard. To prevent spending the holidays in the emergency room, the brothers recommend double-checking that loose ends and loops are neatly tucked away to keep paths and walkways clear throughout your home.

Slippery rugs, mats, and runners are another major safety hazard. Drew and Jonathan recommend reinforcing any pieces that could potentially slide with gripping tabs or replacing them with options that have better traction—especially in bathrooms where wet floors pose a greater risk.

While decorating with Christmas lights is at the top of everyone’s to-do list, your home needs more than a well-lit tree. Dark halls and stairways are major safety concerns, especially when hosting guests unfamiliar with your floor plan. Plug-in nightlights are a great option for improved visibility, and they can be decorative too.

A clear entryway for the holidays is a nonnegotiable. Outside the home, leaves and debris lining your front steps are as dangerous as they are unsightly. Before your guests ring the doorbell, take the time to rake, sweep, and clean as much as you can to ensure all steps, dips, and curbs are visible.

Drew and Jonathan clock in at well over six feet tall, but their guests may not be as gifted with height. If you’re used to storing things up high, the brothers recommend moving essentials like plates and glasses from high shelves and into lower, more easily accessible territory. Not only does this minimize straining, but it also reduces the risk of dropping pieces that could leave dangerous, messy shards in their wake.

#6823. Glen Powell Tussles with Country Music Superstars in The Comeback King Trailer

Powell plays a country singer on the rebound in the upcoming Judd Apatow comedy.

Rodney Dangerfield set the bar for return-to-school comedies in 1986’s aptly titled Back to School. He decried that “If a man has no education, he's got nothing” before proceeding to throw money at all of his problems and hilariously ignore his own advice for the next hour and a half. Then Adam Sandler put his own, unique spin on the film when he sent Billy Madison back to grade school a decade later. And when The Comeback King hits theaters on February 5, 2027, Glen Powell will walk into homeroom as a country singer looking to save his career by finishing his degree.

In the first trailer, which debuted on Wednesday, November 18, Powell plays Aubrey King, a country music superstar dating the biggest pop star in the world (played by Madelyn Cline). His life is turned upside down when she cheats on him and then writes a song blaming him for the deed instead, which sends his career down the toilet. So, his manager convinces him to head back to school and rediscover what he wants to say with his music. Plus, fall in love with a teacher (Cristin Milioti) and joke around with The Comeback King’s insane list of guest stars—including Miranda Lambert, Jelly Roll, Brad Paisley, Chris Stapleton, Shaboozey, and Reba McEntire.

Powell and director Judd Apatow mostly wrote The Comeback King as they filmed it—which is normal for Apatow, but not so much for Powell. “For a guy like me, who likes to be prepared, it’s a nightmare,” Powell told Esquire in our cover story last month. The script came together from the best lines of their improvisational takes. Spitfires of one joke after another until Apatow laughs, or says “That’s funny,” Powell says. But for now, there’s little of the actual schooling revealed in the trailer.

You can catch a lot of the jokes from our celebrity cameos, however, like when Jelly Roll tells a disheveled Powell that he “smells like how people think I smell.” There’s also a great line when one of Powell’s managers, played by Kumail Nanjiani, says that fans answered a poll about him and said that his eyes were too close together, which wasn’t even one of the options. “They wrote it in like you were a Libertarian candidate,” he says. Watch the trailer above.

The Comeback King begins a busy 2027 for Powell, who also has the sci-fi film The Great Beyond coming out in October by J.J. Abrams. Also in the works? A Ron Howard firefighter movie that is reportedly not connected to Backdraft; the third season of his Hulu football comedy series, Chad Powers; a Lou Gehrig film with Richard Linklater; and likely the start of Top Gun 3—whenever Tom Cruise is ready. As Powell joked to Esquire, “Hopefully I’m not the age of Maverick in Maverick by the time I make it.”

#6821. 7 Window Treatment Fixes Designers Swear By

Smart solutions for windows that are anything but standard.

You’d be hard-pressed to find a homeowner who complains about having too many windows, but not all windows are created equal. Maybe you’re saddled with a skinny one tucked in the corner of a bedroom, or an unusually shaped one in a bathroom. The right treatment can make even the most awkward window feel intentional—but the trick is knowing which solution works best for each situation.

Here, interior designers Paige Kelly and Lindsey Walsh share the window treatment fixes they turn to again and again, along with a few clever ideas you may not have considered.

If a room is short on vertical space, Kelly recommends mounting your curtain rod a few inches from the top of the wall, rather than right above the window. “Getting the drapery high and wide is going to make a room feel bigger,” she says.

Tall panels draw the eye up, but make sure they are long enough to skim the floor. “Otherwise, they look like high-water pants, and it just looks wrong,” warns Walsh.

TWOPAGES Liz Linen Pleated Drapes are a full-length option with a tailored pleat that gives the finished look a little extra polish.

Walsh points to “pattern drenching” as a way to make a space feel more cohesive and help soften the edges of an oddly placed window or render an awkward proportion less noticeable. When you carry the same pattern across the walls and window treatments, the window becomes part of a larger visual composition rather than a feature that stands out for the wrong reasons.

Walsh notes that TWOPAGES can work with paper-backed fabric to allow the same material to cover both the walls and windows. A wallpaper installer can apply the fabric to the walls, and a window treatment workroom will install it as drapery or shades, carefully aligning the pattern repeat so the two applications meet seamlessly.

Increasing the fullness of drapery panels can trick the eye so that windows appear more substantial. “You can make yours look wider by using the stack back required for a wider window,” says Walsh. “The panel fabric may just be covering a lot of the wall, but it will look like there’s a window there.”

If the window placement is part of the problem, Kelly suggests extending the curtain rod beyond the window and using a one-way draw. “Gathering a drapery stack to one side feels intentional, and can help balance an off-center window,” she says.

In rooms where you don’t need full blackout, like kitchens and bathrooms, cafe curtains—which hang in the middle of a window along the check rail—are a great solution. “They cover your neighbor’s dirty yard but you still get to see the sky,” says Kelly. TWOPAGES also sells a variety of ready-to-hang cafe curtains, along with the necessary hardware in a gold or black finish.

Long panels aren’t always practical, particularly when a window sits above a radiator, cabinetry, or a piece of furniture. In those situations, Walsh often turns to roman shades. They’re a streamlined way to introduce fabric and softness without taking up wall space.

For a more decorative look, Walsh loves adding a lambrequin, a fixed fabric-covered frame around the window, with a functional shade tucked beneath it. “It’s a great fix when the interior architecture gets in the way of having the kind of window treatment you want,” she says.

TWOPAGES carries a wide range of shade materials—from linen blends and embroidered cottons to bamboo and woven wood—and offers every fold and lift type possible, so you can find the exact form and function to best fit your space.

Walsh likes to use drapery beyond traditional windows, especially if a room feels stark or echoey because of finishes such as marble, glass, or tile. A portière—a curtain hung in a doorway or cased opening—can create a sense of separation between spaces, soften an entryway, or help buffer cold air near an exterior door.

“Even if they’re purely decorative, drapery and window treatments absorb sound and provide texture and visual interest,” adds Kelly.

The right fabric reinforces that effect. A lighter fabric like TWOPAGES Patti Belgian Flax Linen Curtain adds softness without feeling too heavy, while a drape with a more substantial texture, such as the brand’s Birkin Velvet Curtain, adds visual warmth and a richer feel, perfect for the colder months.

The smallest details can make the biggest difference, even if custom treatments are not in your budget. Instead of a traditional curtain rod with finials on each end, which can look dated, Walsh advises using a French return rod, which is mounted on the wall and curves outward. This allows the end of the panels to sit flush against the wall while still creating space for a stack back.

“A French return rod is by far the most elegant way to fake it and make your drapes look professional,” says Walsh. But stay away from grommets—“they are a dead giveaway you did it yourself,” she says—and use rings with clips instead.

Head to twopagescurtains.com for more ideas.

#6818. What Watch Will Robert Pattinson Wear as James Bond? It's Complicated.

Timepieces are almost as much a part of 007’s wardrobe as his dinner jackets.

Perhaps you've heard? There's a new James Bond in town!

Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next 007, and while most of the speculation has understandably focused on how the former vampire/current Batman might approach Britain's foremost secret agent, watch aficionados are asking another question: What will he wear on his wrist?

Watches, after all, are almost as much a part of Bond's wardrobe as his dinner jackets, Aston Martins, and vodka martinis. Sean Connery famously wore a Rolex Submariner, Roger Moore experimented with Seiko's digital watches, and Omega has been 007's watch of choice since Pierce Brosnan strapped on a trusty Seamaster in GoldenEye in 1995. That brand remains, of course, a paid partner of the franchise.

Yesterday's reveal showed no watch on the newly anointed 007's wrist, and Pattinson's own taste in watches is rather different from the rugged, sporty timepieces traditionally associated with Bond.

In fact, he doesn't seem particularly keen on big watches at all.

"Whenever a watch gets too thick and it keeps your cuff up, I don't really understand the appeal," he told one interviewer as recently September. "A lot of guys really like that, but I don't think I can really pull that off. I need to only have a half reveal."

And when asked what he looks for in a watch, he was even more specific.

"I definitely like really thin watches. That's the main thing. In general, I would probably prefer a leather strap."

Which is quite a contrast with the substantial divers we've become accustomed to seeing on Bond's wrist.

The fact is, until recently, Pattinson wasn't much of a watch enthusiast at all. That changed at this year's Oscars, when he wore a then-unreleased rose-gold Jaeger-LeCoultre Master Control Chronomètre Perpetual Calendar. Other actors apparently began asking him about it at the afterparty, and something clicked.

He subsequently became an ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, although his relationship with the brand goes back much further. As a teenager, he borrowed his mother's Reverso to impress his schoolmates. More recently, he's revealed that Bruce Wayne will wear a Reverso in the next Batman film.

On screen, Pattinson's watch choices have been interesting. He wore a Chanel J12 in David Cronenberg's Cosmopolis, while Christopher Nolan's Tenet, in which he played a mysterious secret agent, featured a Bond-adjacent Omega De Ville.

Meanwhile, the announcement has prompted some entertaining activity on Instagram. Within hours of Pattinson being named Bond, Jaeger-LeCoultre posted pictures of its new ambassador wearing the Master Control Chronomètre Perpetual Calendar. Omega, meanwhile, posted an image of its James Bond Seamaster. And today, Jaeger-LeCoultre has been back with more Pattinson pictures.

It's a little social-media tit-for-tat, although there's no reason the two relationships can't coexist. For now, at least, there's a straightforward distinction: Pattinson can wear whatever he likes. Bond has his own watch.

What other shake-ups can you expect from this upcoming season? Here’s everything that has been revealed about Selling Sunset season 10 so far. Starting with…

At long last, we have a release date! Netflix confirmed that season 10 will hit Netflix on December 4, over a year after the release of season 9 in October 2025.

Why the delay? An Us Weekly source previously revealed back in March that the cast was “supposed to start filming and it has been delayed because they are waiting for [Christine Quinn] to finish negotiations.”

In addition to confirming Christine Quinn and Heather Rae El Moussa’s return, Us Weekly first reported that newbie Tara Burns would be joining the cast, with a source saying, “She will be full time and has worked with Jason [Oppenheim] before.”

Now the other new cast members have been revealed as well: Jordyn Braff (who previously appeared on Selling the City and also famously dated Trevor Noah), Sonni Pacheco (who was briefly married to Jeremy Renner and shares a daughter with him), and Sasha Lance (best known as Breonna Strong in All American).

Following season 9, it was widely believed that Chelsea Lazkani would also be exiting—and while she initially shut down those rumors, taking to Threads in March to write, “If you plan on firing me, do it loudly and proudly and state the reason. In May, the Daily Mail reported that—in addition to Chelsea—four other cast members were being cut from the show: Emma Hernan, Mary Bonnet, Alanna Gold, and Sandra Vergara.

#6812. Brad Pitt Wants to Play a James Bond Villain

The announcement finally arrived this week: Robert Pattinson is James Bond. But before we could even come up for air about Amazon MGM and director Denis Villeneuve’s decision to have arguably the busiest movie star in the business today follow Daniel Craig as 007, the Internet had already moved on. Fans started asking more questions. Who will costar as the next Bond girl? Who’s performing the song? And, most importantly, who would play opposite Pattinson as the villain?

Well, how about Brad Pitt? The F1 star likely didn’t expect a James Bond question when he stepped on the red carpet for the premiere of his latest film, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. The spinoff sequel of Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood sees Pitt return as stuntman Cliff Booth under the direction of David Fincher, which couldn’t be further from the life of a British MI6 hitman. Still, Pitt was excited to hear for the first time that Pattinson landed the role when a reporter for ExtraTV shared the news. “I love this idea,” Pitt said. “He’s the real deal.”

Would he ever think about playing the villain? Pitt winked at the camera and said, “Robert? Denis? You know what, I’d like to do that. My man Javier [Bardem] did it so well [in Skyfall] It’s tall shoes, but I’d take that on.”

Later down the red carpet, Pitt answered the question again when Complex asked if he had any advice for Pattinson. “Sign me for the villain,” he said, coming around to the idea even more. “Get Denis Villeneuve on the flip phone. Let’s go!”

Elsewhere, Pattinson’s fellow Dune: Part Three costar Florence Pugh is already pitching herself as a potential villain and/or Bond girl. When Villeneuve presented her with an honor at Elle's Women in Hollywood event on Monday, Pugh congratulated the director on finding the next James Bond. “Nice catch,” she said. “Any villains the size of a five-foot-four-inch female?" I’m sure this is just the beginning.

I’ll admit, Pitt wasn’t my first choice for the next Bond villain. If anything, Pattinson was. But I love how enthusiastic he is about the possibility. Now, I kind of feel like I need to see it.

#6811. How to Reset Your Skin Care Routine After 40

Dermatologists break down the ingredients, steps, and treatments that matter most for skin over 40.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

As we age, there’s seemingly always something new to think about, including adjusting your skin care routine to meet your skin’s evolving needs. You may not need to add a bunch of new products to your current regimen, but increased dryness, changes in texture, fine lines, and enlarged pores may require ingredient swaps that your current lineup can’t deliver. The skin care products you used in your 20s and 30s may have worked then, but once you hit 40, your skin may start to need something different. Experts share how to reset your routine for 40+ skin, including the non-negotiables, new ingredients that can have the greatest impact, and what to avoid to keep your maturing skin looking and feeling its best.

Over 40, skin has already started to thin, at both the epidermis and dermis levels, explains Dr. Suzan Obagi, a board-certified dermatologist, associate professor of dermatology and plastic surgery, and director of the UPMC Cosmetic Surgery & Skin Health Center. “This means that skin will start to appear more fragile, fine lines will start to show, and skin becomes drier. For these reasons, a good skin care regimen should include a retinoid (retinol, retinaldehyde, or tretinoin) to help improve skin thickness, increase extracellular matrix proteins (collagen, elastin, and glycosaminoglycans (GAGs)), and encourage fibroblasts to make more of our Natural Moisturizing Factor (NMF),” Obagi tells ELLE.

Most skin over 40 also has some sun damage, which Obagi says can present as freckles and sun spots. Well before 40 and certainly after, there’s one daily non-negotiable for skin of any age: sunscreen. If the spots have already shown up, Obagi recommends a skin-brightening serum with tranexamic acid (TXA), antioxidants, and peptides to help correct the hyperpigmentation.

Additionally, Dr. Chris Tomassian, a California-based, board-certified dermatologist and founder of The Dermatology Collective, says a retinol at night will go a long way, as will vitamin C in the morning and aggressive moisturization.

As for ingredients, Tomassian says the key players in the post-40 reset will be retinol, SPF, and vitamin C, as already noted, along with PDRN, ectoin, ceramides, and occasionally estradiol.

If you’re not already on a daytime and nighttime routine, now’s the time to start.

Morning: Use a gentle cleanser if your skin is oily or if you didn’t get to a proper wash the night before. Tomassian suggests skipping the cleanse if your skin feels dry when you wake up. Follow with a good antioxidant like an L-ascorbic acid (vitamin C) serum or one with tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate (THD), silymarin, or phloretin. Layer on a PDRN moisturizer and SPF before any makeup.

Night: Before bed, cleanse thoroughly to remove makeup and sunscreen. Layer on a copper peptide serum, ptiox treatment, tretinoin (retinol), and a PDRN moisturizer. Obagi also suggests combining a pigment-correcting serum with a retinoid to help build the dermis extracellular matrix and target hyperpigmentation.

Bonus steps: Exfoliate one to two times each week with a combination peel pad, alpha hydroxy or beta hydroxy acids depending on your skin’s dryness level or if you’re experiencing any breakout. Tomassian warns, though, that post-40 skin should avoid over-exfoliating. “Skin gets drier with age, and breaking down your skin barrier by scrubbing or peeling too aggressively or too often can leave skin vulnerable to drying out,” he explains.

At any age, consistency is key. Even if you’re lucky enough to have minimal signs of aging, both experts agree that these steps will go a long way. “It is still important to incorporate a retinoid, an antioxidant, and a good moisturizer into your daily routine,” says Obagi.

There’s plenty you can do at home to care for your skin after 40, including adding LED light therapy to your lineup to help with fine lines and wrinkles and stimulate collagen—but Tomassian notes these are only beneficial if you use them consistently. An even greater investment is pairing your home routine with regular visits to a professional for in-office procedures like microneedling or ablative and nonablative lasers. These treatments can jump-start your skin to start producing more collagen. For chronic sun damage like redness and dark spots, Tomassian recommends Intense Pulsed Light (IPL), Picosure, or DermaV/Fraxel/CO2 lasers. These devices target pigmentation concerns that skin care does little to improve.

Obagi adds that pro visits are important since collagen production peaks at age 18 and, with each passing year, our skin makes 1 percent less collagen, elastin, and GAGs. “By our mid-30s and early 40s, we would benefit from devices that boost collagen production periodically. These can be noninvasive lasers, microneedling, and radiofrequency devices. These will boost collagen for a short time, but when combined with a well-thought-out skin care regimen, the results can be prolonged,” says Obagi.

You’ve lived with your skin for 40+ years, so you can tell when things start to change. Obagi says you have to listen to your own skin. “If you are on the dry side or have fragile skin, avoid harsh ingredients such as glycolic or lactic acid, strong retinoids, or over-exfoliating with scrubs. These can irritate the skin and drive sensitivity,” she highlights. If you have thicker skin or are oilier, she suggests exfoliating fruit acids and says your skin can tolerate stronger retinoids.

Tomassian’s rule of thumb is that after age 30, use as many ingredients as possible to bank collagen and focus on thicker moisturizers as you get older, since we produce less oil.

Key ingredients: oat-derived surfactants, plant-derived humectants, polyhydroxy acids

Key ingredients: liposomal tranexamic acid (TXA), oligopeptide-68, THD, and hydrolyzed algin to help target the various pathways driving pigmentation

Key ingredients: stabilized vitamin C, hyaluronic acid, panthenol, soothing allantoin, and green tea extract

Key ingredients: collagen, copper peptides, smoothing and brightening niacinamide, retinal, rice PDRN

Key ingredients: low-molecular PDRN, moisturizing squalane, panthenol, and ceramide, brightening niacinamide, firming rose peptide

Key ingredients: glycolic acid, lactic acid, malic acid, antioxidant-rich resveratrol, and green tea extract

Key ingredients: 10 percent Homosalate, 5 percent Octisalate, 3 percent Avobenzone, brightening niacinamide and ethyl ascorbic acid; moisturizing argan oil, squalane, and bisabolol

#6809. How to Make Sure Your Sex Life Keeps Getting Hotter With Age

We get better with age—our sex should, too.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

I’m excited to get older. I keep getting wiser, more sure of myself, and much more confident about speaking up for myself. All of these things are just bound to make the rest of my life better—including my sex life. And I plan on having sex—good sex—for as long as as I possibly can.

And, as it turns out, I can indeed do that, for a very long time.

Despite what you’ve heard from other people, neither men nor women have sexual “primes” in their 20s. Good thing, too, because think about how much unlearning of sexual stigmas and hangups happen in your young adulthood!

“In reality, women in their 40s and 50s often know what they want far better than they did in their 20s,” certified sex and relationship coach and sex educator Gemma Nice tells Cosmopolitan. “The shift is moving away from sex where the goal was just to look good or rush to penetrative sex and moves towards purposeful, sensory connection using more intuition.”

Even when people do hit the average peak for sexual desire—typically 30s and 40s for both men and women—it doesn’t just disappear afterwards. Sure, on average, sexual frequency decreases every new decade of age you enter, but that doesn’t mean your sex life is doomed after your 30th or 40th (or 50th or 60th!) birthday. There are ways to keep your sex life healthy, fulfilling, and hot the older you get. You just have to work at it.

The most inevitable part of aging is that our bodies will change. Now, with proper nutrition and exercise, you can make sure you’re staying as limber and flexible as possible. But some health issues affect our bodies regardless, and eventually there are some limitations to what you can physically do. Instead of framing this as a death sentence for your sex life, you have to learn how to adapt your sex life to your changing body.

When it comes to women’s health issues like perimenopause and menopause, your sex life can be directly affected: You might experience exhaustion, decreased libido, vaginal dryness, or other physical and emotional symptoms. There are workarounds to these, of course, including changing the time of day when you have sex, changing how you have sex, spending more time on foreplay, and lots and lots of lube.

“Menopause does change how the genitals respond but the clitoris doesn't lose nerve endings,” Nice says. “Reduced blood flow just means it takes longer and needs more direct attention.”

Sometimes this means changing up your sex position. Do I love being able to say that I’ve had sex in the Butter Churner position? Absolutely. Do I think that I’m going to really enjoy that move the older I get? Probably not.

Maghan Burge, nurse practitioner and founder of Braise—a platform that helps you design your room based on intimate wellness—says that your sex positions should adjust with your athletic ability. “Positions that were easy at 25 can strain knees, hips, and backs at 50,” she says.

She encourages taking your time and using support pillows and wedges that take pressure off joints. And of course, you need to get out of the mentality that sex is less “sexy” or “fun” just because you need to make some alterations.

“None of it is a sign that something's wrong,” Burge says. “It's maintenance, the same as stretching before a run.”

This maintenance can even be changing up your room so that when it’s play time, all you’re worried about is enjoying sex.

“Night sweats, broken sleep, and hip or back pain make bed the last place you want to be active,” Burge says. “Cooling sheets, a fan, breathable fabrics, and a body pillow (or a pillow between the knees for hip and spine alignment) sound unsexy, but people who sleep well and hurt less have far more interest in being close.”

If you’re with a long-term partner, there’s going to be a lot of talking needed to maintain a great sex life.

Even if there are kids, a mountain of responsibilities, and a packed schedule that seem in the way, Burge says to make an effort to talk more and earlier in the day. “Desire at 10 p.m. usually starts with feeling like a team at 10 a.m.,” she says.

Also, discuss what you both want your sex and intimate life to look like. If every night doesn’t have to end with sex, talk about what sort of nights you can have together to keep intimacy in tact. “Keeping touch and closeness in the routine, without a scoreboard, is what keeps the bigger nights happening,” Burge says.

One simple way to do this is through a somatic tool known as the lap-sit reset. According to Nice, this is where you straddle your partner while they sit cross-legged, look into each other’s eyes, and just sync your breathing for a few minutes. “It releases sexual tension from the pelvic floor, grounds the nervous system into rest-and-digest, and reminds your body that your partner is a safe, sensual space to be,” she says.

You’ll feel less like you need to “warm up” to sex if you’re keeping a physical connection with your partner throughout the week.

This is important with commitment-free hookups too. Not everyone is going to be married or in a long-term relationship when they’re older. Some of us will still be just getting it in when we can—and there is nothing wrong with that.

“When you stop being who you were back in your 20s and start to really know what you want from now, you will be really empowered to go and get that amazing sex you have been wanting for ages,” Nice says. “It can be the most liberating sex of your life.”

Things change as you get older, but we all need to collectively get out of the mindset that it’s for the worse. I plan on aging like fine wine—and I expect my sex life to follow suit.

#6807. The Best Coffee-Table Books to Gift Your Beautiful, Discerning Friends

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

These books will please everyone on your gift list this year

Every year holidays come around, and a slight panic sets in at the thought of finding gifts that the people you love will get excited about—and that will make them feel seen. The real trick is to keep a list throughout the year of everything you see that reminds you of this person or that person. But because sometimes you don’t write things down because you’re “sure you’ll remember,” and because even if you do, we need all the help we can get in discovering cool things, we’ve put together a list of our favorite coffee-table books to give (and to receive, if we’re being honest) this year.

From fashion monographs to punk rock album covers to a guide to medieval wellness, we promise that we’ve found something that will thrill even your most cynical friend.

Richard Avedon was undoubtedly one of the greatest photographers of the 20th century and this collection gathers his work for Harper’s Bazaar from 1944 to 1965. As the world experienced generation-defining shifts, Avedon was zeroed in on his style, creating indelible images that would go on to change fashion. Bonus? It pairs perfectly with Ron Howard’s documentary on the photographer, also titled simply Avedon.

This massive pink tome, assembled by Coppola herself from her own collection of photographs, scripts, collages, and all manner of feminine detritus, offers a revealing and inspirational look at the director’s process and world-building.

With wit and humor, medievalist Larisa Grollemond sheds light on the way humans lived—and thrived(?)—during the middle ages. Is it true they never bathed? Did they have practice birth control? Were witches in fact, doctors? This books holds the answers.

Raymond Pettibon may now be a certified blue-chip artist, but he began his career in the 1970s drawing flyers and record covers for punk bands in Southen California like Minutemen and Black Flag. (He also designed their iconic four-bar logo, which has now been meme-fied.) This book collects his musical body of work, which also includes the Foo Fighters and Lana del Rey—that’s his work on the cover of Norman Fucking Rockwell.

The elusive Martin Margiela may very well be the designer that has most influenced contemporary fashion. Nowhere is that more evident than in this book that looks at the time when the Belgian designer was at the helm of Hermés. The enduring appeal of the collections he created from 1997 to 2002 would go on to set the tone for the whole quiet luxury moment we’ve been living under—except better.

Jeff Goodwin was the makeup artist for David Lynch’s iconic film Blue Velvet. His personal trove of Polaroid photos capture impromptu behind-the-scenes moments and reveal how he refined the makeup looks; they’re accompanied by his own memories of the filming experience.

How many people’s fashion obsessions began as they endlessly dressed and undressed their dolls—be they Barbie, Bratz, or even American Girl dolls? This tome looks at the symbiotic relationship between dolls and real-life grown-up fashion, zeroing in on the works of designers like Comme des Garçons’ Rei Kawakubo and Viktor & Rolf’s Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren, among others.

This is a book designed to inspire. For “Kitchen Piece,” Ono suggests one “hangs a canvas on a wall” and “throws all the leftovers you have” on it, with the caveat that “you may prepare special food for the piece.” After spending time with Ono’s instructions, one realizes there is art to be found literally everywhere.

This is the only book about Carolyn Bessette Kennedy that one may ever need. Sunita Kumar Nair talks to CBK’s friends and, through a carefully curated edit of images, breaks down her style. She also reveals the true essence of the person behind all those infinitely rebloggable images.

Past Continuous is the name of an exhibit at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York that brings together the world of Lee Krasner and her husband Jackson Pollock and looks at their career arcs in tandem. It begins with a selection of their paintings before the pair met, and traces their influences, taking a closer look at how their presences wove in and out of each other’s work.

This tome celebrates America’s 250th anniversary through over 200 pages filled with iconic images that have defined the country throughout its history, from images of cowboys wearing their worn-in Levi’s and immigrants landing at Ellis Island to Martin Luther King and Elvis Presley.

Diane Arbus’s unflinching photographs captured humanity in all its beautiful and exacting rawness. Documents tells the history of her short-lived career through essays, criticism, and other ephemera from 1967 through the present day; it’s a comprehensive guide to understanding her work.

Glen Luchford photographed a few of Prada’s most iconic ad campaigns of the 1990s. This book brings them all together along with alternate shots and test shots, and is an essential for both Prada aficionados and lovers of the decade.

Created in 1909 by Arthur E. Waite and Pamela Colman Smith in London, the appropriately titled Waite Smith tarot deck is the most popular deck in the world. This book looks at its history, uncovering the details and meaning of each individual card—and it comes with its own set of cards.

This year, the Fashion Museum Antwerp is celebrating its 40th anniversary with an exhibition dedicated to the “Antwerp Six,” the name the fashion media gave to a group of designers—Dries van Noten, Ann Demeulemeeter, Marina Yee, Dirk Bikkembergs, Walter Van Beirendonck, and Dirk Van Seene—that arrived in London in the mid ’80s fresh after their graduation from the Royal Academy of Fine Art. For those who can’t make it to Belgium to see the show, the book may prove to be the next best thing, chock full of photographs, illustrations, newspaper clippings, and essays. They may not have all become household names, but their influence can still be felt on the runways today.

Brianna Capozzi’s unique view of womanhood has made her one of the most sought-after photographers in fashion. Her latest monograph features a mix of magazine shots of famous singers and actors with images of impromptu shoots staged with her best friends. The result is a visual shot of adrenaline and a reminder that girls—well, women—just wanna have fun!

Remember when Emma Chamberlain was constantly cranking out vlogs, driving around San Francisco and L.A. while listening to music, drinking copious amounts of coffee, and having photo shoots with her friends? Life was simpler back then, and we are so back because she’s officially returning to YouTube in 2027.

The internet star-turned-IRL celeb has been busy building her empire and being the best-dressed person at the Met Gala over the years, but she’s making a comeback to the video platform with an all-new series. According to The Hollywood Reporter, Emma is launching a docuseries called What Are You Waiting For?, in which she digs deep into the long lines taking over New York City.

“After deciding to take a hiatus from my podcast, I spent the next few months trying to figure out what I wanted to create next,” Emma told the outlet. “The answer wasn’t obvious at first, but I knew for sure that I wanted to make something for YouTube. From entertaining me as a child to allowing me to build a career as an adult, it was a no-brainer that whatever I make next had to go on YouTube.”

As for what the series will entail? She says she discovers “much more about humanity than I ever could have expected,” as she interviews people waiting in queues for different pop-up experiences around NYC.

“What Are You Waiting For? on the surface is about people who voluntarily wait in lines for stuff set in New York City, a phenomenon that I personally don’t understand but seek to understand, and along the way I discover much more about humanity than I ever could have expected,” she further explained, months after going viral for accidentally stumbling onto a line for her former “Sister Squad” member, James Charles’ pop-up.

“The experience of making this was unlike anything I have ever done and has profoundly changed me as a person, talking to strangers all day, working with a crew of unbelievably talented people, and making something bigger than I have ever made before, I feel the next chapter of my life coming to fruition, and I am deeply inspired and grateful,” she gushed.

Apple 2025 MacBook Pro 14-Inch (M5 Pro, 24 GB RAM, 1 TB)

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop, even with the recent price hike from $599 to $699. Right now, the Neo is modestly discounted, although we’re holding out hope that it might drop down to its inaugural price—or even lower—once Black Friday proper arrives. The Neo is an easy recommendation for anyone looking for their first Mac. It runs on Apple’s A18 Pro chip and is surprisingly quick for browsing, sending email, and streaming video. The 13-inch Liquid Retina display looks great for the price, and the battery lasts a solid 16 hours. It also comes in four fun colors, with the yellow-green citrus being a fan favorite.

There are some trade-offs with going with Apple’s budget model, including storage that starts at 256 GB, just 8 GB of RAM, and no keyboard backlight. You also get only two USB-C ports, so getting a USB-C hub is a must if you plan to connect a lot of accessories. Spending an extra $100 gets you a Neo with 512 GB of storage and a Touch ID sensor for quick unlocking. For students or anyone who mostly sends emails and browses the Web, the Neo is hard to beat.

I stepped back into the ballroom, pulse racing. The band was still playing, but my world had tilted. Nothing felt the same.

I was threading through the crowd toward the bar when I heard my name.

I turned to find Helen Gurley Brown, radiant in a sequined mask and velvet gown, a champagne coupe in hand. Of course she’d be here. If there was a room with power to be had and people worth dazzling, Helen would be in it.

“You look marvelous,” she said, studying me with a kind of knowing that felt almost maternal. “But something’s off. You’ve got that storm cloud look.”

I let out a laugh that came out thinner than I intended. “Is it that obvious?”

“Only to a woman who’s been exactly where you are,” she said, steering me toward a quieter alcove away from the crush of bodies. “So. Tell me. What’s on your mind?”

There was something in her tone, the mixture of curiosity and command, that cracked me open. Before I could stop my­self, the words tumbled out: Burt had refused me partnership. Years of loyalty, wins, and sacrifice, and still I was expected to be grateful for scraps.

Helen tilted her head, listening without interrupting. “Men hate sharing power. It’s practically coded into their DNA. I can’t say I’m surprised.” She touched my arm. “My offer still stands, you know. Come run features at Cosmopolitan. You’d thrive.”

The thought was more tempting than ever, but something about it still didn’t sit quite right, either. I didn’t want to inherit someone else’s table; I wanted to build my own.

“I appreciate it,” I said softly. “Truly. But I don’t think I want to be an editor.”

“Then don’t,” Helen said easily. “But don’t waste another de­cade making someone else rich while you do the work. If Burt won’t make room, build your own room. PR is your kingdom; you could start your own agency tomorrow if you wanted.”

The idea struck a nerve deep within me. Start my own. It was an audacious, reckless thought. Suddenly, though, even the champagne in my coupe seemed to fizz with anticipation.

Helen raised her glass to me. “To women who write their own stories.”

We clinked, and for the first time that evening, I felt a jolt of something close to joy.

#6800. The AI Police Are Going After Black Writers

The white powers that be have always doubted our intellect. Now they have a new tool.

Picture a waifish enslaved teen—a girl named Phillis, after the slave ship that Middle Passaged her from present-day Senegal and Gambia—trembling before a room of incredulous, austere white men, the most esteemed thinkers and politicians of colonial Massachusetts. The reason: The gifted girl wrote a book manuscript, and the family that owned her journeyed all the way to London to find a publisher for it. That prospective British publisher, a bloke named Archibald Bell, promised to publish the manuscript if the Wheatleys could prove Phillis had written it herself—an attestation tantamount, of course, to whether an enslaved African soon-to-be American possessed the intellect requisite to producing exceptional creative work.

Present at the trial, which has been described by historian Henry Louis Gates Jr. as the nascent scene of African American letters, was Thomas Hutchinson, the governor of the Province of the Massachusetts Bay; Andrew Oliver, the province’s lieutenant governor; and Mr. John Hancock himself, the future first governor of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. Per Gates, almost all the men forgathered to pass judgment on Phillis Wheatley were both Harvard graduates and slaveholders. No record exists of what transpired, but oh how brilliant Phillis must’ve been as she convinced those 18 eminent Bostonians that she’d indeed written the poems. The confirmation was printed in the front matter of Phillis’s poetry collection—the first book published by an African soon-to-be American—Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773):

We whose Names are under-written, do assure the World, that the Poems specified in the following Page, were . . . written by Phillis, a young Negro Girl, who was but a few Years since, brought an uncultivated Barbarian from Africa, and has ever since been, and now is, under the Disadvantage of serving as a Slave in a Family in this Town. She has been examined by some of the best Judges, and is thought qualified to write them.

As my great-grandmother Edith Larkin Jackson, a woman not two generations removed from chattel slavery, used to say, “There’s nothing new under the sun.” Mama Eddie was a schoolteacher, and I imagine she’d be astounded by artificial intelligence. However, she’d have no trouble whatsoever fathoming a world that called into question the creativity or intellect of her people.

Here we are in this brave new world of AI, an age hurtling headlong toward the peril of superintelligence. Here we are in the 21st century, a time when the ivory-tower panjandrums are engaged in a sinister pattern, if not conspiratorial scheme, of incriminating Black and brown writers with even the suggestion that their work is AI assisted.

For example: In March, Hachette Book Group rendered kaput the U. S. publication of Mia Ballard’s Shy Girl over claims of AI usage.

When Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir’s story “The Serpent in the Grove” was named the regional winner of the Commonwealth Prize in May, Ethan Mollick, a Wharton Business School professor who serves as the codirector of Wharton Generative AI Labs, ran it through the AI-detection software Pangram, touted as the industry standard, and reported that the platform flagged it at 100 percent. Once Mollick shared his findings on social media, several others joined the chorus bemoaning Nazir’s work as a product of AI.

In July, academics studying AI accused H. M. Wolfe of having used a large language model to write her best seller Daggermouth (though its publisher Simon & Schuster has, thus far, stood by the book). Later that month, writer Jerry Falade had a $2 million book deal with Macmillan collapse after his agents withdrew the submission of his debut crime novel citing AI concerns.

In September, Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça ou Mourir (It Was Either That or Die) was proclaimed a standout of the French literary season, won France’s Prix du Roman FNAC, and was long-listed for the Goncourt, the country’s most prestigious literary prize. But then an anonymous X account (later revealed to be owned by a conservative columnist) posted that Pangram had identified all 34 chapters of the book as having been written with AI. That claim spurred accusations that Orélien plagiarized earlier work, leading the Goncourt to nix the book from its long list.

In October, The Atlantic accused writer Simbarashe Kundizeza of using AI to write “The Blue Fighter,” which won the Caine Prize, Africa’s most prestigious short-story accolade.

Germane: While Nazir is Trinidadian, Ballard, Wolfe, Falade, Orélien, and Kundizeza are all Black.

Although all those writers have denied claims of using AI to produce their work, I’m not here to dispute whether they did or to what degree they used it, nor the epistemological paradox of using AI to determine whether a writer used AI to write a story. Of equal importance is that, if we ain’t reached the point where all published writing is scanned for possible use of an LLM, what’s the logic informing which writers are investigated for AI use and which aren’t, as well as the attendant issue of which accused writers suffer the most severe fallout, including the scarlet letter of damaged credibility?

The plight of Black and brown writers in the age of AI must be judged in light of what’s being described as an era of postliteracy. Of the specter of AI sloptimism becoming so ubiquitous it overruns human output. Of the cataclysmic doom of superintelligence approximating the creative work of a human brain to such a degree that the difference will be negligible to the undiscerning masses.

The plight of Black and brown writers in the age of AI must be apprehended against the beef between the publishing industry writ large and AI. Against 10,000 authors having copublished an “empty” book in protest of their work being pirated to train its models. Against America’s Big Five publishers suing Meta for copyright infringement. Against the recent unsealed documents that reveal OpenAI executives knew they were training their AI on copyrighted material and, furthermore, that AI-authored books were apt to displace in the market ones authored by humans. “There will be a point where a bunch of artists express worry about what we’re doing here, and we’ll likely ignore their concerns and release anyway,” OpenAI policy director Jack Clark wrote in an internal memo back in 2020. The predicament of Black and brown writers should be weighed against the long and calculated history of portraying them as lesser intellects.

Casting doubt on the possibility of Black literary brilliance is in the spirit of a hubristic Saul Bellow asking, “Who is the Tolstoy of the Zulus?” Of 45/47 portraying beaucoup Black people as “not that bright.” Of attacking DEI to paint us as unworthy or incapable, less we are sanctioned by people in power. The same insidious forces—linked to right-wing Cambridge professor James Orr and conservative billionaire Peter Thiel—stoked the allegations that ended in Cambridge professor Jason Arday dying by suicide. (Arday has been posthumously cleared of plagiarism.)

In stark contrast, best-selling novelist and screenwriter Anthony Horowitz has admitted using AI for his work. Best-selling biographer Katie Prescott extolled AI as invaluable in writing her book on Mike Lynch, the late British tech entrepreneur and AI pioneer. And while she’s been called among other things a “grifter” and a “villain,” South African writer Coral Hart has published more than 370 books using artificial intelligence since 2025 and defended her use of LLMs despite criticism and threats. While she later clarified she used it only for research, Nobel laureate Olga Tokarczuk caused a ruckus revealing she queried AI for writing help. Other than Santiago Schnell, a white Latino, resigning as the provost of Dartmouth for using AI in his published articles and The New York Times cutting ties with Alex Preston for an AI-assisted book review, beyond vocal to tepid criticism, white writers aren’t suffering material consequences on par with those of their Black peers.

Poor Phillis Wheatley never published a second book. Despite advertising six times in the newspaper to find a publisher. Despite announcing she’d dedicate it to Benjamin Franklin. Despite General George Washington extolling her as “favored by the muses.” In fact, in 1784, Phillis died at 30 years young, destitute, having placed the last advertisement for her second manuscript just a few months prior.

Because Big Tech is big-time thriving and race is evermore an oppressive tool, critics are bound to keep casting the work of Black writers as AI assisted, in effect electing themselves nouveau versions of those privileged 18th-century Bostonians. Best believe their indictments are a tacit way to portray the work of Black people as unworthy of patronage, acclaim, awards—aka inferior. But be forewarned: If Big Tech succeeds at AI turning the creative work of human brains passé if not obsolete, it’s near foregone that most writers will lose their ability to earn a living. Indeed, the sad-ass upshot is that if AI prevails, all writers—race be damned—will be fated a Phillis.

#6798. How to Maintain Long, Healthy Hair Over 50, According to Experts

From top treatments to when to plan your next trim, here’s everything to know

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

There’s something undeniably chic about a head of long, luscious hair. Think glossy, waist-skimming, bouncy, voluminous lengths that make extensions an option rather than a long-term commitment. What’s more, long hair provides the ultimate canvas for experimentation, with styling possibilities that feel limitless.

As hair matures, however, maintaining the same level of shine, strength, and vitality can require more attention. As texture changes and dryness increases, the key is to adapt your routine to give your longer lengths the care they deserve. “Long hair can look beautiful at any age, but keeping mature hair glossy and healthy-looking is all about replenishing moisture and maintaining shine,” says celebrity hairstylist Naomi Brooks. “I always recommend prioritising hydrating products that help smooth the hair cuticle, improve softness, and enhance shine, alongside regular trims to keep the lengths and ends looking healthy.”

If you’re considering making the transition and letting your bob grow out, look to a host of celebrities for inspiration. From Demi Moore and Naomi Campbell to Andie MacDowell and Claudia Schiffer, countless iterations are proving just how effortless long hair can look on women over 50. As Brooks explains: “Demi Moore is a fantastic example of how beautiful long hair can look at any age. Her hair is consistently glossy, healthy-looking, and full of movement.”

While genetics certainly play a role, Moore’s glossy lengths are also the result of great care and strategic products. Her hairstylist, Dimitris Giannetos, revealed on social media that he often relies on Kérastase’s Gloss Absolu Glaze Drops Anti-Frizz Hair Oil to reduce frizz, boost shine, and ensure hair remains sleek without looking too heavy. Indeed, experts recommend investing in a high-quality hydrating treatment to ensure mature hair is treated with extra care. “Mature hair can become drier, finer or more fragile over time, so maintaining moisture and shine is important,” says Warren Edwards, creative director at Warren & the Hare.

Additionally, for those with gray or silver hair, session stylist Danilo Giangreco recommends incorporating a clear gloss into your routine to enhance shine. This can also help counteract any unwanted brassiness, ensuring hair appears brighter and healthier.

Another expert-approved tip is to keep heat styling to a minimum where possible. If you do rely on hot tools, applying heat protectant can help shield strands from damage while preserving moisture, strength, and shine.

Finally, contrary to popular belief, long hair thrives on regular maintenance. Though it may seem counterintuitive when trying to grow your hair, routine appointments are essential to keep split ends at bay and prevent the ends from looking too thin or tired. In turn, this helps keep long, mature hair looking fuller, healthier, and overall more glossy.

#6795. Penélope Cruz Says It’s Time for Women Directors to Be the Norm

With Bunker, The Invite, and La Bola Negra all out this year, ELLE Women in Hollywood honoree Penélope Cruz told three very different stories through her characters. She dedicated her speech at our Women in Hollywood event to the writers and directors behind those projects, along with her The Invite co-star Seth Rogen. She also called out the lack of women directors in Hollywood, saying it’s time for things to change.

“I wanted to share this recognition with all the people that over the years have given me the opportunity to make a living out of this profession. That was my prayer every night,” Cruz began. “I also want to share it with four directors and two writers. Florian Zeller [who directed Bunker], thank you for your talent and for your trust and for allowing me to express through a character my anger and sadness about the fact that a story where people are building bunkers to save themselves is not a story of science fiction anymore. Thank you, Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrosi, my new best friends, for giving me the treasure of a character that is Nené Romero in your incredible, genius film, La Bola Negra. And Guitarrica is here, and so [I’m] sharing [this honor] with you and all the cast of the film.”

“I want to thank the incredible Olivia Wilde. You are brilliant,” she added of The Invite’s director. “I really loved making our film. The only thing that I didn’t like about it is that once again, when you are being directed by a woman, you get to do all the press, that is still the number one question: Does it feel very different to be directed by a woman? And I feel really like after 30 years working, when are we going to get to the day where that is not worth [it] to ask anymore because it’s just a normal, common thing? That is truly a very strong wish that I have.

“Seth [Rogen], I don’t know where you went, but what a privilege it has been to sing Sade for you in this film. What a privilege to work with you, with Edward [Norton], with Olivia, to be part of a film that brings people to the theater and makes them laugh and cry at the same time for two hours. People are stopping us in the streets now to tell us all their secrets about their relationships. And others, and I’m not joking, are sending us letters to inform us about their very recent divorce—in a good way. So, the process of making this movie was interesting. Everything had to happen very quickly, but thanks to the generosity of the writers Will [McCormack] and Rashida [Jones] and the generosity of Olivia, it happened. It was one of those miracles where everything gets put together very quickly, and it happened. And truly, it was important for me today to name Will and Rashida because I haven’t met in my career people with that amount of generosity and zero ego, so this is also for them.”

Cruz ended her speech by shouting out her longtime agent, team, and her brother, who attended the event with her.

Watch her full speech above and read her Women in Hollywood cover story here.

#6790. The Fearless Sensitivity of ‘Mouse’ and ‘Clarissa’ Star Sophie Okonedo

Sophie Okonedo is one of those performers whose very presence can make a scene feel more alive. The Tony Award–winning British actor projects both warmth and watchfulness, moving swiftly from humor to hurt, or authority to vulnerability, without announcing the shift. Even in a supporting role, she has a way of making you lean in.

This winter she leads two independent features opening theatrically after an international festival run: Clarissa, by brothers Chuko and Arie Esiri, and Mouse, by husband-and-wife team Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson. Though shot nearly a year apart, the two films are arriving within weeks of each other—a quirk of the release calendar that makes for an unusually timely double feature.

Mouse, out now, is a coming-of-age story set in 2002 Arkansas, in which the teenage Minnie (Katherine Mallen Kupferer) develops a complicated relationship with her best friend’s mother (Okonedo) after an unexpected tragedy. Meanwhile, Clarissa—in limited theaters December 18—transposes Virginia Woolf’s novel Mrs. Dalloway to contemporary Nigeria, a project that brought Okonedo to a country she hadn’t visited in two decades. (Her late father, whom she was mostly estranged from, moved back to his home country when she was young.)

Filming in Lagos proved consequential in ways that extended well beyond the work itself. “The journey I had in Lagos was so immense, personally and professionally, that I remember thinking on the wrap day that even if nothing else happens with this film, I’ve already gotten everything I wanted,” she tells Vogue.

Both films were made on tiny budgets, and as Okonedo points out, a conversation about one inevitably opens up a conversation about the other. So we talked about both.

Vogue: Let’s start with Mouse. How did it come to you? What was it about your character, Helen, or about the directors that made you say yes?

Sophie Okonedo: I didn’t read anything about them. I read the script completely cold. By the time I got to the end, I rang my agent and said, “I’m absolutely doing this. I don’t know who’s directing, I don’t know what’s happening with the film, but I’m doing it.” So he sent me their last film, Ghostlight. It’s such a brilliant film, and it was made for pennies. These are two really interesting filmmakers who are talking about America in a way I haven’t seen—very quietly. There are no explosions, no big movie stars, and it’s deeply significant. Kelly’s writing is subtle and real. But films like this can slip by without anyone noticing. I have to galvanize everyone and get them behind it because I think it’s so good.

Helen ends up mothering her daughter’s friend, Minnie, in a way that’s unnerving at times, as if she’s grieving and replacing her at the same time.

It’s totally inappropriate at times. She even says it at one point: “Oh my God, I’m the adult here.” She uses Minnie to ease her own grief, then backtracks, then moves forward again. It’s a messy situation, but there’s hope in it. The film is funny too. Kelly has that gift for finding levity in dark situations. But they never get you to play the comedy. You play the seriousness of it all, and it’s funny as it goes along.

I realized after watching the film that the woman playing Katherine’s mother is her real-life mother. What was that dynamic like on set?

She wasn’t even meant to play the part at first. Tara [Mallen], her mother, is a theater actress. She runs a theater company in Chicago and was there as Katherine’s guardian. They’d cast a great local actor, but on the first day we realized it wasn’t right. By the second day, Tara stepped in. Everything was so homegrown. My baby in the film is actually Kelly and Alex’s baby. They removed all the blockers you normally have as an actor on a film, where you spend three hours in hair and makeup. Sometimes you need those things, but this film didn’t. You just rock up and start filming. It was very seamless.

Katherine Mallen Kupferer and Sophie Okonedo in Mouse

You shot on location in North Little Rock. Had you been to Arkansas before?

Never. I got there a little early to check it out because I was playing an outsider but an outsider who’d lived there for 15 years. So I had to know the place and feel familiar with it. All the locations came from [O’Sullivan’s] childhood. You could ask her, “What happened here?” and she’d tell you. Many people with small parts in the film knew Kelly from high school and were now playing mothers. The dance we see at the memorial was one Kelly actually performed herself. We even brought back the dance teacher who taught her so she could teach it to the two girls in the film.

Does playing an outsider give you something to work with? You didn’t do the method thing, keeping yourself apart from everyone, right?

No. I totally get that some people do, but I’m too shy to stay in character! I feel too silly. What I do is think very deeply about every single word I say in the script before I arrive. Because I’m theater trained, the script is my bible. All answers will be there. I spend a long time thinking about everything I say and everything everyone else says, and I go through it many, many times. An internal world builds up inside me. I can’t really explain how it happens. When I get to set, I forget any notes or journals I’ve made. I drop it all, empty myself, and see what happens. I feel buoyant and flexible, not stuck in any particular way.

Mouse is so specific about 2002, down to the Michelle Branch music cues. I was a bit younger than the characters then, but it all felt right. What did setting it in that moment bring to the story?

I’m older, but Kelly was that age in 2002, so she had all the references. She knew exactly what she was listening to, what she was thinking and feeling. The main difference is there were no cell phones back then. If you wanted information, it had to come to you through someone taking action. The jogger has to tell Minnie something, then she has to run to the house to see if it’s really happened, then she has to look for a phone book. Now it would just be someone posting “RIP Callie” on Instagram. It’s so much more interesting to film people taking an action than all these constant shots of phones and texts, which I see in movies all the time now. It’s so boring.

In Mouse, Helen and Minnie come from very different backgrounds. Class is also woven into Clarissa, where you play the titular role. Was that a connection you were conscious of while working on the two films?

Class is massive in Britain. We live and breathe it. It runs through every vein of everyone’s body here, probably more than anything else, so I’m very aware of it. But there’s another weird parallel between the films: Mouse is directed by a couple, and one of them is the writer. Clarissa is directed by two brothers, and one of them is the writer. With both, I had an instant, visceral response. I didn’t need to think about the whys and wherefores. It was just yes, yes, yes. With a lot of other work, I have to get myself into the right position or work it out. What’s also amazing is that the scripts for Clarissa and Mouse barely changed between that first draft and the start of filming—the same was true of Janet Planet. These are filmmakers who have thought deeply about what they’re writing. There weren’t a million drafts or endless revisions; all three films were already in a remarkably evolved state from the start. Even though Mouse looks improvised in places, I’m sticking to the script.

But parts of Mouse were improvised, right? I’m thinking of the scene where Helen attends a grief group.

It was a real grief group. I knew the man handing me coffee at the beginning was an actor, though by coincidence he was also in a grief group. I was just outside the room; they put two cameras in there, and someone called action. I walked in, and during the scene it slowly dawned on me—someone had forgotten to tell me these weren’t actors!

The scene is short, but that take lasted an hour and 10 minutes—the exact length of the group. If it were scripted, I probably would have talked and broken down. But I couldn’t speak; their stories were so extraordinary. I kept talking to them afterward, thinking the cameras had stopped, until I realized they were still filming. Alex will do that. You don’t even know. There’s no “cut.”

Both films are concerned with motherhood, though in very different ways. In Mouse, there’s an absent daughter; in Clarissa, she keeps her living daughter at arm’s length. Did these characters speak to each other in any way?

It’s a good question, because I find that when I do a part, it usually feeds into the next one. The next role I played after Clarissa was Natalya in Turgenev’s A Month in the Country, in London. She’s a woman of a certain age looking back, wondering whether she made the right choices, and she has a very separate relationship with her son. I was thinking that a lot of Clarissa was in her.

I read that Arie and Chuko drew on their own mother in shaping the film and that you got to spend time with her. How did that influence your performance?

When they cast me, I wondered if I could do this. I told them I didn’t recognize the Lagos in the script and that I had such a fractured relationship with the country. They said, “If nothing else, we’ll bridge that for you.” That meant a lot. Before filming, Chuko invited me to stay with him and his mother. I ended up staying the whole shoot and got very close to her. I used her a lot, more than she realizes, perhaps. Like Clarissa, she employs staff [in her home], and I observed how she interacted with them. I didn’t want to turn her into a caricature out of Downton Abbey. You can just be real with them, the way she was.

You also just don’t see stories like this coming out of Africa, and I say that broadly. The subject matter is usually very narrow: Africa is depicted as war-torn, impoverished. Here was a film about people. There’s a backdrop of war and social and economic circumstances, but that isn’t the main thrust. I long to see films where we as Africans, as Nigerians, get every part of ourselves represented, just as our white Western counterparts get films about everything. It’s the same with queer films and Black films: They shouldn’t only be about being queer or Black. That shouldn’t have to be the whole story.

And on top of that, Clarissa is character driven and not plot driven.

The thought of going to Lagos and making an arthouse film on 35 millimeter was incredible. It’s an impossible book to film. People have tried many times, and mostly it doesn’t work. I was taking a punt. I just wanted to be part of it. I hardly say anything but say a million words with my face.

What is it like to project that kind of interiority? It’s sort of a paradox: Clarissa is deep in thought, but she also doesn’t let you in much.

She’s hard to read, but you have to make her really easy to read for the camera. She’s protective, but you have to let the camera in. I didn’t think about it that deeply. I just have that sort of face. I’m really sensitive, hypersensitive, which is so difficult in my normal life, but it’s great for acting. My grandmother used to say, “Your face changes like the wind.” Everything shows. Chuko or Arie would only have to whisper the slightest thing in my ear, and it would show.

People always say to watch an actor’s eyes, but I noticed so much happens in the lower half of your face. It holds everything.

That’s why I could never do any of that stuff to my face. I’d be too frightened! I know I only have to think the glimmer of a thought and it’ll show. I don’t know what happens to my face because I don’t really watch myself, but doing something that would stop that would be the end of my career.

The story famously centers on your character throwing a party. Are you more of a host or a guest?

I’m quite a good host, actually. I don’t do it often because I go overboard and it’s exhausting. I love cooking and making lovely things. I used to spend the whole time panicking in the kitchen, but I’ve learned it doesn’t really matter what you serve. It’s about how you engage with guests. They just want you to be part of the party.

Did you watch any of the other adaptations of Mrs. Dalloway to prepare for Clarissa?

I watched about three minutes of one with Vanessa Redgrave and realized we’re not doing this type of film, so I didn’t carry on. Chuko and Arie would have watched everything, though. They’re complete cinephiles.

Did they give you suggestions on films to watch to prepare then?

They probably did, but I forgot because my brain is a sieve. They gave up on me. They’d mention really famous films, and I’d say I hadn’t seen them. I don’t know what I do with my time. I don’t fill it wisely. I just seem to mess around most of the day, and then it’s gone!

It sounds like you’re living your own stories instead of watching other people’s on screen.

You’re putting it nicely. As my husband says, I spend a lot of time daydreaming. I’ve got a really nice view. [Turns her laptop to the window to show the view.] I spend a lot of time just looking out at the trees with my dog.

After this double-header year, what are you looking for next?

Because I’m getting older, I don’t see an eternity stretching out in front of me anymore, and I find myself asking how I want to spend my time. I’ve decided that my heart is really in independent films and theater, so I’m going to wait until the right thing comes along. You might find me still unemployed a year from now. Nothing has come up yet that’s been worth getting on a plane for.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6789. Taylor Swift Swaps Her Signature Red Lipstick for “Cinnamon Latte Lips”

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The old Taylor can’t come to the phone right now

Over the years, Taylor Swift has changed her hair often, switched up her style, and gone through many eras, but one constant has been her iconic red lip. Swift has worn the notable blue-red color for decades—through multiple tours, relationships, and possibly even at her wedding—but more recently, she’s branched out and ditched her signature red for something a bit juicier.

On Monday, the Recording Academy announced the 2027 Grammy nominations, and Swift made a surprise appearance on the livestream to announce two of the categories, “Album of the Year” and “Song of the Year,” but her appearance wasn’t the only surprise. Instead of her classic red lip, Swift wore “cinnamon latte lips”—a burnt-orange shade that may be our favorite hue for the fall season. One might assume “cinnamon latte lips” would skew more brown, but the way Swift wears it, the color has a bit of orange. The lipstick shade also resembles the one Swift wore when announcing her recent single “Patient Zero” back in September.

Although Swift swapped her red for a warm brown-orange hue for the Grammys announcement, she still wore her classic winged eyeliner and bangs—two other staples of her beauty look. This isn’t the first time she’s shaken up her lip look. More recently, Swift has leaned more neutral, with a petal-pink lip at the sixth annual Academy Museum Gala and the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards. But she’s not completely forgoing her red lip, as it still seems to be a staple look, especially at her husband Travis Kelce’s Kansas City Chiefs games.

Swift hasn’t explicitly shared what lipstick she is wearing in the video. However, her makeup artist, Lorrie Turk, has previously confirmed that she often wears the Nars lipstick in Morocco, a warm, neutral cinnamon shade with an orange undertone, so she may have worn the same shade during the Grammys announcements.
