#6788. When to Tuck Your Trousers Into Boots This Fall and Winter

Consider this your cheat sheet for every pants-and-boots combo.

Every fall, the same fashion question finds its way back into our closets: Should you tuck your pants into your boots, or let them fall over the top? As a Southerner, who loves a good cowboy boot, I’ve been debating this topic for years. It’s a deceptively tricky styling decision. One minute, you’re channeling an effortlessly chic equestrian look; the next, you're wrestling with a pair of jeans that won’t stay put inside your knee-high boots. And sometimes, if you’re like me, your pants just aren’t able to squeeze into your boots, so you have to let it all hang out.

Whether you're reaching for riding boots, chunky combat boots, ankle booties, or a slouchier silhouettes, the secret is knowing when a tuck works—and when it's better to let your pants do their thing. Below, please see my definitive guide on when to and when to not tuck those pants into your boots. And there’s no better time than today to figure it out, since we’re deep into fall and heading toward winter.

I know there’s a debate every day on the internet about skinny jeans being dead, but they are alive and well during the winter months! You need a good skinny jean for all your tall boot days. Yes, boyfriend jeans and ’90s baggy are popular, but those cuts are not sliding into your leather knee-highs.

Maybe because I love a good lazy girl fall, there’s nothing better than tucking your baggy sweats into your Ugg boots. It works great for the overall vibe you’re curating and keeps your pants from dragging on the dirty ground.

A straight-leg jean is sublime with this style of pointed boot. Whether it’s actually a bootie or rises to your calf, keep these untucked for a classic day-to-night moment.

Similar to straight leg, there are very few occasions where I personally believe you need to tuck some flare pants into a boot. They are the star of the look, creating a silhouette that you’d lose if tucking them in. This is also the case for flare jeans with cowboy boots. Let the boots poke out a little while the jeans do all the work.

Similar to sweats and a shearling boot—but opposite of the straight leg—if you’re going to rock one of my favorite styles, the slouchy boot, you’ve gotta tuck. It’s so fab and gives that cool girl, 2016 era, full-beat party girl energy. So, if you plan to go slouchy in the next few weeks, make sure your pants are baggy enough to handle the tuck.

Aiyana Ishmael is the style editor at Cosmopolitan magazine. In her work, Aiyana focuses on the culture of fashion and how it intertwines and shapes the zeitgeist. #6785. Stylist and Creative Director Akari Endo-Gaut’s Guide to Tokyo

Perhaps no city juggles the past and the future as nimbly as Tokyo. Sleek skyscrapers meet centuries-old shrines; a rich culinary tradition blends with contemporary innovation (it’s no accident that this is the city with the most Michelin starred-restaurants in the world). The fashion, of course, exists in a similar dichotomy, expertly blending traditional techniques with the avant-garde. There’s never a wrong time to visit the Japanese capital—but in winter, when ski resorts a quick day trip away are in full swing and New Year’s celebrations are on the horizon, it feels particularly special. All you have to do is narrow down your itinerary.

In fact, there’s so much to discover that you could spend an entire trip dedicated to shopping alone—according to Akari Endo-Gaut, a Japan-born, New York-based stylist and creative director who studied in Tokyo, it may be worth bringing a second suitcase just for souvenirs. From the vintage shops to put on your radar to the best place to stop for a glass of natural wine, here’s a glimpse at Endo-Gaut’s Tokyo little black book.

For a one-of-a-kind clothing find: Since I was student in Tokyo, one of my favorite areas to hang around was Minami-Aoyama. We used to have amazing Corso Como store there; now, the Comme des Garçons store, the Issey Miyake Pleats Please shop, and the Auralee store there are still where you can go to find a special piece.

For vintage gems: There are so many good vintage shops in Tokyo, and it goes deep. BerBer Jin is always my first stop, and I also check luxury resale shops like Komehyo.

For unique souvenirs: You can find the best curated products, from ceramic bowls to German knives, at Arts and Science. And beautifully wrapped sweets at Higashiya are the best gifts.

For a worthwhile investment piece: Wako Arts and Culture is a new space conceived by artist Hiroshi Sugimoto in the basement of a prestigious department store in Ginza. It’s all specially curated, a great spot to find a special piece from fashion to Japanese craft.

For the magpie: My very talented friend Charlotte Chesnais from Paris recently opened a shop in Tokyo; it’s a must-visit. Or, if you’re looking for best-condition vintage watches, you can go to ECW Shoto.

For your next great read: Japan has a big book culture—go to Komiyama bookstore for vintage books, or spend a full weekend browsing at Tsutaya Daikanyama or SKAC.

For stylish home goods: You can find traditional but beautiful kitchen goods at Kiya and, of course, at Muji. Or, spend a fun day exploring all the kitchen goods stores in the Kappabashi area, which is a shopping street dedicated to restaurant owners.

For the quickest way to impress an out-of-towner: Hakujitsu houses a beautiful collection of ceramics in an old dentist building. My secret favorite is Yanaka Matsunoya—it has the best baskets and tote bags.

For a fabulous dinner reservation: I love Japanese-Chinese food or yakiniku, so I go to Chugoku Hanten with local friends or to Jojoen with my sister. If I have foreign guests, they usually have fun dining experience at Narukiyo.

For a bakery treat: Sawamura is our best local bakery cafe in Hiroo. After a soba lunch at Kanda, stop by Omiya Western Sweets Shop for the cutest pastry; for traditional Japanese sweets at an upscale, architecturally beautiful spot, go to Toraya Akasaka.

For the art-lover: Taka Ishii and Tomio Koyama are the best fine arts galleries in Tokyo. I like the artists from Kosaku Kanechika too, and at Licht gallery, you can see the best design pieces.

For an apéro.. or a nightcap: For the architecture lover, a drink at Imperial Bar, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright, is a must. When I’m hanging out with local friends, I’d go for a natural wine at Le Cabaret or Tabac.

For your packing list: Honestly, you don’t need anything, since you go to Tokyo to buy the best of all items! Bring flat shoes for walking, and an extra suitcase for shopping. An eye mask and melatonin for the 13-hour time difference will come in handy, as will a handkerchief; it’s part of local etiquette to carry one. And I always like to bring a running outfit for the famous Imperial Palace run.

#6781. Best Harrington Jackets 2026: Preppy, Punk, and Ultra-Functional

Few jackets have managed to cross as many style tribes—and decades—as the Harrington. In fact, if you were to enroll in Classic Menswear 101, the Harrington jacket would be a prerequisite. The transitional season staple—a favorite of Elvis, James Dean, Steve McQueen, and every member of The Clash—is constantly found across lookbooks and style Instagram accounts, because it does so many things so well.

For one, it's incredibly practical: Water-resistant, pocket-forward, lightly insulating, and ever-adaptable to the day's conditions thanks to its full-zip and collar. But the almost-cropped length—and popped collar, if you so dare—is also a style swerve that makes every wearer feel one dose cooler than they did before. No wonder it’s been embraced over the decades by everyone from golfers to preppies to A-Listers and punks.

The original Harrington—a Baracuta G9—is still available almost a century on from its release, and still excellent. But if you’re looking to broaden your horizons, today’s Harrington jackets aren’t resting on their laurels. Below, the standout versions worth adding to your rotation before we’re into parka territory.

The classic Baracuta G9 golf jacket is as British as beans on toast. This is the original tartan-lined, ribbed-cuff Harrington, the jacket you picture when you think of Steve McQueen or Paul Newman, and the brand that insider-y menswear favorites like Engineered Garments and Noah have collaborated with when they wanted to make Harringtons of their own. Baracuta got its start making raincoats for other brands—Burberry included—before branching out with its own designs, and the G9 is still made in England today. Crafted from a water-resistant cotton-poly blend, and featuring the signature Fraser tartan lining and iconic umbrella back yoke (which keeps rain off your back while letting air circulate) it really doesn't get any better than this.

Uniqlo delivers a whole Harrington jacket without sacrificing anything, and in fact saves you some precious dollars along the way. We’re talking a slightly cropped, slightly relaxed silhouette, a touch of stretch, classic slant pockets and even a genre-affirming plaid lining. And while it’s not water-resistant like some other options, it makes up for it with a durable cotton fabric that’ll dry off in no time, and still keep you protected from a few unforeseen raindrops. If you’re after the workaday Harrington aesthetic without spending a lot, this one gets the job done and then some.

If you're looking to purchase a Harrington jacket that'll serve you for seasons to come, but don't particularly want to spend half your rent check on it, J.Crew's faithful take on the Harrington is as true as it gets. And this is no compromise pick: It still comes with plenty of details to get excited about, from the handsome, buttoned interior chest pocket to the warming full lining, leather zip tag, and 10-ounce cotton twill that's already been washed a few times by the brand to make it feel lived-in and well-loved from the jump. It also comes in multiple colors, partly because J.Crew is confident you'll be back for more. Oh, and if you want a winterized Harrington, check out the corduroy iteration, which also has a quilted, Primaloft-stuffed lining.

A pared-down, easygoing take on the classics, Quince’s Harrington strikes a smart balance of polished and sporty, without even the faintest fuss. Offered in khaki, navy and black, this one is the modern minimalist’s Harrington—a clean, contemporary style that does what a staple should do: make you look good without causing a scene. Oh, and that twill outer will break in wonderfully over time, in case you were wondering.

One of the best parts about a Harrington Jacket is that the idea is fully formed. As such, it can be a hard style to riff on, mostly because the source material is so dialed in that it’s often best to leave well enough alone. Ernest W. Baker designers Reid Baker and Inês Amorim, however, couldn’t care less about that tradition and went nuclear with this one: it’s a true-blue Harrington complete with a cropped fit, ribbing at the waist, barrel cuffs and a point collar. But then the inclusion of a leather collar and Western-inspired yoke details in lieu of the classic back vent turns it into something else entirely, without changing the fit one bit. And they nailed it. It’s transformative without being performative, utterly distinct and eminently familiar and, most improbably, contradiction free.

This has most of the trappings of your classic Harrington—stand collar, cool back vent, functional cuffs—but it also eschews the classic ribbed hem for a cinched waist, which adds a little bit of drama to the notoriously no-drama silhouette.

Todd Snyder often plays it straight—Ivy-ish classics with just the right details. Here, they’ve ditched part of the trad playbook and leaned into the modern with water-resistant tech cotton-nylon blend, but it's also a bit cropped and fits very much like you'd remember. And now, it's also on sale.

A Harrington is already pretty pared down, but Barbour trimmed every ounce of fat on this one, leaving us with a slightly longer silhouette, all the *essential* bells and whistles and a brown cotton outer that gets to take center stage.

We could get into the buttery leather collar or the insane Italian wool serge fabric that Wanze deployed on this stunner, or even lock in on that two-way RiRi zipper, but that'd be burying the lede because you're not going to get a red like this anywhere else.

We wouldn't typically include different versions of the same style in one guide, but when our Best Overall version also comes in a buttery suede, exceptions are made.

Stone Island traffics in the unexpected, so, in a way, it should come as no surprise that the Italian label's take on the classic is a Gonzo, teched-out one—one made with a garment-dyed fabric that's been treated with an "anti-drop" finish.

The Harrington is an icon of preppy style, so of course Ralph Lauren has blessed us with its lightweight cotton take, complete with the signature Polo pony on the chest. It’s preppy, American, and exactly the kind of jacket your kids will proudly say “This used to be my Dad’s” about.

You might not think of a Harrington as a "winter jacket," but hear us out: it can be. This Percival joint, for instance, is made out of a hardy birdseye wool blend that will hold up to some chilly weather and layer up nicely when calling things "chilly" is understatement.

The funniest thing about the Harrington? It wasn’t originally called a Harrington at all. The original—and, as you've read above, our favorite—was called the “G9.” It was cooked up by Baracuta in 1937 in rainy old Manchester, England, as a golf jacket—the “G” stands for “golf.” (The idea was to make a garment that could take a beating from British weather without cramping your backswing.) But the jacket earned its now-iconic name thanks to Rodney Harrington, a character from the 1960s TV show Peyton Place, who wore one so often that the name just stuck.

The traditional Harrington jacket fits close to the shoulders and chest, but still has enough room for a full range of arm motion—it is a golfing style, after all. The hem then typically sits either at the waist, or for a more stylized look, just above the belt line. It should be easy to spot from product shots whether the designer in question has stuck to this traditional shape, or elongated the style a touch. From that point, the only thing left to consider is whether you plan to wear it over thick sweaters, or lighter T-shirts and shirts. If it's the former, you may want to consider sizing up.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6780. ‘The Traitors’ Greatest Key to Success: Drama Without Romance

And just like that, another season of The Traitors is about to come to a close. The two-part finale of New Blood airs Thursday and right now it could be anybody’s game. Victor has been the only Faithful making smart decisions this season, but now in the final stretch he’s put his trust in the worst possible person. Shane is now a Traitor and completely off Victor’s radar. Mr. Sweaty Boy could end up getting taken out by his biggest ally in the game. The stakes could not be higher, but let’s be honest—chaos and drama are where this series thrives.

Yet despite the vast array of emotions and personalities that have graced these hallowed halls, The Traitors’ most impressive accomplishment, by far, has always been its refusal to incorporate romance into any part of its narrative. You’d think confining a group of individuals inside a beautiful, remote Scottish castle with an open bar would be a hormonal powder keg waiting to happen. (Think Love Island, but with murder and Alan Cumming in fierce looks.) But The Traitors has made a point to never cross that line.

In four seasons of the celebrity version and one season of the civilian version, there have been no secret hookups, no lover alliances, no steamy makeout sessions in the wine cellar—just platonic game play. That’s a unique approach considering how many reality shows like The Bachelor and Too Hot to Handle fully lean into the whole love and dating genre. Even more strategy-centric “gamer” shows like Big Brother are known for their iconic showmances. Yet The Traitors partakes in none of it, because it doesn't need romance to create must-see drama.

That’s not to say that flirtations and crushes never take place to some degree. (We were all thankful for Rob Rausch’s overalls last season.) Yet the show does not rely on hookups or romantic entanglements. Instead, Traitors has always preferred to highlight the close-knit friendships that develop among the contestants each season—making any potential fallout all the more satisfying to watch unfold.

Just look at Season 1’s winner, Cirie Fields. No one ever suspected her or said her name at the round table because she had formed such solid alliances with so many of her fellow players. The three other remaining finalists were convinced they were splitting that money. They weren’t worried at all that a Traitor could still be among them. That’s how fully they trusted Cirie, which made her treachery such an epic and truly heartbreaking revelation.

Meanwhile, Season 4’s finale saw Rob Rausch completely blindside Maura Higgins when he revealed himself as a Traitor and won the game. These two did flirt a bit on camera, sure, but they also seemed to develop a real friendship throughout the course of the season. Maura put all of her trust in Rob and he proved to be a snake in the grass. (You know he’d appreciate the snake comparison.) Romance and heartache may go hand-in-hand, but to be hurt by a good friend? That’s a different kind of pain, and arguably a lot more fun to watch implode.

Maura was a good sport about it in the end (the show is literally called The Traitors, after all), but the genuine shock that she felt made for some great television. Her quip about how he’s never going to get a girlfriend after this because he’s so good at lying was legendary and deserves a place in the Sick Burns Hall of Fame.

Ultimately, this show knows how to play to its strengths. It’s never been about finding a love match. It’s about murderrrrrrr. Why deal with matters of the heart when it’s much more entertaining to watch these contestants stab each other in the back? Metaphorically speaking, of course. (Or maybe not?) Either way, we love you just the way you are, Traitors. Never change.

#6778. Inde Navarrette Credits Actresses Who Gave Her ‘Permission to Be Free’

For ELLE Women in Hollywood honoree Inde Navarrette, playing Nikki in Obsession was about far more than landing her first leading role. In her acceptance speech at our annual event at the Four Seasons Hotel Los Angeles at Beverly Hills last night, the actress spoke about putting everything that she had into playing the character. “I needed to break through every glass ceiling either school, peers, society, or even I put on myself,” she said. “I needed to be connected with that rage that I used to find solace in. I needed to be reminded that my voice, whether soft or loud, holds weight and creates tension that I get to be in control of. I can play a girl who has an internal world—crazy!—whom is the lead of a film and whom is not the perfect victim. Nikki was my opportunity to show the world what I knew I could do and to that, I have to say thank you.”

She went on to thank Obsession’s writer and director Curry Barker, along with all actresses who inspired her early on (including Bryce Dallas Howard, who presented Navarrette with the award). “Thank you not only to Curry Barker for writing a role that allowed me that chance, but thank you to all of the women that took that chance before me,” she said. “Thank you to Jessica Lange for showing me and all of her work that there is beauty in madness and to just give it to the world. Thank you to Natalie Portman for Léon: The Professional. It was the first time I got to see a kid in a movie being more than a kid. She was me. Thank you to Sally Field and Steel Magnolias for daring to portray grief honestly and the hardships of motherhood gracefully. Thank you, Bryce Dallas Howard and The Help, for portraying how intersectional womanhood can divide us and that women who look different than ourselves are no different than ourselves. Thank you to Florence Pugh, Carrie Coon, Julianne Moore, Elizabeth Debicki, Samantha Morton, Rosalind Eleazar, Penélope Cruz. Thank you for daring to be wild. Thank you. Incredibly, you have all given me permission to be free. Let’s all shine a light in each other.”

#6777. Where to Stay in Antwerp, Belgium’s Design-Filled City

Antwerp isn’t a loud city. You don’t come here to be awed by ancient ruins or to tour record-breaking skyscrapers. There are no leafy stoops with picturesque brownstones enshrined on TV. Antwerp’s charm unfolds quietly alongside its cobblestoned streets and narrow brick townhouses; I’d argue it’s a place most stumble upon when traveling through Europe, rather than specifically seek out. Those who do make it a point to visit, however, will easily be won over by its unassuming beauty and artistic milieu—after all, there’s a reason why it’s long attracted a certain kind of creative. (Painter Peter Paul Rubens called it home in the 16th century, fashion designers Raf Simons and Pieter Mulier do so in the 21st.)

Winter is an especially lovely time to visit—even when it drizzles (trust me, it will), Antwerp feels delightfully festive: Christmas markets take over the Old Town square, with glowing lights strung up all over the city. The ongoing Antwerp Six exhibit at the MoMu makes a trip this holiday season particularly timely; the group’s first major retrospective closes on January 17, 2027.

The best places to stay in Antwerp offer a chance to adjust to the city’s quiet rhythm—whether that means finding calm in a former convent, or slowing down in one of the many well-appointed Airbnbs that dot the center. Like most major European towns, you can confidently skip the car rental; much, if not most, of Antwerp, can be comfortably discovered on foot and by bike.

An Augustinian convent transformed into a design lover’s dream, the work of famed Belgian architect Vincent Van Duysen makes for a serene refuge after a long journey. Modernist touches and an earthy color palette underscore the property’s monastic qualities, and the rooms are thoughtful but efficiently put together. (The artfully rumpled bed linens are one highlight; the exposed timber beams in the larger suites, another.)

Couples wishing to explore the grounds can unwind with a treatment in the spa—which includes an intimate swimming pond—then dine in the on-site restaurant. (If weather allows, try to book a table in the outdoor terrace.) While the hotel is located in one of Antwerp’s quieter neighborhoods, het Groen Kwartier, you’re still within walking distance from most of the action, including two local favorites: Bar Vert for a low-key lunch, and Funk (an essential personal bookmark) for breakfast pastries.

Photo: Courtesy of Antwerp Botanic Sanctuary

It doesn’t get more central than this. Antwerp’s Botanic Sanctuary, the sole five-star property in town, gets its name from its location: It’s a former monastery nestled besides the city’s Botanical Gardens. Rooms are awash in calming neutrals with multiple large suites available for families—some of which overlook the adjoining 15th-century chapel. Food-motivated travelers are spoilt for choice: Start with drinks at Henry’s Bar, then take your pick of one of three Michelin-starred restaurants for dinner. (Ed note: The property’s marquee wellness facilities are currently temporarily closed due to a recent fire.)

Hotels in European Old Towns aren’t exactly known for their modern charm—and yet, Hotel Julien is brimming with exactly that. Set across two former historic buildings, it precedes the opening of its sister property August, but remains a worthwhile destination for its location alone. Rooms are cozy but pared back, punctuated by touches of red, and you’ll appreciate all the sightseeing there is to do, starting with the rooftop terrace that overlooks the Cathedral of Our Lady—an exalted edifice of Gothic architecture. It’s the ideal cozy home base for a trip spent exploring: “Antwerp is a very historic city, so it’s worth spending a day wandering through its streets, admiring the old architecture, and stepping into the many independent boutiques and antique shops,” adds de Geyter.

Originally a mansion built in 1890, Boulevard Leopold has found new life as a bed and breakfast since 2006. It’s very much no-frills—the aforementioned breakfast, a daily spread that includes croissants and fresh orange juice and is served each morning in the orangerie, is pretty much the only standard “amenity”—but that doesn’t mean it’s sparse. On the contrary, this jewel box of a space is full of charming little touches everywhere you look, the effect of which is a collected feel akin to that of a slightly eccentric aunt’s home.

To wit: crystal chandeliers that play against antler mounts, taxidermy birds that mingle with ornate, gilded candlesticks, a large bamboo fan moonlighting as a headboard that sits above a spartan cot. There are just five bedrooms to book, one of which is a gold-painted suite that takes up the entirety of the first floor. If you’re looking for a quiet, design-forward spot, this B&B is it.

Art is the main motivator at Hotel Pilar, a stylish boutique stay in Antwerp’s hip Het Zuid area, where each of its 21 rooms is designed around unique works. Oil paintings and glossy photographs contrast exposed brick and raw concrete in some; colorful prints juxtapose stainless steel and marbled tiles in others. Lively cafés and bars surround the property, which also happens to overlook the Royal Museum of Fine Arts (KMSKA). For the intrepid gallery hopper, the Museum of Contemporary Art (M HKA) is similarly close by; so is the Ann Demeulemeester flagship if you’re down for a side quest. An art-filled salon adjoins the hotel’s ground-floor restaurant—you’ll want to bookend the day here on one of its velvet couches, no matter where you dined that night.

Set in a 19th-century building in the heart of Antwerp’s fashion district, this light-filled apartment is a more than comfortable base from which to explore the city. It sleeps up to four, with a large dining room and sweet little kitchen that encourages culinary creativity. Original features, like a marble fireplace and antique wood floors, mix seamlessly with modern amenities; you will feel instantly at home.

Stained glass windows, zellige tiling, gilded mirrors… there are more than enough special decorative touches in this home to keep the eye busy. This stay is ideal for a family: It sleeps 10, with five distinctly designed bedrooms (the flamingo pink one, complete with a crystal chandelier and brocade drapes, feels especially grand). It’s well-located, too, with a green park nearby and several main tramlines on your cobblestoned doorstep.

#6776. John Mulaney Wore Joe DiMaggio’s Watch to Host 'Saturday Night Live'

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

Between sniffing out paternal autism and perfecting his Robert F. Kennedy impression, you may have noticed that John Mulaney was wearing an extraordinary watch while hosting Saturday Night Live this weekend. It’s a beauty—a gold vintage Patek Philippe with swoopy Breguet numerals—but its backstory is even more impressive. On December 12, 1948, New York Yankees legend Joe DiMaggio purchased this timepiece and owned it until his death in 1999.

The Patek Philippe, a ref. 130 circa 1947, is already a rare bird before you add in its Joltin’ Joe provenance. The model is one of just 180 made in yellow gold with Breguet numerals, and only 55 with this same combination have ever reached the secondary market. In late October, dealer Eric Wind of Wind Vintage put this specific watch up for sale with a $1.2 million asking price. “I think it’s the greatest Patek that’s known and tied to any athlete,” Wind told Robb Report last month.

For his seventh time hosting SNL, Mulaney came to Wind in search of “an important watch,” the dealer explains now. After surveying Wind’s entire catalog, the comedian landed on this piece, whose ties to a legendary New Yorker felt right for helming one of the city’s most hallowed institutions. To be clear, Mulaney only borrowed the watch for the show, which means its legend will have only grown by the time it reaches an eventual buyer. Talk about an illustrious provenance: A DiMaggio-owned Patek that also appeared on Saturday Night Live. “It was a very special moment and another cool moment of history for this important Patek Philippe,” Wind says.

As a known history buff and devoted baseball fan, the watch likely appealed to Mulaney on several levels. But its eggshell-hued dial also happened to go perfectly with the brown suit Mulaney sported during his opening monologue. “John has classic styling,” Wind says, “and the Joe DiMaggio Patek Philippe was the chef’s kiss on his wrist.”

Over the past several years, Mulaney has emerged as one of Hollywood’s most prolific and tasteful watch collectors. He is an eager and omnivorous admirer, bouncing between his beloved Rolex Air-King, loud Chopard chronographs, and glamorous Grand Seikos.

Mulaney, styled by Michael Fisher, wearing Cavour

During our watch-focused interview last May, Mulaney told me that he steers away from more obvious models like your garden-variety Rolex Submariner. “I don’t ask any questions about it, I know what it is,” he explained. “And I’m just more interested in watches that [are a little more] mysterious.” As an example, Mulaney specifically referenced a Patek Philippe Calatrava his wife Olivia Munn bought him.

The DiMaggio Patek is full of intrigue. The watch obviously has important provenance, but it’s historic on its own accord, too. The ref. 130 is named for the movement inside, known as the Calibre 130. That engine was the basis for Patek’s 1518, the first serially produced watch to combine a perpetual calendar and chronograph.

Funnily enough, this isn’t the first Mulaney, DiMaggio, and SNL crossover. In his 2018 special Kid Gorgeous at Radio City, the comedian explained what it was like working with famous SNL hosts during his time as a staff writer. “It’d be like if you went into your childhood bedroom and Joe DiMaggio was sitting there,” Mulaney quipped. “Yeah, he’s Joe DiMaggio, he’s a legend, he had sex with Marilyn Monroe, but only you know where the bathroom is.” And only Mulaney has had DiMaggio’s watch on his wrist, for now.

#6774. Carrie Coon Speaks Out About Women’s Representation at ELLE’s Women in Hollywood Event

Carrie Coon had a question for her fellow Women in Hollywood honorees: “Can we start a studio?”

On Monday night, the actress took the stage at ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood celebration in Los Angeles, where she called for women in the entertainment industry to come together and create more opportunities for themselves.

Coon was introduced by her Gilded Age co-star Louisa Jacobson, who celebrated her recent career achievements.

“Carrie is a crusader, always fighting tirelessly for artistic integrity in a landscape that seems to value high gloss and profit over honest, nuanced storytelling,” Jacobson said. “And if you know Carrie, you know that she is completely allergic to superficiality.”

In her acceptance speech, Coon reflected on the importance of women’s stories, drawing inspiration from feminist literature and End Times Fascism, a book by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor.

“Patriarchy, capitalism...these are hierarchical systems of domination that rely on fear,” she said. “And in this paradigm, women and girls, like our natural resources, are a disposable commodity—and as such, according to philosopher Kate Manne—our stories are interchangeable and of equal power. But of course, they’re not. That’s not true. And we’re not a monolith.”

Coon went on to discuss the performances of her fellow honorees, arguing that their work represented something extraordinary. “In these women, I see the fight for the living world. I see moral clarity. I see imagination. I see courage,” she said. “And these are, in fact, the antidotes to fascism. That’s how important this storytelling is.”

Toward the end of her speech, Coon questioned how women in Hollywood could create lasting change beyond events celebrating their individual achievements.

“How do we forge our collective safety and solidarity in an ethic of communalism?” she asked. “Okay, so this is the part of the speech where I don’t actually have the answer to that question, but I make the appeal that nights like these shouldn’t be one-off nights.”

She concluded with the aforementioned proposition for her peers: “And so I’m going to start with a really stupid question, but I’m not afraid to ask a stupid question: Can we start a studio?”

#6773. Why ‘DWTS’ Fans Think Harry Shum Jr.’s Elimination Ties Back to Some Behind-the-Scenes Drama

We’ve finally made it to the Dancing With the Stars finale—and fans aren’t entirely pleased with last night’s results.

The five celebs who are still in the running for the Mirrorball Trophy are Connor Wood, Ezra Frech, Maura Higgins, Amber Glenn, and Tatyana Ali. Which means Harry Shum Jr. has officially been booted from the ballroom—even after his touching homage to his late Glee co-star, Naya Rivera.

While fans are distraught by Harry’s exit, some are convinced that his elimination was driven by some behind-the-scenes drama from earlier in the season.

“Personally, I liked Harry and his dancing,” one fan wrote on Reddit. “Yes, he had dance experience but he was very good and he made things his own. I think he had a great story to tell and genuinely is a good guy.”

They then theorized what might have contributed to his elimination on Tuesday night’s episode—and it all ties back to Jenna Johnson and Val Chmerkovskiy’s drama earlier in the season.

The fan alleged that Val’s Mariah Carey Night braids and social media activity played a part, as well as Jenna and Harry’s LiftGate debacle, which led to Val’s “Fresh Prince” comments toward Carrie Ann Inaba.

“I think because of Jenna’s inability to take criticism from a judge and then Val’s social media (getting dreads and referencing hitting Cari Ann) Harry got voted off. Val only ‘apologized’ when he got pushback from the public,” they pointed out before separately suggesting that Harry might have survived longer with a different pro partner.

While some agreed, others weren’t immediately aligned with the theory.

“Honestly, for both Jenna Dewan and harry I didn’t feel the connection to the viewers as compared to the other dancers,” someone added. “So for me they were easy to not vote for because I didn’t feel anything towards them emotionally.”

Another added, “Harry got voted off because he wasn’t people’s favorite. It’s really not necessarily that deep. Not everyone is chronically online and know what’s going on.”

While none of this is confirmed and it probably came down to votes, Harry seems to be content with his DWTS journey, as he wants to “make more art” with Jenna outside of the show.

“I want to make more art with her, and that's what it's really about. I like making art that people enjoy,” he told E! News after his elimination. “So, to me, I felt that energy [in] the people that I did see and the people that really loved what we were able to do in this dance. I’m now a trained dancer because of her.”

#6771. The OG 'Thomas Crown Affair' Is an Essential Menswear Movie. How Will the Reboot Stack Up?

Between a stacked roster of Hollywood icons in their prime (Newman, Poitier, Redford) and a cadre of auteur directors on the come-up (Kubrick, Peckinpah, Coppola), the late 1960s produced some of the 20th century’s most stylish movies. Right up there with the best of them is The Thomas Crown Affair, a 1968 caper film directed by Norman Jewison and starring Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway. Fast-forward a few days and the same could be said about the 1999 remake starring Bond-era Pierce Brosnan, which is worth watching for the suits alone.

Now, in other news of a formerly Brosnan-led, menswear-centric franchise being rebooted: Oscar winner Michael B. Jordan is the producer, director, and star of a third riff on The Thomas Crown Affair, as he announced at CinemaCon back in April. Judging by the first trailer that dropped last week, the film aims to uphold the sartorial reputation of its forebears.

Hitting theaters in March 2027, Jordan’s The Thomas Crown Affair remake follows the same premise as the 1968 and 1999 versions: a wealthy playboy businessman plots art heists for fun while being pursued by a sexy insurance investigator, played in this iteration by potential future Wonder Woman Adria Arjona. There’s crime, there’s glamour, there’s sexual tension—but most of all, in the spirit of the Thomas Crowns before him, there appears to be plenty of high-octane menswear. The movie’s style credit is bolstered by Ruth E. Carter, the two-time Oscar-winning costume designer of the Black Panther movies, who also dressed Jordan for his Oscar-winning turn in Sinners.

But how will MBJ’s high-fashion Thomas Crown land? In the trailer, he can be seen wearing a stiff gray shirt with a matching tie and trousers by Bottega Veneta. The shirt, marked by the luxury brand’s signature triangle pocket detail, had an odd fit: taut around the torso yet puffy around the biceps. Here’s hoping we’ll see some sharper tailoring in the next preview.

Still, to understand Thomas Crown’s legacy as one of the best-dressed guys in film, and why the forthcoming reboot will likely be a smorgasbord of big-time menswear, it’s worth looking back at what made the original such a gem of classic American style. Beyond Jewison’s use of Mondrian-esque split-screen and a very cool soundtrack by French composer Michel Legrand, McQueen’s wardrobe is a perfect embodiment of late 1960s cool, and a how-to for anyone looking to capture it.

Equal parts finely tailored and adventurous, Crown is the ultimate man’s man: He closes million-dollar deals by day, but also flies planes, plays polo, and does donuts on the beach in a juiced-up dune buggy. Likewise, his wardrobe is split between incredible tailoring and a supremely dialed-in lineup of casual pieces. Crown’s suits are a primer on old-school Savile Row: structured, traditional, and precisely tailored, and his shirts, ties, and pocket squares are equally on point. Crown’s double-Albert style watch chain (attached to a Patek Philippe pocket watch, naturally) is a decidedly advanced swerve, but his Cartier Tank Cintrée looks as good in 2026 as it did in 1968 (or 1928, for that matter).

Steve McQueen and Faye Dunaway in The Thomas Crown Affair (1968).

Off-duty Crown’s casual looks include a parade of hall-of-fame menswear pieces like the Baracuta G9 Harrington jacket (classic navy blue with a red tartan lining), brown suede desert boots, and Persol aviators he wears while piloting his glider (gliders—also extremely cool). Club rules be damned, he plays golf in a non-regulation long-sleeved tee, whacks polo balls in an outfit straight out of a Ralph Lauren campaign, and later dons an Aran sweater for a romantic evening clambake at his beach house. It’s often said that Steve McQueen could look good in anything, and that might be true, but the clothes in this movie hit hard enough to make anyone look several orders of magnitude cooler.

Set to the funky bars of Fela Kuti’s “Gentleman,” the trailer for Jordan’s forthcoming Thomas Crown Affair offers several tantalizing tidbits of what’s in store, including a Ferrari F40, several razor-sharp tuxes, and a glimpse at a watch that’s almost certainly a vintage Piaget. That monochrome Bottega look aside, between Jordan’s leading man chops and Carter’s knack for high-concept menswear, we’re assuredly in good hands.

#6769. I’ve Tried Dozens of LED Masks—Here’s Why I’m Obsessed With CurrentBody’s Newest One

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Here’s my full, in-depth review while it’s 20% off for Black Friday.

A few months ago, I got invited to a very insider-y dinner with CurrentBody, a brand I’ve loved for years already for its LED masks and red-light hair-growth devices. The invite promised a new look at the brand’s latest red-light mask innovation that I, admittedly at the time, snoozed at. I’m no stranger to the beauty device game. I’ve tested more than a dozen in my eight years as an editor, and I figured that they really couldn’t get any more exciting, especially considering that the key to these masks working at all is consistency. What could CurrentBody do in a new mask that could make it any better than its previous iterations?

As I sat gnawing on table bread and sipping a glass of wine, I ate a big ol’ slice of humble pie, realizing that I was so wrong about what CurrentBody could have up its sleeve. The brand introduced me to its LED Face Mask: Series 3, featuring six wavelengths and, most importantly, MyDose, an app-controlled feature that gives you free rein to create custom treatments based on your skin’s needs and goals.

I waited patiently for a sample and have been using my Series 3 LED mask consistently since September. And it has entirely replaced every other LED mask I own (so much so, I gave them all away). Let me explain why it’s so good and all the reasons I love it.

BTW, CurrentBody’s Black Friday sale is running right now, where you can get this brand-new, high-tech LED mask for more than $100 off. If you’re considering trying it out, now’s your chance (I predict this will sell out before Cyber Week is over).

To understand the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask, you have to quickly understand what LED masks do in general. LED light—whether it’s red, blue, green, or yellow—delivers low-level wavelengths of light into your skin, which get absorbed by your skin cells and boosts cellular energy. How it affects your skin depends on the wavelength (aka color) of light. Red, for example, can help trigger collagen and elastin production in your skin to reduce fine lines and firm skin. Blue, though, targets acne-causing bacteria to prevent and treat breakouts, while yellow light can potentially soothe redness, and green light targets the melanocytes in your skin to fade hyperpigmentation.

FWIW, red is the most studied, but there still isn’t enough information out there yet on the potential further benefits it can have for skin and body (like decreasing inflammation and promoting faster wound healing). There’s also near-infrared and deep infrared, both of which penetrate the deeper layers of your skin to encourage tissue repair.

Now that you understand LED, let me get into this mask’s specs. It’s a full-face flexible silicone mask with a chin strap that covers your jawline and the area directly under your chin (I’ll wax poetic about this more later). In total, there are 750 LED bulbs, all of which can take all six wavelengths of light, meaning you don’t have to have multiple LED masks for your different needs.

The most defining characteristic of the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask is the introduction of MyDose. When you connect the mask to Bluetooth and use the CurrentBody smartphone app, you can customize your own treatments based on where you want the wavelengths to go. When you use the brand’s smartphone app, you can create your own treatments by painting on the exact spot on your face that you want certain wavelengths to go. And because MyDose automatically calculates the optimal (and safest) dose for your skin, you can actually use multiple wavelengths at once in one area. If you wanted, you could honestly do all six at one time, and the device will manually adjust the wavelength settings so it’s safe. If you don’t wanna create your own custom setup, you don’t have to—there are four preset treatment options (advanced anti-aging, advanced clearing, complexion corrector, and balance & brighten).

The key with LED masks is finding one that’ll convince you to use it most days. LED is only as good as your consistency. And unfortunately, I haven’t been all that consistent in the past. But! All of the below qualities of the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask really convinced me to use this regularly. For the past two months, I’ve used it at least three days a week. Most weeks, I try to get in at five days; a few weeks, I was lucky to hit six or seven. But best of all, I’ve used it consistently enough to (1) see results, and (2) have a lot of experiences to pull on to review.

Most of the time, I used my custom treatments, but I also tried all of the preset options at least once.

When I was first introduced to the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask, this feature was what made me immediately want to try it out. It’s easily the most advanced LED mask I’ve ever laid my eyes on, let alone used. It allows me to make the mask my own and use it how my skin needs. Some days, when my skin is really breaking out, a combo of blue, yellow, and green is my go-to. On days I remember that I’m almost 30, I crank up the red light. It’s like mood reading, but for your skin. And I freakin’ love it.

This feature is actually what earned the Series 3 LED Mask a coveted 2026 Cosmo Acne Award. I was able to create my own custom treatments to help my hormonal acne (specifically, one for my luteal phase where I’m most prone to breakouts and skin dullness). What’s really cool is that you can actually share treatments you’ve created. So if you want to try Cosmo’s custom treatment for acne-prone skin, just use code TXRXR in your app.

As someone with acne-prone skin and a dream of a chiseled jawline, the ability to get LED therapy on my jaw and under my chin is extremely helpful. I’ve used a lot of LED masks, but none of mine cover this much surface area, unless I add on an extra neck mask. I usually load up on the blue light here, but red light is also a great addition, as over time, this can tighten skin and reduce jowls.

The silicone itself feels great on my skin, but I especially love that the LEDs don’t make me overheat. Some LED masks I’ve used can make me feel a bit claustrophobic when I have them on, and the longer I wear the treatment, the LEDs can get a bit hot and make me sweat. Not ideal, especially if you are prone to melasma. But with the CurrentBody Series 3 LED Mask, I can comfortably sit for the entire 10 minutes of my treatment with no issues. Speaking of...

CurrentBody did the research to figure out just how long you would need to get the maximum benefit from the wavelengths in this mask, and I’m pleased that it’s only 10 minutes. I usually do my treatments in the morning, after swiping my face with some micellar water. It’s become a ritual I look forward to. I’ll sip my coffee and write out my to-do list for the day (or, occasionally, scroll on my phone—duh). Before I know it, the mask can come off. The device itself is also extremely easy to figure out, even if you’re not tech-savvy.

The device itself is cordless (meaning you don’t have to plug it into a wall), but there is a rechargeable box with a touch screen on a short cord for choosing your treatment. It’s really intuitive and easy to use (which I love), but the box is a bit bulky. It has a slot on the back that should allow you to slide it onto your clothes so you can go hands-free and walk around with the mask on (like, while you’re doing dishes or folding laundry). But I have a bit of a hard time getting it to stay when I do that.

It’s not a deal-breaker, obviously, but something to keep in mind if you like to wear your mask up and about. If I have to be seated for 10 minutes of my day, so be it.

I’m normally app-averse when it comes to beauty devices (and any device, tbh). I have enough damn apps on my phone! But because I don’t mind this one for the customization capabilities, I do wish the app included a tracking feature. Just a way to see how often I’m using the device in one place would be nice, especially if it could track which treatments I used. Not to sound like a biohacker, but I’d love to see how my skin fares using different treatments consistently.

What is the difference between the CurrentBody Series 2 and Series 3 LED masks?

If you already have the CurrentBody Series 2 LED Mask, you don’t need the series 3 by any means. But if you’re deciding between the two of them, I absolutely recommend Series 3. First of all, there are more than 500 more LED bulbs in the Series 3 than the Series 2, meaning you’re getting a lot stronger of a treatment for only a little over $100 more. The biggest difference, though, is that the Series 2 only offers red, near infrared, and deep infrared wavelengths, not the blue, green, or yellow light functions. Plus, the app-controlled MyDose function is only available on the Series 3.

Right now, the CurrentBody Series 3 mask is actually only $455 with the brand’s 20% off Black Friday deal, making it less than the Series 2. We probably won’t see a deal like that again until next year, so if you were considering upgrading or just jumping in to the latest model, now’s your time.

How soon can I expect results with the CurrentBody LED mask?

LED therapy is a marathon, not a sprint. The brand says you can see results in as soon as eight weeks. But it really depends on what you’re aiming for. I noticed within just a few weeks that my breakouts were curbed and my skin was a bit less inflamed. But collagen synthesis, which is what softens wrinkles and firms skin, can take time and consistency. I wouldn’t expect to see major results on that front for about three months.

The topic of “is it worth it” is difficult without knowing someone else’s financial situation. But on the LED mask front, I believe this is the best one out there right now. The combination of the 750 LEDs with the MyDose technology is really unique to many of the masks I’ve tested. And it’s also one of the most comfortable to wear too.

Currently, while the device is 20% off, I would definitely say it’s worth it. The $455 price tag puts it on par with a lot of LED masks, which is fantastic when you consider how advanced this one is. Is an LED mask essential to have good skin? No, but it is a great extra tool to have in your toolkit and one that all of our Cosmo editors agree on. And if you are going to drop the money on one, the CurrentBody Series 3 is my favorite.

FYI: CurrentBody also came out with a Series 3 Neck and Décolletage Mask that has all the same MyDose features but for your neck and chest. And if you’re serious about skin health, you can get them both in a discounted Series 3 Mask and Neck Bundle right now for Black Friday. It’s a whopping $300 off, so I wouldn’t wait.

#6768. The 63 Best New Perfumes and Fragrances of 2026

We sniffed, we spritzed, we sprayed. Only the perfumes below left a lingering impression, earning them a spot on our annual best-of list.

Everything smells like vanilla. At least, that’s what perfume naysayers will tell you. And it’s somewhat true: If you’re judging by what’s popular, ubiquitous, or cool with the youth, then sure—vanilla scents and sweet gourmands are still trending.

But hundreds of other fragrance launches in 2026 deserve a spot on your vanity and a spritz on your skin, and many are far less sweet. Gourmands took a turn for the weird and fruity this year, with notes like lychee and rice milk popping up in otherwise innocuous formulas. Woods and ambers continued to reign, as did spice-forward and citrus scents with unexpected depth. Perfumers are meeting our demand for newness in increasingly interesting, artistic ways, and we smelled hundreds of their creations to choose the 63 winners of our annual fragrance awards.

See all the winners of the 2026 Harper’s Bazaar Fragrance Awards, plus quotes from our beauty editors on what makes these formulas worthy of your next blind buy.

#6767. Samantha Morton on Being a Woman in Hollywood: ‘We Are Here as a Family’

The Odyssey costume designer Ellen Mirojnick delivered some of the actress’s remarks on her behalf.

Yesterday evening, The Odyssey star Samantha Morton was unable to attend ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood celebration, remaining at home in London instead. But the honoree had the film’s costume designer Ellen Mirojnick deliver some of her moving remarks on her behalf. Morton reflected on the honor of playing Circe in The Odyssey—and the greater lesson she has learned about what being a woman in Hollywood means, decades into her acting career.

She wrote, “Thank you so much to Nina and ELLE for this amazing honor. And to Ralph Lauren and Bulgari for supporting this wonderful event. My huge thanks to Alex White, Norman Jean Roy, and the wonderful team who made me feel so fantastic at the cover shoot. To Jenny, Nicki, Kat, Billy, Scott, and Ashton for being there for me every step of the way and for helping to make my dreams come true.

“To be even a small part of a phenomenon like The Odyssey was an experience that cannot be matched. Circe is a role that I felt deeply blessed to play, to bring her voice to life for Christopher and Emma and their incredible team, John Papsidera, Ellen Mirojnick, Luisa Abel, and Andrew Jackson.

“And to get to work with my favorite actor in the whole world, Matt Damon, the peerless Matt Damon…the most suave, sophisticated, talented, handsome, generous, kind, and gifted Matt Damon. Thank you for helping me to find Circe on that Scottish hillside and for standing in for me this evening. It takes a village and I am certain this wouldn’t have happened without all of these wonderful people and more…I am so desperately sad not to be able to be there with you all to celebrate.

“I want to congratulate the other amazing women being honored tonight. What an incredibly talented and formidable group. Rosalind, my Harlots sister…you inspire me so much.

“And as women in this industry, we know what we do isn’t easy. Yes, we love it, we are passionate about it and we are fortunate to do it; it’s great when it all comes together. But we know this isn’t always the case and there can be many obstacles and pitfalls along the way in an ever-changing and sometimes cruel business.

“I keep asking myself what it means to be a ‘Woman in Hollywood.’ It was a childhood dream for me to be here. To work in this business. To act in films that would travel the world and be remembered forever. For almost 30 years I have visited and worked here and for a time I called this city home, returning every year to the same house in Beechwood Canyon, a house built by Dolores del Río, the first Mexican movie star, yet I never fully felt that I belonged, that I had ‘made it.’

“Tonight shows me that to truly be a woman in Hollywood is not about location but community. It doesn’t matter where you come from…your race, your faith, your sexuality, your social or economic background. We are here as a family, a community of creatives, and we must support each other, help each other, and fight for our right to work in a safe environment. To be treated fairly and respectfully. To keep pushing for fair and equal pay and parity for female actors and filmmakers. We will get there.

“And ultimately to pass on the baton and because of this I want to thank my beautiful daughters Esmé and Edie for their brilliance and support and the difference their outspoken and courageous generation is making to our glorious industry.

“I dedicate this award to all the women in our community, fighting to carve out their own path and to create, free from fear and exploitation.

Watch Mirojnick deliver an abbreviated version of Morton’s remarks above and read the actress’s Women in Hollywood cover story here.

#6765. Exclusive: The World’s Top Players Look Back on a Wild Year in Men’s Tennis

It was Friday the 13th, and Turin, Italy, the site of the Nitto ATP Finals, glowed with cobalt light as a fingernail moon hung in the air. It looked almost like a Tintoretto painting.

At the Piazza San Carlo, a blue carpet had been laid out lengthwise for the world’s eight best (and currently active) men’s tennis players as fans called out for autographs and selfies. Carlos Alcaraz in Louis Vuitton and Ben Shelton in Ralph Lauren walked among them; missing was the home favorite, Jannik Sinner, who qualified for the field but is sidelined with a knee injury. The scene delivered a surreal, Hollywood-esque half-hour of public stagecraft—paparazzi flashbulbs, police escorts—with all of it designed to celebrate the end of a very notable, and sometimes odd, year in men’s pro tennis.

Speaking of the dreamlike: the evening included an ATP-commissioned portrait session with the photographer Szilveszter Makó, a man who has skyrocketed to industry prominence for having shot multiple covers this year—including for the American, British and Italian editions of Vogue. Makó’s aesthetic itself is rather painterly; photographs as aged frescoes, both cerebral and unusual. Within Turin’s Inalpi Arena, he forged two vignettes with his signature box sets. We stepped in to take a look as Arthur Fils, wearing Balenciaga, was instructed to stand tall and lift his right foot, balancing it on the heel. (“It’s kind of weird, no?” Fils asked, before leaning in.) Makó lensed seven of the eight athletes; due to extenuating circumstances, Alcaraz was unable to stop by the makeshift studio.

But, no matter. In a mad dash between the Principi di Piemonte Hotel, the Piazza San Carlo, a jam-packed van ride across gridlocked roads, and, finally, the Arena, we caught up with all eight players, who together offer an apt representation of the deep and diverse present state of the world’s elite-most men’s tennis. What was discussed: everything from self-reflections to coaching change-ups to cellys to the popularity of the Maldives.

2026 was the biggest year of Zverev’s career: he won his maiden Slam at Roland-Garros, then followed it up with a victory at the US Open. The German also reached the world number 1 spot for the first time (it’s worth noting here that Zverev also holds a super-rare tennis title: an Olympic gold medal, from Tokyo). At 29, he is a half-generation older than the sport’s current dominant duopoly of Sinner and Alcaraz, but if he keeps his current level of play up, he’ll make a strong case for another “Big Three”(the nickname assigned to Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic during their long run of supremacy). Despite the settlement of a domestic abuse lawsuit involving his ex-partner Brenda Patea, a new case was brought to light just a few days ago: the tennis writer Ben Rothenberg reported that Patea has sued Zverev for public misrepresentations. It’s been a career year, but it has to be said that Zverev remains a polarizing figure.

The finest Canadian tuxedo I’ve ever seen.

When you wear head-to-toe denim, yes. You’ve had an incredible year. What worked—and is working—best for you mentally, looking back on it now?

I made a decision with my team last year to change my game style—changing the way we play. I think it was quite a bold move at the age of 29. But we said: it had been working, I’ve had a great career, but it wasn’t working at the final stage of Grand Slams. It hadn’t worked to achieve the dreams and the goals we had. So, sticking to the new game plan, I think that was the biggest thing. Sticking to it and being brave enough to accept it. I think, in the end, it paid off.

Definitely. Two Slams this year, the number one ranking. Are you happy with your game right now, or is there anything you want to improve in 2027?

No, I don’t think I’m complete at all. There are always things you have to improve—and at the end of the day, everybody else is improving, too, so you have to keep with it to stay relevant.

You had some frustration a few weeks ago in Paris in having to defend your number one ranking. Are you still reckoning with that?

I think in Paris it was all just quite new, and I was mentally a little bit tired. There were a lot of new things. And of course, it’s a different kind of pressure. But, I think it’s all settled down, and I’m very happy to be here among the best in the world. It’s an honor.

What’s your vacation plan once the season ends?

Alcaraz—men’s tennis’s brightest star—nicely bookended an otherwise turbulent 2026. The Spaniard, 23, won his first Australian Open all the way back in January, and has enjoyed a surge of recent title wins (in Vienna, Tokyo, and Paris) after returning to the tour from a bout with wrist tenosynovitis that kept him offline for nearly five months. His return at the US Open—where he reached the quarterfinals—brought with it a much-hyped collaboration with Nike’s Cactus Jack line and a tousled new hairstyle. One interesting note going into Turin: Alcaraz has not yet won an ATP Finals, and will be hungry to add that to his resume.

What’s your best 2026 memory off of the court?

Oh, well, I have a couple, to be honest. One of the highlights I had this year was attending the World Cup final. Seeing Spain win the World Cup was unbelievable. So yeah, I’m going to say that! Ferran Torres’s goal, that was the turning point of his career. From that, I would say his stock is really high.

You’ve come back from injury, and you’ve had a strong tail-end of the year, winning Tokyo and Paris. After being hurt, did your mentality change at all? Any hesitation?

I knew that, coming back, I needed matches. I needed competition. I need to feel I was back in the rhythm of competing, and I’m still [building that back]. I need to go out there and feel those nerves of competition. I’m still working on being strong for these difficulties.

With the season ending, what will you try to do in the offseason?

Well, I am not allowed to play golf yet, because my team [won’t let me]. Probably the first thing I’m going to do after the season is over is play golf.

Shelton, 24, had two standout moments on the court in 2026: he defended his Canadian Open title and reached his first Major final at the US Open. Though he lost to Zverev there, it was still a considerable level-up for the Florida-born phenom. Shelton made recent industry news by tapping Juan Carlos Ferrero—Alcaraz’s former coach—to join his team in 2027 (Shelton’s father, Bryan, will remain his coach as well).

You’re bringing on Juan Carlos Ferrero as a coach. Talk us through that decision.

Yeah. Even in the early stages, I think we’ve done a good job of putting together a schedule where I will have two coaches. I don’t want either of them to have to travel 40 weeks a year. So I think we’re putting together a really good formula where they’re both traveling about half the weeks. That’s the ideal scenario for us.

What’s the strongest, most resonant moment you’re taking with you from 2026?

Defending my title in Canada is one. I thought that was the best tennis I’ve played in my career. I didn’t drop a set all week. I was clinical. It was fun for me to see that I can play at that level. But, I have to say, walking out on court for a US Open final and feeling the energy of that stadium on that day, even though I took an L, was pretty special.

I’m just going to play it by ear. I might go on vacation with Arthur Fils, but we’ll see.

The tennis world is happy to see Medvedev, 30, back in elite form. After a less-than-stellar 2025, the lanky Russian has been playing significantly better in 2026, having won four titles and returned to the top 10. Yes, he still has outbursts, and yes, crowds will either go with him on them or boo relentlessly. But that’s just part of the Medvedev Experience. What’s helped on a deeper level: coaching change-ups, and a newfound self-assurance. Don’t forget: Medvedev is a Slam winner (US Open, 2021), a former world number one, and an ATP Finals winner (2020).

Looking back at 2026, what’s the most significant thing you fixed?

What I was looking for was probably finding confidence in myself. Sometimes that requires changing things, and I wanted to take a bit more responsibility. That was probably the biggest fix I managed to make, closer to the end of the year.

Was that rediscovering your old confidence, or was it something new?

Rediscovering in terms of tennis, yes. But more in terms of… I want to say, it’s more like confidence in a tennis life path. I was listening to my old coaches a lot rather than trusting myself fully. So there was always a bit of back-and-forth. Where do I trust them? Where do I trust myself? And now it’s more about trusting myself fully, and then discussing that trust with the team, if that makes sense.

You’re known for your heated interactions with crowds. At this stage in your career, how much of that is just a reaction versus a choice?

It’s never a choice. It’s always a natural reaction.

Any indulgences you’re looking forward to after the season ends?

I have a photo shoot with Lacoste, and then I’m in the Maldives the next day. I would love to go to Hawaii, I don’t know, or wherever. But it’s way too far from where I live.

Cobolli, 24, had the best year of his young career in 2026. His breakthrough: reaching the final of the French Open, where he lost to Zverev in five sets. In Turin, the Italian naturally received the loudest cheers on the blue carpet. With Sinner absent, he’s the home favorite. Cobolli is well-liked on social media, too; the ATP sometimes jokingly calls him their “admin.” He’s had some struggles with fatigue as the season nears its conclusion, but here’s hoping the Florentine can turn on the jets in Piedmont.

At Wimbledon this year, you made some headlines for doing Matheus Cunha’s “surfing” celebration. Should tennis have more cellys?

No, you know why? Two weeks ago, Cunha beat AS Roma. He beat my team, so I’m really pissed with him. [Laughs] But no… I think [for celebrations] if I have something on my mind, I just do it.

You’re the home favorite in Turin. What does that feel like?

It means a lot to me to play here and to win in front of the Italian crowd. Of course, we miss Jannik a lot. He deserves to be here. So I play for him, for the country, for my team, for myself, and for my family. I just want to play for everybody!

Fils, the 22-year-old Frenchman, struggled in the beginning of the year with a back injury that forced him out of the Australian and French Opens. But he had a strong enough summer to qualify for the year-end tournament, winning his first Masters 1000-level title at the Cincinnati Open. In tennis circles, many believe Fils has the natural talent to eventually challenge the Tour’s stalwart top three Sinner, Alcaraz and Zverev. But he’s already matched them if not exceeded them in aura: in Turin, Fils stepped out on the blue carpet in a full Balenciaga look—he has a deal with the brand—and space-like sunglasses. Audiences went wild.

What are you most happy with regarding your play this year?

I’m serving better, moving better. I mean, I knew I was a great competitor. But I didn’t know I could be that good in competitive moments.

When the season is said and done, what’s going to be your first indulgence?

I’m going on holiday in the States, so I think I’m going to go with… having some ribs.

Tell us a little about working with Balenciaga.

They’re changing [internally] now, I know. But I love the brand. It was kind of a dream when I was a kid to sign one day with a huge fashion label. I feel very comfortable wearing them. It’s a new world for me, but I enjoy it.

Tiafoe, 28, has reached the ATP Finals for the first time. It’s testament to his grit and commitment—what he calls a re-established sense of “showing up” day in and day out. “Big Foe,” as he’s endearingly called, has had a productive year; he won his first 500-level tournament in Halle, reached the semis at the US Open, and recorded the fourth-most match wins of any man on Tour. He was all smiles in an expertly tailored Giorgio Armani double-breasted suit on the blue carpet, too.

You’re having a great season. What are you most happy with, not necessarily numbers wise, but in terms of your play?

I think I just found a flow state. I found this peace, and I’m showing up every day. I think sometimes you try to figure out this whole thing of how to get to X to Y to Z, or how to do X, Y and Z together. And it’s kind of just: you show up, man.

Every day looks different, but you just go out there and give your best and be okay with the result. Every time I’ve been able to lay it out there and lost, I was cool with it, rather than having regret that I could have done a little more. I was also focused on my preparation, and once preparation meets opportunity, you get the results.

During the long season, what was a favorite memory away from the court?

I saw the Chris Brown and Usher concert in D.C. and it was out of control. One of the biggest things was getting to meet Matthew McConaughey at the US Open. He’s a special individual.

What are you looking forward to during the break?

Jodar, the youngest man in the Turin field, has been lightning in a bottle this year. He broke men’s tennis’s record for the quickness of his ascent: from his tour debut to hitting the top 10, Jodar needed only 296 days. With that in mind, the Spaniard can be forgiven for speed bumps along the way: a highly publicized outburst at a ball kid during the Shanghai Masters, and a gamesmanship debate around equipment changes. He’s among the youngest of tennis’s new guard—a quarter-generation behind Alcaraz and Sinner, even—and his future feels bright.

So much has been said about the speed of your year, and how quickly you’ve risen. Is there anything you wish would slow down?

Well, I think how it works is that if you do well on Tour, you’re going to have more expectations. That’s something you just have to deal with when you’re doing well. Not every day you’re going to be in a happy mood. But at the end of the day, you just have to handle the situation in the best way possible, and keep focusing on and trying to get better at the game.

What do you do with your limited free time?

I think I’d say spending some time at home and doing some activities in Madrid. Probably, the thing I want to do most is go to the Bernabéu to watch Real Madrid. That’s when I disconnect completely from tennis, and focus on the football game.

#6761. Robert Pattinson’s Hair Is Already 007 Material

Whether you like it or not (or placed bets on Kalshi), Robert Pattinson is our next James Bond. During the years-long process in casting 007, we used our best detective skills to narrow down the field to who would join His Majesty’s Secret Service. And if you were going by hair type alone, well, Pattinson makes a rather compelling case.

Let’s review the canon for a moment. In the 1957 novel From Russia, with Love, Bond creator Ian Fleming describes the spy’s mane thusly: “The hair was black, parted on the left, and carelessly brushed so that a thick black comma fell down over the right eyebrow.”

Pattinson’s hair might be naturally light brown, but a darker ‘do is hardly out of the question for the actor’s upcoming transformation. For his turn as Bruce Wayne in The Batman, he dyed his hair to a darker, almost pitch-black hue. The rest of Fleming’s description fits the actor nicely, particularly the bit about being “carelessly brushed.” In real life, the actor’s hair is rarely anything approaching immaculate. Even at more formal engagements, it tends to retain a certain studied dishevelment, with stray strands escaping an otherwise respectable comb-through. Fleming’s famous “comma,” after all, isn’t a carefully sculpted curl. It’s simply a lock of hair allowed to fall where it pleases, which just so happens to be very on trend in 2026.

We got our first glimpse of the 40-year-old actor taking on the role in a video posted by the official James Bond X account where he’s seen stepping out of the shadows pointing a gun at something (or someone) just outside the frame. It’s hard to tell whether the golden lighting is playing tricks on his hair color, but the accompanying promotional image certainly seems to suggest a shade of black. Plus, his hair’s parted on the correct side.

It’s worth noting that Daniel Craig’s casting as Bond was initially met with considerable resistance, much of it centered on one detail: He’s blonde. Fleming’s Bond, after all, was famously dark-haired, and Craig represented a departure from the physical template established by the novels and previous screen incarnations. We know how that turned out. Craig went on to deliver one of the most celebrated interpretations of 007, proving that a little deviation from the source material needn’t be a deal-breaker.

Pattinson will still need to prove himself to be agile in a tuxedo, nimble behind the wheel, and thirsty for a martini or two, but one thing’s sure: He's got the hair down pat.
