#6760. 40 Years On, the Musée des Arts Décoratifs’ Fashion Collection Remains Ahead of Its Time

An anniversary exhibition revisits key moments from MAD’s history

On my first trip to France in the mid-2000s, the Musée des Arts Décoratifs (MAD) became my go-to destination in Paris for a fashion-museum fix. With each subsequent visit, the intellectualized fashion scene became more saturated, as maisons increasingly invested in their heritage with public-facing venues (Fondation Azzedine Alaïa, Musée Yves Saint Laurent Paris, and Galerie Dior), plus the opening of Palais Galliera’s permanent galleries. As far as I’m concerned, when it comes to fashion exhibitions, the more the merrier. But I remain loyal to my first love. For art and design lovers like myself, it’s hard to top MAD’s interdisciplinary approach—and, of course, that prime Rue de Rivoli address.

This fall, the museum’s self-contained fashion collection—the Musée de la Mode et du Textile (originally Musée des Arts de la Mode)—celebrates its 40th anniversary with an exhibition titled “Look: 40 Years of Fashion at the Museum,” open through April 4, 2027. While the museum’s central hall, the Nef (“nave”), pays homage to 40 of its 70-plus shows by spotlighting a look to represent each, the surrounding galleries invite visitors behind the scenes of an atelier and the museum itself.

“As the custodian of France’s National Fashion Collection, it was really important for us to show people their heritage, as well as the diversity of the collection,” Sophie Lemahieu, the museum’s curator of fashion and textile collections after 1947, told Harper’s Bazaar. Co-curating the exhibition with MAD director Bénédicte Gady, Lemahieu sought to convey the skills of the many professionals who made each garment a reality, as well as the museum workers who care for and prepare them for display.

The multilayered approach represents a consecration of fashion as art—a concept MAD’s Musée de la Mode et du Textile has been instrumental in transmitting since its inception, when such a notion was far from the prevailing opinion. “40 years ago, it was not obvious to have fashion in the museum, even in Paris. There were many curators and art historians who were extremely mad because all these floors could have been used to show Islamic art or other decorative art collections,” said Lemahieu. “It took time to legitimize fashion history as an art history field, but now every museum wants to have fashion exhibitions because they’ve seen how meaningful they can be. People identify with fashion because it’s part of our lives. We all wear clothes.”

For context, MAD was founded in 1864 and contained textiles and fashion prior to the official establishment of the Musée des Arts de la Mode. The decision to formalize its fashion collection was twofold: first, it marked the union of two monumental collections, the Union Centrale des Arts Décoratifs and the Union Française des Arts de la Costume. More broadly, during the 1980s, under President François Mitterrand, the French government began advocating for fashion as national cultural prestige, rather than a purely commercial entity (though it was undeniably one of the country’s leading exports). In 1982, the Louvre’s Cour Carrée courtyard became a designated venue for French ready-to-wear shows, making a powerful global statement. To quote Lemahieu, “Fashion became political.”

For the Musée des Arts de la Mode’s inaugural exhibition, “Moments de Mode” (1986)—which in “Look” is illustrated by a pristine 1760 robe à la française, the oldest garment in the show—MAD pulled out all the scenography stops. Working with theater professionals, curators presented an immersive history of fashion, including a mannequin, clad in a 19th-century cycling suit, in continuous movement on a mechanical bicycle. While today, such a display would never happen due to conservation requirements, it set the tone for MAD’s myriad innovations showcasing garments at their finest.

Another fascinating example from Moments de Mode is MAD’s usage of invisible mounts, which make garments appear as if they are floating. Visitors to Fondation Azzedine Alaïa may recall that these spectral mannequins have become somewhat of a signature for the institution. Lemahieu said this is not a coincidence: “Mr. Alaïa actually came to the exhibition in 1986 and thought this was an absolutely wonderful way to show a dress, so he asked the same person to do the mannequins for his foundation.”

Elsewhere are odes to MAD’s many monographic shows, from its first, Yves Saint Laurent in 1986, to its traveling blockbuster “Christian Dior, Couturier of Dreams” in 2017. Dior is one of the few designers to have multiple MAD exhibitions—another is Schiaparelli, who was the subject of shows in 2004 and 2022. Similarly, MAD staged two exhibitions about the 1980s—in 1989 and 2022. Lemahieu noted in all cases, however, MAD never repeats its approach to the same subject.

She also pointed to several exhibitions conceived by her colleague, Denis Bruna, curator in chief of the Fashion and Textile Department, who favors a more sociological approach. “The Mechanics of Undergarments: An Indiscreet History of the Silhouette” (2013), for example, explored techniques used by women and men to shape their bodies, while “Proper Attire Required: When Clothing Causes a Scandal” (2016), focused on controversies that marked turning points in fashion history.

Nearly all the garments in “Look” were previously featured in their corresponding exhibitions. The one exception is a tricolor bodysuit that Gilles Asquin created for the 2024 Paris Olympics Opening Ceremony (several young designers contributed looks for the momentous event). The garment, which the French National Olympic and Sports Committee entrusted to MAD, is displayed to represent the exhibition “Fashion and Sport, From One Podium to Another,” 2023. Lemahieu said the bodysuit’s inclusion demonstrates how museum exhibitions can open pathways for future donations.

Acquisition, documentation, storage, conservation, and mannequinage (the art of mounting a garment) are some of the internal museum processes discussed in the “How Clothing Becomes a Work of Art: Backstage at the Museum” galleries. Meanwhile, “Backstage: Creating Couture” focuses on inspiration, fabrication, ornamentation, and photography. It’s here where MAD can proudly show the range of its holdings (more than 150,000 pieces from the third century to the present day), which include preparatory sketches, fashion illustrations, embroidery samples, and more. Rarities include a mannequin upon which Madeleine Vionnet draped her fabrics, as well as pleating boards used by Maison Lognon, a historic Parisian pleating atelier founded in 1853.

Running concurrently this fall at MAD are exhibitions dedicated to the Thai court’s fashion evolution, Brazilian photographer Rafael Pavarotti’s cutting-edge imagery, and Marion Delarue’s wearable art created during her residency at the museum. Forty years on, this mix of shows, in scale and subject, has become MAD’s unique strength, as Lemahieu described: “It’s important for us to not just make bigger and bigger exhibitions. We need to be involved in what happens in haute couture, but we also need to be here for young designers and to be aware of what’s happening in fashion socially.” It’s that distinctive cocktail of programming—not to mention all the period-room interiors, jewels, and posters—that still keeps MAD at the top of my Paris museum list after all these years.

#6758. I Got the Love and Dating Life of My Dreams After Transitioning

Forget everything you’ve heard about how hard it is to date while trans. I’m the belle of the goddamn ball.

I’ve been dating since I was 14, several years before my transition and before the guys I dated would see me as a woman. But even back then, I was cognizant of the way men reacted to me instantly—usually it was a cute guy in class who seemed to immediately take a liking to me. The issue was that, as a girl who didn’t present as such, I was often kept a secret, relegated to late-night phone calls and texts or one-on-one hangouts.

As I got older and the men around me became less constrained by the rigidity of small-town surroundings and conservative societal norms, I began to date them more publicly—they’d meet my friends and family and ask me to meet theirs. Still, I knew none of these partners were what I really saw for myself. Now an adult woman who still didn’t present as such, I ultimately wasn’t going out with the kind of men I wanted. Instead, I was dating dudes on the DL—bi men who were keenly interested in the fact that my body was male and others who were in their “experimental” phase.

But I wanted to experience sex and love as a woman—ultimately, I wanted to experience everything as a woman. That would mean not dating men who were trying to repress latent homosexual desires but dating those who were looking for a woman as a partner. I wanted to be courted properly while wearing something fabulous. I wanted autonomy.

During the pandemic, many of us thought about how we wanted to live our lives post-COVID. Trans people came out publicly and began their medical transitions. I happened to be one of them. I came out on my 30th birthday to both my friends and family. I would do the same at work the following week. And once I’d grown my hair and had it braided in an African salon around the corner from my apartment, I decided it was time to come out in my dating life as well—to present as myself on the apps.

That’s when I realized, fairly immediately, something a certain kind of Bud Light–boycotting member of society would hate to hear about trans dating: Men are not only open to but actively pursuing trans women. And no, I’m not talking about the ones who saw me as some kind of novelty—I had zero interest in being an experiment or tourist attraction for dudes who were clearly fetishizing me or looking to recreate a scene from a porno. I’d suffered enough of that already, thanks.

Sure, I encountered a few of those, the ones who’d open with intrusive and inappropriate questions (“Pre-op or post-op?” Block!). But by and large, most men I connected with seemed surprisingly well-versed in being with trans women. These were people who had actual experience dating women like me and wanted more of it, guys who knew how to navigate my body. There’s a stigma that comes with dating while transgender—this idea that it somehow narrows your options or makes you less widely desirable. But as soon as I changed my photos on the apps to reflect my transitioned self, the massive uptick in engagement was instant. In fact, even the dating apps themselves, not just the men on them, were suddenly more interested in me. Raya, which I’d been on a two-year wait list for, let me in the day after I reapplied with new photos in which I presented as my female self.

Not long after the first week or two on the apps, I’d built up a roster of men I was dating regularly—and yes, they all knew about each other (thanks, polyamory). There was Eli the lawyer/writer in an open marriage, Dave the finance bro who lived in a fabulous Upper East Side building and sent Uber Blacks to pick me up, and the NFL player who couldn’t keep his hands off me. Date nights became inventive and impressive, like a food crawl through Chinatown or cocktails at The Carlyle. I garnered attention everywhere I went. Finally, I was dating the way I’d always wanted to date, just like my cis girlfriends and acquaintances.

Pre-transition, I was still getting hit on and my inbox held messages from men on social media, but it always felt like I was something to be embarrassed of. That was no longer the case. Now men were taking me out to crowded, well-known restaurants, picking me up from my apartment, and shooting the breeze with my cis male roommates like a real-life version of New Girl.

I was seeing the way men treated women when they wanted them firsthand. I’d watch the ways my dates would try to impress me—flexing their biceps as I held on, walking to an enviably hard-to-get dinner reservation or the Guggenheim. I’d wake up to music in my Instagram DMs, songs that made an admirer think of me.

What really changed, though, was that these suitors were asking me to be their girlfriend—no more closeted, casual, half-hearted dating. And, eventually, one of them won me over. Nearly four years since my whirlwind dating life began, my now-boyfriend and true love of my life is everything I’d wished for. He’s classically handsome, rugged, tall (in my highest heels, we still aren’t eye level—he’s 6'3"), and while I’ve seen him hoist furniture and move it around like it was nothing (*swoon*), he handles me with such grace and care. We share traditional sensibilities—he wouldn’t let me pay for our meals out for most of our first year together and I always made sure I was in lingerie and coquette-coded dresses when we were together. (Though, of course, he’d be just as happy to see me “in sweatpants, hair tied, chillin’ with no makeup on.”)

I mention all of this to say that I got everything I wanted from transitioning. I live as my authentic self, the one I always pictured somewhere lounging in a man’s lap, a diaphanous dress spread out over my legs, his big arms around me while he kissed me on the forehead. In a world where you can be whatever you want, choose it and chase it.

#6757. The 8 Best Hotels in Santa Fe for a Winter Escape

Whatever expectations you might have for Santa Fe, nothing really prepares you for the magnitude of its beauty. The blue sky is enormous—with impossibly fluffy clouds—stretching on and on until it melts into the distance. The surrounding Sangre de Cristo (“blood of Christ”) mountains are especially striking, named by the Spanish who were spellbound by the peaks that turned a vivid red during sunrise and sunset. There’s the traditional adobe architecture the Southwest is famous for, earth-toned and low-slung, and the piñon-juniper woodlands that add to the landscape’s dreamlike quality. It’s a magical place where chiles and pine nuts are on every menu, and the craft scene is so prolific the city was designated a UNESCO Creative City of Crafts and Folk Art. For travelers who have their sights set on New Mexico’s capital city, the best hotels in Santa Fe celebrate its many riches.

The city’s high-elevation desert climate makes visiting throughout the year a distinct experience. In winter, Santa Fe puts on its party hat and transforms into a holiday snow globe with glowing farolitos and city streets perfumed with piñon pine drifting from kiva fireplaces. Whether you choose to position yourself downtown in proximity to galleries and restaurants, or on the outskirts with wild acreage as your backyard, a winter spent in Santa Fe is certain to be a memorable one.

As you plan your upcoming travels, let Vogue’s guide to Santa Fe’s best hotels, below, serve as motivation to spend the cozy season in the Southwest.

Originally settled over 150 years ago by Jean Baptiste Lamy (the first Archbishop of Santa Fe), this property is now home to a luxury retreat surrounded by 317 acres bordering the Santa Fe National Forest. Guest rooms occupy adobe-style structures, with interiors that lean into the southwestern aesthetic—think, kiva fireplaces, wood beam ceilings, and decor sourced from local artists. The resort’s Adventure Basecamp acts as a meeting point for the day’s excursions, which range from horseback riding and guided hikes to a dedicated Ski Santa Fe experience in the winter.

For travelers who prefer a hotel amidst all the action, Vogue’s Senior Fashion and Style Writer Christian Allaire suggests Rosewood Inn of the Anasazi. “If you’re looking to explore around downtown Santa Fe, there are few better locations than here,” he says. “Situated right on the plaza, it's just steps away from all the action—but you may not want to leave, given how cozy the hotel is! The rooms come with wooden beams and fireplaces, and the restaurant serves up classic New Mexican fare with a modern twist.”

Despite its central location, the property feels like its own world once you step through the hand-painted, carved-wood doors. The interiors pay tribute to ancestral textiles and works by local indigenous artists, and chef Cristian Pontiggia (a James Beard Award semifinalist) blends New Mexico ingredients with global influences.

Set on 57 acres in the Sangre de Cristo foothills, Four Seasons Resort Ranch Encantado is a destination for travelers who want to be completely surrounded by nature (yet still situate themselves a convenient 10 minutes from the downtown area). There are 65 casita-style rooms designed with traditional materials like stucco exteriors, wood beams, and kiva fireplaces—plus private outdoor spaces for taking in bird chirps and the afternoon breeze. Thanks to the surrounding wilderness, activities run the gamut, from jeep tours to snowshoeing. Once you’ve worked up an appetite, head to Terra for roasted poblano leek bisque and an Ember & Adobe reposado cocktail.

With its convenient Barrio de Analco location and jewel box interiors, it’s no surprise The Inn of the Five Graces has won several prestigious design and travel awards over the years. “Each room is a feast for the eyes,” Abbas says, “a tapestry of colorful textiles, mosaic tiles, and handcrafted antiques that combine Southwestern decor with East Indian and Tibetan influences.” (If you fall in love with the decor and want to bring home a souvenir, the owners are also behind the furniture store Seret & Sons, which houses their grand collection.) For travelers staying on the property this winter, don’t miss seasonal activities like holiday tea time, fireside cocoa, and a holiday makers market.

This is not your average motel. This adobe roadside motor court was originally built in 1936 and is now home to one of Santa Fe’s most compelling boutique hotels. El Rey Court sits along old Route 66 and offers 86 rooms on five acres of old-growth gardens. No two adobe rooms are identical, and amenities like a heated outdoor swimming pool, a tree-lined lawn, and al fresco fireplace offer plenty of opportunities to soak in the natural surroundings. Be sure to spend at least one of your evenings at Le Reina, their mezcal and tequila bar that serves up a mean margarita.

This legendary hotel on Santa Fe’s iconic plaza sits on land that has played host to an inn since the early 17th century. La Fonda’s current structure dates back to 1922, and is now a member of the Historic Hotels of America association. Original details like hand-carved beams, terracotta tile, and stained glass skylights set a thoroughly romantic tone, while guest rooms keep it cozy with hand-painted headboards and earth tone decor.

For a home-away-from-home kind of getaway, this welcoming bed and breakfast offers eight rooms tucked among lush gardens. El Farolito is close to the city’s best attractions—to name a few: the historic plaza, farmer’s market, and Georgia O’Keefe Museum—yet sits on a tranquil street away from the bustle. The inn features original artwork throughout, as well as handmade furnishings like wood-carved headboards. And be sure to set your alarm for breakfast: It’s served from 7:30 to 9:30 every morning and can be blissfully enjoyed on the patio next to a gurgling fountain.

Unlike local lodging that leans into Southwest design aesthetics, the ryokan-style accommodations at Ten Thousand Waves offer a distinctly Japanese perspective. The spa is surrounded by 20 acres of piñons and junipers, and guest rooms are situated within a historic ranch house. This retreat is best for wellness-focused travelers, as the private hot tub suites and shared soaking environments are just a few steps away from the rooms. (Don’t sleep on the myofascial facial or shiatsu massage, either.) For cuisine, Izanami is an upscale izakaya serving seasonal small plates meant to share.

#6752. Frog Closures Are the Unexpected Detail Defining Fall Jackets

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s all in the details, from intricate knots to elaborate braiding

There are plenty of ways to make a statement with your outerwear, from an oversize silhouette to a high collar or bold color. But this fall, designers are turning their attention to a smaller detail: the fastening. Jackets featuring decorative knots, elaborate loops, and ornate toggles have emerged as one of the season’s biggest outerwear trends, offering an alternative to standard buttons and zippers.

In particular, frog fastenings are having a resurgence, bringing a fanciful finishing touch to everything from minimalist wool peacoats to tailored military-inspired jackets. Typically constructed from fabric or braided cord, the fasteners consist of a knotted button and a loop. Originally designed to secure garments, the closures have evolved into a more ornamental role with intricate shapes and floral-like designs.

While they may seem new for the season, frog-fastener jackets have a history that spans centuries. In Chinese dress, knotted closures known as pankou have long appeared on garments such as the qipao and tangzhuang. By the 18th and 19th centuries, frogging had also become a feature of European military uniforms, worn by cavalry regiments whose fitted jackets were adorned with braided cords.

Fashion has revisited the detail since then. Oscar de la Renta incorporated frog fastenings into his designs in the 1990s, while Valentino explored versions for its fall 2015 couture collection. More recently, for fall 2026, designers reinterpreted knotted closures: At Kallmeyer, black toggles punctuated a gilded jacquard jacket, while Kim Shui incorporated the detail into fur-trimmed blazers and opera jackets. Meanwhile, labels like Khaite and Ann Demeulemeester embraced military-inspired looks featuring ornamental braiding and embellished fronts.

Today’s store-rack versions range from collarless blazers with understated knots to dramatic outerwear designs featuring detailed cording. Brands like Róhe have introduced contemporary takes on frogging, while Hong Kong–based fashion label Sau Lee has reimagined traditional Tang-style jackets with modern silhouettes.

Rather than reinventing jackets entirely, designers are proving that something as minuscule as a fastening can make a familiar silhouette feel new again for the season. Ahead, shop our favorite takes on the look.

#6750. The 40 Best Wedding Dresses for Every Ceremony Style and Venue

You can plan out the perfect menu and spend hours curating playlists; but when it comes down to it, there’s really just one item that’s front and center on the big day, and that’s your wedding dress. From picking out the right style to managing alterations to juggling multiple options (do you really want a different dress for the ceremony and the reception? For the after-party? How many gowns does one person need?), it’s a lot—even if you’re planning a courthouse affair. We’re here to streamline the process, with our edit of the best wedding dresses you can buy online.

If you don’t have a dream design in mind and are feeling stuck on where to start, you may want to consider your venue. Are you hosting a beach ceremony? If so, opt for breezy, looser styles in airy fabrics that err on the laid-back side to be in line with the seaside setting. (Think: off-the-shoulder styles in shell white or an asymmetrical dress, loosely knit with pearlescent beadwork.) Are you headed to City Hall? Go sleek, modern, and maybe even short—without the confines of a strict dress code, this is your chance to experiment. If you’re planning a more formal fête, you may want to lean into tradition with a bridal look that stars full-skirted organza and floor-sweeping styles. Not all white dresses are created equal.

It starts with getting a sense of what’s out there; so to help kick off your search, we pulled together a range of wedding dresses that’ll suit every setting, dress code, and personal style.

Looking to go traditional? There’s no beating a classic, fairytale-inspired dress. These designs are built to be showstoppers, whether you opt for a bubble-skirt gown from Danielle Frankel or a style with subtle drama by Self-Portrait, Emilia Wickstead, or The OWN Studio.

Sleek, minimalist, and effortlessly elegant, a column wedding dress works for an array of dress codes. Sculptural, contoured versions by Marmar Halim and Safiyaa are perfectly polished for traditional venues, while Simkhai’s sleeveless number seems just right for a city ceremony.

Strapless dresses are an especially lovely option if you’re getting married in a warmer climate, though the silhouette is appropriate year-round. Rachel Gilbert’s corseted gown is great for more formal dress codes, and gives the illusion of a fuller skirt with a hand-draped sash. You can also lean into unexpected shapes with Magda Butrym’s architectural neckline or Balenciaga’s draped design.

For civil ceremonies and backyard weddings that take a more casual approach, why not choose a short-sleeve style? Rixo leans romantic with a v-neckline, ruffles, and floral detailing; Heirlome and Khaite offer modern takes with open backs, while Jacquemus goes asymmetric with a single sleeve.

One-shoulder, off-the-shoulder, fringe trim… the more irregular, the better with this kind of wedding dress, which places emphasis on the neckline and is great if you’re going with a simple updo. Naturally, Vivienne Westwood excels at draping with a sweetheart neckline; for a touch of drama and movement, go with Taller Marmo. Or if you need a courthouse look, Altuzarra’s shift dress has you covered.

For brides who consider sleeves a non-negotiable (or are hosting a wedding in a colder climate), a long-sleeved wedding dress should read as elegant and assured, never frumpy. Brandon Maxwell makes the case for demure sensuality with a body-skimming crepe gown, while Bernadette keeps things slightly casual with a midi silhouette.

Whether you’re exchanging vows at City Hall or simply not convinced you want a full-length gown, a tea-length dress is worth considering. Look to Prada and St. Agni for easygoing options suited to warm-weather nuptials, or Leo Lin for a more formal take that works in any season. (This is the occasion to pay particular attention to your bridal shoes; they’ll be on full display!)

Torn between a ball gown wedding dress and something a little more on-trend? Consider a drop waist, one of bridal’s most popular silhouettes. Markarian offers a classic look with a fitted bodice and an off-the-shoulder neckline; Ilkyaz Ozel suits the bride who wants to make an entrance; Danielle Frankel brings a whimsical touch in flowy organza; Amsale turns heads with its double-tiered skirt.

A halter neckline channels the pared-back ease of ’90s minimalism. In liquid satin or fluid silk, styles from Givenchy, Reformation, Ralph Lauren, and Halfpenny London feel aisle-ready—and they’re just as fitting for the dance floor, so consider this your ceremony and reception look in one.

If all you want from your wedding dress is a little something special, look to designs that stand out from the crowd with some element of the unconventional. Whether it’s a lace Dior gown embroidered with bows, Clio Peppiatt’s crystal-studded maxi with a draped scarf neckline, or Christopher John Rogers’s sequin paillette-embellished, mermaid-like gown, the appeal is in the details.

What should brides look for in a wedding dress?

Start by getting to know the many (many) wedding dress silhouettes, from ball gowns and A-lines to mermaid styles and beyond; your ceremony setting will likely help narrow things down. From there, look to fabrics. Silk and satin are classics that, depending on the style, can be both structured and soft (though beware wearing them in hotter climates, as they’re more prone to showing sweat stains), while airy materials like chiffon, organza, and tulle offer a delicate look.

It’s also a good idea to have a few wedding dress designer names in your back pocket to reference in your research. Oscar de la Renta, Danielle Frankel, Vivienne Westwood, and more are Vogue favorites, and you can find many of them online at trusted retailers like Net-a-Porter, Neiman Marcus, and Bergdorf Goodman. One last thing: If you’re shopping online for your special day, don’t forget to double- and triple-check the shipping and returns policy to avoid surprise fees.

Making such a consequential purchase from the comfort of your couch can feel like a risk—and if you can, it doesn’t hurt to try on your dream look in a store before you buy—but there are benefits to wedding dress shopping online. For one, you’ll have a clearer idea of the cost upfront and can filter by price; it’s also easier to browse by style, material, and even length. Not to mention, if you’re shopping with time constraints, it’s more convenient to see products that are in stock and ready to ship, taking out the guesswork and minimizing delays.

When should brides order wedding dresses (and when should alterations begin)?

While the general rule of thumb is to buy your gown eight to nine months before the wedding day, online shopping offers a little more flexibility when it comes to speedier delivery. Getting the purchase done early also allows more wiggle room for alterations; experts say to book those well ahead of the 10-week pre-wedding mark.

Should brides buy two wedding dresses for the ceremony and reception?

This one’s completely up to you—every bride and every ceremony is different. If you’re on the fence, why not consider a bridal gown rental? The practice is rising in popularity and is a smart solution for anyone who wants multiple looks but doesn’t want to be stuck with multiple gowns (or, at the very least, shoulder the cost of multiple gowns).

What are the most popular wedding dress styles and silhouettes?

The classics are classics for a reason: A-line silhouettes and ball gowns, mermaid silhouettes and fit-and-flares, and sophisticated column silhouettes remain bridal dress mainstays. But lately, drop waists, corseted bodices, and bias-cut styles, along with shorter hemlines for civil ceremonies and receptions, are seeing a surge in popularity. The best shape ultimately depends on your venue, dress code, and how you feel in your chosen piece, so be sure to try on a few shapes before committing to the final look.

Robert Pattinson is the next James Bond, and Florence Pugh is throwing her hat in the ring for the opportunity to star alongside him—not as a Bond girl, but as the villain.

The East of Eden actress attended ELLE’s 2026 Women in Hollywood event on November 16 and was introduced by Dune: Part Three director Denis Villeneuve, who is also helming the next Bond film starring Pattinson. During her acceptance speech, Pugh took a brief moment to shoot her shot at starring in the next 007 movie.

“I sent Denis a message this morning. I said, ‘Congrats on finding your Bond. Nice catch. Any villains with the size of 5’4”?’” she told the audience, who laughed at the joke. “Anyway, I’m reminding you just in case!”

The joke was a timely one—just earlier that morning, Pattinson was announced as the lead of the next Bond film, after several outlets reported that actors like Josh O’Connor, Nicolas Hoult, Callum Turner, and Jack Lowden auditioned for the role. Now, the speculation has turned to who will star opposite him as the female lead, a.k.a. the Bond girl. Pugh’s name has been on some prediction lists, but she seems to have her sights set on a different character.

Elsewhere during Pugh’s Women in Hollywood speech, she thanked all the people who assisted her journey as an actress, telling those in attendance, “I think of the crews I’ve been lucky enough to work with, who create the space and the stage so I can do what I do comfortably. I think of the casting directors at the beginning of my career, who took a risk arguing for me, claiming that it didn’t matter that I had no qualifications and only one film credit. Or for the dressers, who would fib and say there was a costume malfunction when they could see I hadn’t had enough time to eat my lunch—this was pre-SAG membership. So don’t panic, SAG. Or to the glam teams all over the world who join because they believe in you and what you do. The makeup artists and hair stylists who wash and clean brushes well into the night just for you, tomorrow at 5 A.M.”

“I think of all of these people who protected me on my journey,” Pugh added. “And it would not have been possible without every single one of them. Just in case you’re listening now and you’re not aware how grateful we are and how important you are, I just received an ELLE Women of the Year honor, and I didn’t get here on my own. I only took stock in myself because I could see you doing it for me first.”

#6748. Sorry to My Sweatpants, But These 8 Thanksgiving Outfits Are Just as Comfortable and So Much Chicer

Pass the pie and the compliments, please.

Thanksgiving is just a couple of weeks away. Aside from figuring out which dish you’re going to bring to the gathering (Mashed potatoes! Stuffing! Pumpkin pie!), you’re also charged with finding the perfect outfit. Not one look fits all occasions; it’s heavily influenced by the caliber of the celebration. Is the table set with fine china and crystal glassware, or are you watching the football game over finger food? You also have to consider who’s in attendance. If it’s a group of your girlfriends, you might opt for a flirty dress and save the knit sweater for a family brunch.

To take something off your plate and leave room for all that food, we’ve curated a lineup of eight versatile and effortlessly chic Thanksgiving outfit ideas for all types of occasions. Each one can be achieved by reaching for simple style combinations, so keep scrolling for editor-approved inspiration—but remember that the ideal look is one you feel most comfortable and confident in.

Styling a long, draped sweater dress with heeled boots is always a good idea. For an extra cozy look, consider a ribbed style featuring intentional details, like a turtleneck and asymmetrical hemline. Belts, clutches, and jewelry help dress it up.

This is the perfect in-between look for a semi-dressy dinner. The bold coat—whether faux fur, color-blocked, or fringed—elevates the ensemble when paired with sleek, closed-toe pumps. You can fill in the gaps with virtually any other basics, including denim, tees, and slouchy bags.

If a game of football and an afternoon nap on the couch is in your future, then slip on a pullover sweater and track pants. Wear a T-shirt underneath and maybe swap your dress shoes for casual sneakers. In a matter of seconds, you can master a laid-back outfit change.

Thanksgiving is a day meant for cozy vibes, so slip on your favorite fleece-lined slippers or booties. Pair them with a warm-toned flannel, and dress it up (just a smidge!) with relaxed jeans and a suede coat.

Make a scene this holiday season with a bold, printed dress and over-the-knee boots. The shorter the hemline and taller the footwear, the more dramatic the final look.

Sometimes, less is more. A coordinating sweater-and-pants combo looks instantly polished. If your look is light and airy, add visual interest with dark, moody shoes and accessories and vice versa.

When two aesthetics clash, fashion magic is created. A feminine ruffled dress directly contradicts a heavyweight bomber jacket, making it an intentional and trend-forward look.

Slip a pair of sheer tights underneath your favorite skirt to give the outfit a little oomph. From there, you can let your fashion imagination run wild and reach for everything from timeless coats to loud animal prints.

#6745. Kate Middleton Shopped From Brentwood to Belgravia for Her Royal Tour

Last night, the Prince and Princess of Wales took to the red carpet for this year’s Earthshot Prize Awards, the centerpiece of their three-day tour of Mumbai and New Delhi. The ceremony awarded five environmental projects—tackling everything from forever chemicals in France to the protection of marine life in the Pacific Islands—over $1 million each to further their work. Making her first appearance at the event since she travelled to Boston in 2022, Catherine wore a hand-embroidered anarkali by Mahima Mahajan, which she is believed to have purchased for a modest—at least by royal standards—$892 from Lilly’s Boutique in Essex. (Perhaps during her visit to The Forward Trust in nearby Southend-on-Sea back in September?)

But this morning, on the final day of their trip, the Kate Middleton we know was back on more rarefied ground, stepping out in a tailored, fit-and-flare dress of cherry-red wool crepe by Sloane Street-based designer Emilia Wickstead, priced at $2,461. From Brentwood to Belgravia, then; two very different sides of the British retail landscape, both represented in the same suitcase. Alongside her trusty suede Manolo Blahniks and coordinating DeMellier Small Hudson bag were the additions of a hand-embroidered shawl and beaded bracelet, presented to her during a visit to the Chanakya School of Craft in Mumbai, which trains women from underserved communities in traditional Indian techniques and has paired up its graduates with the likes of Dior, Fendi, and Valentino. The Princess then traveled to the Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital, known for offering affordable care to women from all walks of life.

Whether Catherine has another outfit change in her suitcase—she and William are due to attend a bilateral meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi before returning to Windsor—remains to be seen. What this trip has made clear, though, is that the future Queen Kate Middleton is as intentional with her wardrobe as ever. Consider the rewears—sustainable choices, yes, but also ones that avoid headlines about new purchases that might distract from the work at hand—or the range of price points, from relatively accessible DeMellier handbags to priceless jewels from the royal collection. Above all, though, is her continued ambassadorship of British fashion—a concept as ever-changing and expansive as the country’s identity itself—as demonstrated by an Indian-designed dress bought on an English shopping street.

#6744. Milan Laser’s Black Friday Deal Takes 60% Off Laser Hair Removal, and I've Never Seen a Discount This Good

Did you know you can get in-office beauty treatments on sale during Black Friday? In fact, it’s my secret for getting a good deal on things like Botox, skin lasers, and facials that I would already be buying full-price later in the year. And there’s no time like winter to get your beauty treatments, when your skin is out of the sun and mostly hidden beneath thick layers of coats and scarves.

One of the best deals I’ve seen so far this season is for Milan Laser, a spot that our editors just started trying in NYC that’s available with 400+ clinics across 38 states in the U.S. Right now, through November 28, Milan Laser is offering 60% off all body areas for laser hair removal. In all my time as a beauty editor, I’ve never seen such a good deal on laser hair removal in general, let alone an in-office service.

Let me explain laser hair removal first. In a laser hair removal session, your provider will use a handheld laser device that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) all across your skin where you want less hair to grow. The laser uses concentrated beams of light to target the melanin in your hair follicle and destroy it using heat. This slows down hair growth and can even prevent future growth for a limited time. IMO, laser hair removal is the key to super-smooth, clear-looking skin from head to toe.

Although the lasers are stronger and don’t require as much upkeep as an at-home laser hair removal device, they can be pretty expensive. But with this solid 60% off deal, it really cuts down on the cost. To get the deal, sign up with your name, phone number, and email address and make an appointment at your nearest location (reminder: there are more than 400 around the country, so there’s likely one wherever you are, not just in big cities!). At your appointment, you’ll have a consultation about the right package and treatment for you based on your skin type and goals.

What’s super cool is that Milan Laser offers something I’ve never seen before: an Unlimited Package, which gives you a lifetime guarantee and unlimited sessions per body area and free touch-ups for life. You won’t have to worry about not having enough to get the desired effect you want, because remember, laser hair removal isn’t truly permanent and will require touch-ups. You also need quite a few appointments depending on your hair type. Some with thick, coarse hair could need up to 16 appointments, while those with fine, thin hair might only require eight. It’s really personal, which is where an unlimited package can take away some of the stress.

I usually shy away from recommending deals with providers you’ve never tried before (like grabbing a cheap Groupon), but because you get a free consultation first, it takes some of the stress out of figuring out if this is the right place for you. And Milan Laser is more than just a random med spa. They perform more than 90,000 laser hair removal treatments every month across all of their locations, so it won’t feel like you’re walking into a place that isn’t experienced. They also use only licensed medical professionals (and have a physician overseeing everything) to ensure safety.

If you were ever considering laser hair removal, now is the time to do it too. In the summer, it can be difficult to keep up with treatments when your skin is inevitably exposed to the sun. While you’re bundled up and stuck inside this winter, laser hair removal treatments can make you feel one step closer to warm days.

This deal only lasts until November 28, so make sure to book your appointment ASAP at one of Milan Laser’s 400+ locations.

#6742. Julianne Moore Says Her Fellow ELLE 2026 Women in Hollywood Honorees Are ‘So Effing Good’

When Julianne Moore accepted her ELLE Women in Hollywood honor, she used her time onstage to not only thank Jesse Eisenberg for taking a chance on her and casting her to star in The Debut, but also to spotlight the wealth of talent among her fellow honorees.

Moore took the stage at the event, which took place at The Four Seasons Beverly Hills on November 16, and praised the director for being willing to tell his life story from a woman’s point of view.

“Jesse wrote me the part of a lifetime, and now he’s running around, telling everybody that I’m the only person who could do it,” she said during her speech, which Eisenberg introduced her for. “I didn’t know this when we were shooting The Debut, but this story and the character of Mona are based on Jesse’s experiences in community theater as a kid in New Jersey....What was evident to me when I read it was how beautifully Jesse had written a female character that was at the center of a narrative.”

Moore continued, “To be very clear: A man wrote a screenplay about his personal journey and transmuted his experience into the body of a middle-aged woman. He didn’t ask me to play the mean mom, or the ex-wife, or the ‘attractive but she doesn’t know it’ girlfriend. (We all know that part, right? ‘Oh, I don’t know how beautiful I am; I just don’t know.’) He wrote me the part of the lead, a part he could’ve played beautifully himself. He did what female actors crave—he put me in the center of the narrative. I will always be so grateful to you for that.”

In the latter part of her speech, Moore recognized the talent of all the other ELLE Women in Hollywood honorees.

“Florence [Pugh], when I saw you for the first time in Midsommar sobbing on the phone, I was like, ‘She is effing good.’ Samantha [Morton], dragging that body around in Morvern Callar, I was like, ‘She is effing good.’ Elizabeth [Debicki] as Princess Diana—how did you even do that? So effing good!” she gushed. “Carrie [Coon] in the first second of Liberation, so heartbreaking and effing good! Penélope [Cruz], from the moment I saw you as a teenager in Jamón Jamón and then watching you say, ‘Don’t touch me!’ in La Bola Negra, so effing good. Rosalind [Eleazar] coming out of the bathroom after doing coke and talking to Chris Rock [in Misty Green], all glassy-eyed, I was like, ‘so effing good.’ Inde [Navarette], completely committed and imaginative in absolutely outrageous circumstances. I was like, ‘She is so effing good.’ All of you are effing great. I mean it. I am so honored to be among you and know you as my peers.”

#6739. An Inside Guide to Kate Middleton’s Royal Tour Wardrobe in India

India had sat at the top of Kate Middleton’s bucket list ever since she married into the royal family in 2011. Or so said Prince William during their 2016 tour of the subcontinent, for which the then Duchess of Cambridge packed a wardrobe that brought together the fashion heritage of both India and the country she represented.

First came an Alexander McQueen dress, its paisley print drawing on the textile traditions of India and Persia, followed by a pink-and-pistachio tunic dress by Mumbai-based designer Anita Dongre, worn to play cricket at the Oval Maidan with children supported by local charities. Then along came a Jenny Packham gown, hand-beaded by Indian artisans, to a Bollywood gala, and a blue-and-white embroidered sheath dress by Cumballa Hill-born designer Naeem Khan for a visit to the Taj Mahal. Together, the looks offered Kate’s ever-clear understanding of clothing as a diplomatic tool.

Catherine, the Princess of Wales, wearing Alexander McQueen at the Taj Hotel in Mumbai, 2016.

Catherine, the Princess of Wales, at the Oval Maidan in Mumbai, 2016.

A decade on, the couple returned to India on Monday morning, where Prince William hosted the sixth Earthshot Prize summit and awards ceremony in Mumbai. The annual Earthshot Prize gives £1 million ($1.3 million) each to five winners tackling some of the world’s most pressing environmental problems, and India has produced more finalists than any other country since its founding in 2020. It was Catherine’s first appearance at the event since Boston in 2022, while the inaugural Children’s Earthshot Awards provided familiar territory for the princess, whose charitable work has long focused on the next generation.

Beyond the prizes, though, the Prince and Princess have undertaken a series of engagements across Mumbai (and New Delhi), highlighting the cultural ties between Britain and India, including cricket, film, and, of course, fashion. For her last appearances, Kate has also turned to favorite brand Edeline Lee, whose signature bubble-flou fabric can be scrunched into a suitcase and spring back to life without a crease.

Scroll down to see how Kate Middleton approaches diplomatic dressing 10 years later.

Prince William wearing a Manish Malhotra bandhgala, while Kate opted for an anarkali by New Delhi-based designer Mahima Mahajan, paired with a necklace and earrings from Queen Elizabeth II’s emerald tassel suite and a burgundy velvet Prada minaudière.

Wearing a tailored Emilia Wickstead dress with suede Manolo Blahnik pumps.

More tailoring, this time by Edeline Lee, and paired with eye-catching architectural earrings by Chalk.

Wearing a blue linen suit by Gabriela Hearst, which had an outing earlier this year at Wimbledon.

In a Veronica Beard blazer over cropped Alexander McQueen trousers and Camilla Elphick flats.

#6736. Fall Is Almost Over, So I Rounded Up the 7 Celebrity Outfits I Still Want to Copy

Like much of the TikTok generation, I spend way too much time looking for style inspo on social media. While that sometimes means letting the dishes pile up in favor of a few extra minutes of scroll time, I rarely miss a street-style moment. Whether it’s Hailey Bieber in a date-night outfit or Taylor Swift in this season’s hottest color combination, I’ve been stowing away fall outfit inspiration for the final stretch of the season.

Hollywood’s cool girls are squeezing every last wear out of fall, wearing silk midi skirts, sheer tops, and cape-like scarves. Beyond fall essentials like trench coats and dark-wash denim, they’re also reaching for this year’s breakout trends, including maraschino-cherry-colored accessories and striped pullover sweaters, keeping their seasonal rotation fresh before winter takes over.

While I can’t recreate every ensemble on the internet, I can round up the seven autumn outfits most on my mind, ranked by how eager I am to make them my own before the temps drop for good. Keep reading for late-fall outfit inspo to carry you into the holiday season.

On the set of Die Alive, Zoë Kravitz made a case for laid-back elegance and an unexpectedly bright fall color choice. The slinky midi skirt is polished, while the basic gray tank is casual. The trench coat makes the outfit perfect for chilly weather, with a pair of chocolate pumps elevating the style. Consider this your go-to look for weekend brunch plans and cocktails with the girls alike.

Selena Gomez put a fresh spin on the capsule wardrobe, creating a monochromatic outfit using closet staples, including sleek capris, mesh pointed-toe heels, and a quilted cinched bag. However, instead of a basic black tee, she reached for a sheer iteration, turning the simple ensemble into a fresh and fun look. To pull it off for a chilly night, I’d add a leather bomber jacket.

Kristen Bell managed to wear just about every style trend at once—without it looking like a slop wardrobe. Her striped pullover served as the base, with coordinated fall-coded colors sprinkled throughout the rest of her outfit. Her dark-wash, wide-leg jeans reminded me why denim is an autumn classic, and I officially want her glove flats. However, it was Bell’s cherry-red beanie and merlot Chanel handbag that injected personality into her look.

I’m all about a cozy fall wardrobe, but when date night rolls around, I want something a bit more elevated and sleek. Ashley Graham understood the assignment, wearing a silky plunge halterneck top and draped, gray trousers. While she opted for open-toe sandals, pointed, closed-toe pumps can beat the chill.

Karlie Kloss’ chic look is a nod to office wear. Her polished autumnal look features closet basics, including a white button-up shirt, above-the-knee skirt, and ballet flats. Kloss added an extra dose of flair by intentionally draping a black shawl across her shoulders, making it the perfect look for strolling Fifth Avenue and museum hopping alike.

Sometimes the best looks are the simplest. Daisy Edgar-Jones layered a classic white T-shirt underneath a sapphire-blue trench coat, taking a closet basic and elevating it with an unexpected twist. Light-washed, straight-leg jeans elongated her frame, and timeless black pumps turned a casual look into a polished ensemble.

Elizabeth Debicki played with fall textures, reaching for a bold leopard-print turtleneck sweater and slick leather pants. Leopard print is both timeless and trendy, which makes it especially easy to style. It’s the ideal outfit for a night on the town, perfectly cozy yet fashion-forward.

#6735. Leighton Meester Is Still Having Fun

Nearly 20 years after Gossip Girl, the Guarding Stars actress is just glad to be here.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

When Netflix released the trailer for its new holiday movie, Guarding Stars, with Leighton Meester in a lead role opposite Jared Padalecki, better known as Dean from Gilmore Girls, it was catnip for millennial women everywhere. “Blair is back on my screen and I’m seated,” one commenter wrote, referencing Gossip Girl’s Blair Waldorf, the role that made Meester famous. “Put Leighton in anything and I shall watch it,” remarked another. Others chimed in with “Inject this straight into my veins” and “We’re all showing up for Leighton right???”

It’s been nearly 20 years since the September 2007 premiere of Gossip Girl, when Meester won our hearts as the sharp-witted, immaculately coiffed queen of the Upper East Side, and she says now that she’s just as happy as we are that she’s still appearing on our screens. “I’m so lucky. I think about it every day, how so many people don’t get to do what they want to do. It’s so wonderful and rare,” Meester tells me over Zoom from her home office in Los Angeles. “Obviously, there are lots of elements that are really hard. Sometimes it’s negative 20 degrees, it’s muddy or cold or raining, and you’re sitting in a tent, trying to warm your hands. But to me, overall, it’s pretty damn glamorous.”

In Guarding Stars, which is based on the 2022 novel The Bodyguard by Katherine Center and drops on Netflix today, Meester plays a no-nonsense bodyguard charged with protecting one of the most famous actors in the world (Padalecki) while he visits his family in Montana during the holidays. The catch is that, in order to keep the actor’s mom from worrying about him, she must pretend to be his girlfriend. You can see where this is going…but unlike your typical Hallmark-esque tale, Guarding Stars also features action scenes as Meester’s character protects her charge from a stalker. There’s an explosion; there’s a horse race scene. “I’m really proud of it,” she says. “It has all the stuff that I like in a movie. There’s action, there’s romance, there’s definitely comedy, and it feels very cozy, like a place you want to live and stay.”

In a way, Meester manifested the role. “I feel like I somehow summon things,” she says, telling me about a junket where she was asked what sorts of projects she was looking to take on in the future and she mentioned the genre. “I was like, ‘I’d like to do something where there’s action.’ And then, right away this came about.” She did many of her own stunts in the film. “I got to ride a horse—I got to run and jump in-ground explosive thing that blows up—and I also got to flip a stunt person and do some wrestling.” (Near the beginning of the film, her character flips Padalecki’s character onto the ground to showcase her skills when he doubts her ability as a bodyguard.) “I’m pretty sure the stunt person can do a backflip from standing, so it wasn’t really me,” Meester says, “but it still felt super powerful.” (The horse stunt, however, was less of a confidence booster: “Horses don’t respect me, and I learned that, but that’s okay,” she adds.)

They filmed last winter in Calgary, Canada. “I remember the cameras would freeze and they’d be like, ‘We can’t film,’ because it was 25 below Celsius,” she says. “But you get so much cinematic value from shooting in actual snow. A lot of the time, winter scenes are not shot in the cold. You do it in June and there’s pretend snow on the ground and you’re wearing a sweater even though it’s sunny and hot. This was truly cold and I think you can tell the difference.” But the frigid temperatures did require some creative costuming. “The wardrobe department was very prepared,” she adds. “In every scene, you have to understand, I was wearing at least four pairs of pants, all layered on top of one another, and then multiple pairs of socks.”

She’s hoping the film will make its way into the holiday movie lexicon. “We could use a Christmas classic this year,” she says. “And it feels very much like no matter what you’re looking for in a movie to cozy up with, this kind of has it. I would tell people it’s a Christmas cowboy action Hollywood rom-com—it’s kind of just all those things mixed together in a beautiful garland of a film.”

Blissfully, Guarding Stars is just the first project starring Meester on the horizon. She will also soon appear in Basic—her first theatrical release in years—another rom-com written and directed by Chelsea Devantez that premiered at South by Southwest earlier this year and will hit theaters in February. According to Meester, in Basic, she plays “a basic bitch” who does stand-up and fights with her co-star Ashley Park over a man they both dated. “She wears workout gear 24/7, drinks matcha all day, and speaks in hashtags—that’s who she is,” she says. I joke that it’s somewhat of a return for her—Blair wasn’t basic per se, but she could certainly be a bitch. “Somehow it comes easy to me,” Meester says with a laugh. “Don’t know why!” She notes that two of the characters she played in recent guest-starring roles—as a “try-hard” influencer on Nobody Wants This and as a “girl boss” on I Love L.A.—are also quite basic. “I guess I just really like doing it,” she shrugs.

As she did with Blair, Meester manages to give nuance to the women she portrays. “I try to wade through and find common ground and humanity and dignity within a character and relate to it,” she says. “I often start with, how can I bring myself into this so that I can embody this person? And somehow through the course of playing a character, I find her within myself and I’m like, ‘Oh, actually I have this inside of me.’ So we sort of find each other.”

I’m curious what she thinks of the “she’s back,” “Leightonaissance” narrative that seems to emerge every time she’s cast in a new role. She says the warm reaction from fans is nice and she doesn’t have a negative association with it, but she also doesn’t really feel like she left. “I have done many shows and projects through the years, but I think maybe they just weren’t as visible,” she explains. “They weren’t seen or loved as much.” Even after having kids, she returned to work when her first child was 6 months old. “So, I didn’t take years off or anything,” she notes.

It’s all part of riding the waves of Hollywood. “Anything that I’ve done, I’ve definitely wanted it to be seen,” Meester says. “Like I’ve been on a couple shows that I was like, ‘Oh, I’m really proud of this. I want people to see it.’” She cites Making History, a time-travel comedy that aired on Fox in 2017 for one season, and Good Cop/Bad Cop, another comedy—this one about a family of detectives—that premiered on The CW in February but was canceled after an eight-episode run, as two projects she wishes would have gotten more attention.

I ask if being married to a fellow actor—Adam Brody, her husband of 12 years—helps her weather the ups and downs in the industry. “Yes, I think it does help, but I also feel like he’s the best person in the world, so no matter what job either of us did, I would think the world of him,” she gushes. “But I do think that having that in common is really nice. It gives you a shorthand of being able to talk about it and support each other, for inspiration and input, and just an ongoing dialogue about what it all means.” I tell her that, in a recent interview with ELLE, Brody was asked what he’s learned from being married for over a decade, and I’d like her to answer the same question. She says she’s been most surprised by how it just keeps getting better. “It’s amazing that when you marry someone, you’re so, so, so in love and you think of the future and you fantasize and talk about it and plan, but then you find yourself in the future and somehow you’re even more in love,” Meester says. “The intimacy and the love and the depth of the relationship is that much more, and you’re like, ‘I never thought that I could love you more.’ Life is filled with ups and downs and going through everything together, you get closer and it’s kind of hard to believe that’s possible.”

“I know that I felt this way when I met him, but even more so now, my life is better living it with him,” she continues. “And to be loved and understood by somebody, especially when you think the world of them, it’s kind of surreal and it’s the best thing in the world.” I mention that losing their home in the devastating Los Angeles wildfires in January 2025 was probably one of those hard things that made them stronger. “We are very, very lucky because we have each other and that’s the main thing,” she says. “Actually, that’s the only thing, full stop, that we all have each other. It’s just true that nothing else matters.”

When it comes to Meester’s enduring popularity, it’s not just Gossip Girl that holds lasting appeal. Her debut solo album, Heartstrings, released in 2014, is also beloved online. I ask her if she has plans to release more music. “I have been writing and actually recording music over the years. I took a beat last year, but I’d really like to wrap it up and put it out,” she says. “So, I do have new music to put out, but when that will be, I have no specifics.”

Before we part, I tell her I have to give the people what they want and ask whether she would ever reprise the role of Blair Waldorf. “I’ve been asked this exact question forever, but I never have a good answer because I just am always like, ‘I never say never because I don’t know,’” she says. “Obviously that character meant something to me. And I’m grateful that it meant something to other people. So you never know, but I really just don’t know.” She is aware that Cecily von Ziegesar, who wrote the Gossip Girl book series the show was based on, is currently writing a new standalone sequel novel called Blair; in fact, Meester says she has already read the first seven chapters. I say that perhaps it, too, will be adapted into a show, which would give her the chance to play Blair now. But all Meester does is smile.

Whatever role comes next, she seems content so long as they keep coming. “I’m sure that this is cliché at this point, but every time I finish a job, I don’t know what my next job is,” she says. “There’s nothing that’s guaranteed, so every time you get a role, you’re like, ‘I get to do this again. Here we go.’” Every part is a chance to put herself in someone else’s shoes and see what happens. “I’m like, would I want to be a detective? No, but I would like to play one. Would I want to be a bodyguard? Probably not, I want to play one. And so it’s just truly playing make-believe all the time,” Meester says. “To be an actor is such a dream, and it’s never lost on me. I’m almost nostalgic about it because I can’t believe I still get to do this. Not to sound like a crazy person, but sometimes before I do a scene, I will tell myself, ‘This is my dream, and my life, in one way or another, has led to me being able to be there when they yell ‘action!’”

#6733. Suki Waterhouse Has Been Dropping James Bond Clues for Months

In an interview in the December issue of British Vogue, Judi Dench, of M fame, suggested that the next James Bond should be “a young actor we’ve not yet heard of.” There has, of course, been no shortage of speculation about who might inherit the role of 007 since Daniel Craig bowed out following the release of No Time to Die in September 2021, with Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O’Connor (bless) all touted as potential successors. But, lo and behold, it has just been announced that the lead in the new Denis Villeneuve-helmed era of the spy franchise will go to little-known up-and-comer Robert Pattinson.

And perhaps it should have been obvious all along, thanks to the woman on his arm: his wife, Suki Waterhouse. In the two years since releasing her second studio album, Memoir of a Sparklemuffin, the singer has cultivated a vintage wardrobe of Penny Lane coats, flares, and newsboy caps. But around June of this year—when she stepped out in New York wearing a Saint Laurent tuxedo jacket, cycling shorts and patent pumps, perhaps just as Pattinson was starting his own campaign for the role—Suki Waterhouse took a dramatic style pivot, swapping her bohemian signatures for something altogether more cold-blooded.

Consider also the outsized Zimmermann blazer she threw over a lingerie-strapped bodice for a Manhattan outing in September; the almost-transparent lace minidress she wore to the Venice Film Festival that same month; and the cut-out Michael Kors bodycon dress she chose for the CFDA Awards just two weeks ago. The Pattinson-Waterhouse household would doubtless have been bound by some of the world’s most punishing NDAs, but as any spy worth their double-O status knows, secrets hide in plain sight.

All this is to say: while the role of Bond girl has yet to be cast, might we suggest a woman you’ve definitely heard of?

#6732. How ‘Rivals’ Created an Age-Gap Relationship We’re Actually Rooting For

R ivals has returned to our screens, and Rutshire’s residents are hornier than ever. But Rutag fans might have to hang on a little longer to see them enter their relationship era. Frustrating? Not necessarily, as maybe this intense slow-burn is exactly the reason Rivals has managed to create an age-gap relationship we’re actually rooting for.

There is a lot of awareness around age-gap couples in pop culture right now, and audiences seem very done with the classic younger woman, older man dynamic. Movies like A24’s Babygirl and Amazon’s The Idea of You have gone some way toward challenging outdated tropes around age-related power dynamics, but that still doesn’t erase how Hollywood handled things in the past (Pretty Little Liars and Fifty Shades of Grey come to mind).

Rivals is a bit of an anomaly in how it has tackled Rupert and Taggie’s age-gap relationship so far, and the slower pace seems to have played a very necessary part in that. Rutag’s slow-burn underpins the entire foundation of their connection. What’s working for me personally is that Rupert hasn’t been rushing Taggie emotionally or physically to match where he’s at in his current stage of life. In fact, even though he seems besotted with her—she’s sort of become his moral touchstone—he’s doing his best to stay away from her. He seems to find the idea of letting her down (or fully letting her in) absolutely terrifying, despite how much he clearly cares.

Rivals gains further grace from viewers for its willingness to openly acknowledge Rupert and Taggie’s age gap as being an obstacle to overcome in their relationship, rather than just glossing over it or choosing to pretend it doesn’t exist. Rupert even acknowledges the age gap as being an issue himself by making a promise to Declan in season 1 that he’ll stay away from Taggie. By showing us these hurdles early on, it gives deeper insight into what a relationship would eventually mean for these two and what they’d be up against.

Watching Taggie gain life experience and have her own adventures of self-discovery—not everything has to involve Rupert—has helped them remain exciting to us as a potential couple. Her catering business seems to be thriving, for example. The slow-burn gives Taggie the opportunity to forge her own identity and ambitions, which would be important to have going into a relationship with Rupert, given their differences in life experience. Taggie is slowly blossoming into herself, without falling into that cliché trap of trying to change who she is to impress a man, and that’s empowering and necessary.

As long as Rivals continues to explore the age gap with care and consideration, I think fans will keep rooting for Rutag’s romance, no matter how long the slow-burn takes.

#6730. Do Monsters Lurk Around Us in Plain Sight? Gentle Monster’s Director Worries They Do

Bazaar spoke with Austrian director Marie Kreutzer about her Cannes favorite starring Léa Seydoux and Laurence Rupp

A newspaper clipping about a ring of pedophiles captivated the attention of Austrian filmmaker Marie Kreutzer one morning six years ago. The article detailed the buildup and the arrest in explicit detail, but one description felt more haunting than the rest.

“It was shocking because most of the guys in that ring of criminals were normal family dads,” Kreutzer tells Bazaar on a recent call. “It made me so much more aware of how close these perpetrators are, more than we want to think, and that I must almost certainly also know one.… When I read that article, and it described how the police officers were standing at the doorsteps of these guys, my first thought was, ‘How would that be for me if it were my husband?’ ”

Kreutzer decided to channel this shock, the all-consuming fear that we cannot trust those we love the most, into her latest film, Gentle Monster. Releasing on Netflix on November 18, the film tells the story of Lucy Weiss (Léa Seydoux), an experimental pianist who leaves her life behind to raise her young son with her doe-eyed husband, Philip (Laurence Rupp). The trio exists happily in the German countryside, complete with all the comforts of a cozy domestic life. Lucy and Philip love each other and their son, enjoying a sex-filled marriage that appears to have only the regular bumps. This illusion is disrupted when police knock on the door, arresting Philip for his alleged participation in a child pornography ring. Kruetzer designed the couple introduction to feel as if the rug were pulled out from under the viewer.

“It was obviously very important to have all these scenes where they interact before everything happens and where we see that they have a very natural, loving relationship,” she says. “For me, [Rupp] has nothing secretive or mysterious about him. He’s very there. And that’s what I wanted for the role, because I thought it would be good to see him and never really be open to believing that that guy would really do something like that.” She remembered telling Rupp, “It’s not like you’re playing a petty criminal. You’re playing a liar.” Kruetzer wanted him to “make us want to come back to you.”

In this way, Rupp embodies an uncanny confidence throughout the entire movie. He, of course, carries a sense of guilt, yet an audience can’t easily parse out the weight of his internal feelings. Kruetzer also refrains from giving too much direction about his innocence or guilt. Even when he is released from prison the first time, his nonchalance diffuses any skepticism; you might believe him when he says he has nothing to do with it. And when evidence mounts, including actual files, he twists the story again, telling Lucy he did it for the money. Rupp’s sympathetic portrayal is confusing—enough so that you can understand Lucy’s turmoil. Kruetzer remembers telling him to “play it as if you just messed up the taxes,” and later he told her, “I didn’t really play the monster; I played the gentle.”

This portrayal adds weight to Seydoux’s indelible performance as Lucy. The entire film orbits her reaction to this horrific revelation. Seydoux’s anger and forgiveness oscillate at a frenetic pace throughout the movie, pulling the viewer into Lucy’s point of view, as well as what Kreutzer first felt when she read the newspaper clipping.

Casting Seydoux, the director says, felt intuitive. The French actress dove headfirst into the script, expressing great interest in the character and the story. “The subject matter is tough, but the fact that it’s through the woman’s perspective—and not through the victim or perpetrator—it’s through her emotions that the story unfolds [is what interested me],” Seydoux says in Bazaar’s profile from last week. One bone-rattling scene in particular, where Lucy faces off with Philip in a light rain and directly confronts him about his arrest, underscores why she’s considered one of the best living French actresses. “As soon as we turned the camera towards her, it was really surprising what came out of her and what poured out of her,” Kreutzer said. “I remember that the crew was in shock.”

The main storyline provides enough anxiety and suspense, yet Kreutzer wrote a side plot for Gentle Monster to offer perspective. One of the cops who knocks on the Weiss family door, Elsa (Jella Haase), provides a removed point of view on Lucy’s internal dilemma. The character provides a broader understanding of the crime at the center of this story, emphasizing how widespread and hidden this problem is. “For Lucy, her life is falling apart because of this, whereas for Elsa, it’s just one of many cases, and it’s not even a bad one,” Kreutzer says. “It was important for me to show the magnitude of the problem and to not let the audience lean back and think, ‘Okay, that’s very dramatic, but it has nothing to do with me.’ ”
