#6711. Which Ultra-Processed Foods Are the Worst for You? A Dietitian Breaks It Down

From hot dogs to whole-grain breads, here are the ultra-processed foods worth limiting first.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Research over the years has shown exactly how ultra-processed foods (UPFs) negatively affect the body. What’s still being studied is how many of these specific foods, and how much of them, impact the rise in certain cancers and other diseases. Although the internet is rife with stats showing an uptick in certain cancers among younger adults, a recent study conducted among a massive 460,000 Americans debunked one of the many fear-mongering rumors that ultra-processed foods are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk specifically. But before you place your next fast food delivery order, Caitlin Hosmer, MS, RD, LDN, a registered dietitian and co-founder of MenoPantry alongside Mark Gilbert, nutritionist from The 1:1 Diet by Cambridge Weight Plan, explains which parts of the meal are potentially the most harmful, and what you should know about the study’s findings to understand which ultra-processed foods are actually the worst for you.

Most researchers use a system called NOVA, developed by a Brazilian epidemiologist, Carlos Augusto Monteiro, who coined the term “ultra-processed foods.” Hosmer explains that NOVA sorts foods into four groups based on how much they’ve been processed and not by their nutrients.

Gilbert argues that the system is questionable. “Even nutrition experts were unable to categorize foods reliably or consistently into one of [these] four categories, from unprocessed to ultra-processed. Other systems, including IFIC, Nutri-Score, and the proposed CHIPS system, exist but are similarly controversial,” says Gilbert.

To better understand what these foods are exactly, Hosmer says the simplest way to put it is that a processed food is still recognizably food that’s been preserved or prepared. An ultra-processed food has been taken apart. “These foods are designed to be cheap, shelf-stable, convenient, and very easy to overeat. The key caveat is that NOVA describes how a food is made, not how nutritious it is. So the Ultra-processed category can hold both a hot dog and a packaged whole-grain bread,” says Hosmer.

Gilbert further explains that the processes many of these foods undergo often reduce healthy, essential nutrients, remove fiber, and make the resulting food easier to consume, absorb, and digest, leading to untoward blood sugar levels, less satiety and, in the longer term, poorer metabolic health.

Gilbert notes that it’s difficult to deem any one type of UPF as “worst” simply because genetic and environmental risk factors to various diseases and ill health vary so vastly. “So, just like no single diet is ‘best’ for everyone, no single food is necessarily worst. For instance, if someone has a high heart and vascular disease risk, they might benefit from less saturated fat. If someone has a high risk of diabetes, they should avoid sugar and other refined carbohydrates that raise their blood sugar levels,” Gilbert explains.

However, Hosmer points out that when researchers break ultra-processed foods into subgroups, processed meat consistently comes out on top. The aforementioned study of more than 460,000 adults, conducted by the National Cancer Institute (NCI), found that ultra-processed food intake overall wasn’t linked to colorectal cancer—but higher consumption of meat from ultra-processed food sources was. Hosmer references a 2024 Harvard analysis in The British Medical Journal that found the same pattern for mortality.

“Across more than 30 years of follow-up, meat-, poultry-, and seafood-based ready-to-eat products showed the strongest and most consistent associations, followed by sugar-sweetened and artificially sweetened beverages, dairy-based desserts, and ultra-processed breakfast food. That category includes processed meats such as hot dogs, deli meats, bacon, sausages, and many frozen breaded meat products,” Hosmer summarizes.

Second to processed meat are sweetened drinks—both sugar-sweetened and artificially sweetened. “Sodas, sweet teas, energy drinks, and diet drinks give you sweetness and calories (or the expectation of calories) with no fiber, protein, or real food structure. They show up consistently across heart, metabolic, and mortality research,” Hosmer notes.

Sugar-laced and dairy-based desserts alongside sugary breakfast foods follow on the list. “Many sugary cereals and pastries are basically dessert dressed up as breakfast,” says Hosmer.

These foods won’t necessarily give you cancer or lead to other diseases; Hosmer explains that the more useful message is that “worst” means low in what the body needs and high in what it doesn’t. In the NCI study, higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium from ultra-processed food sources was linked to a lower incidence of colorectal cancer. “A packaged whole-grain bread and a package of bologna are both “ultra-processed,” but they are not the same choice,” she adds.

Many UPFs are often made to be irresistible, meaning you’ll likely eat more than the recommended serving size. Gilbert explains that this leads to large spikes in blood sugar and doesn’t reduce satiety as much as most whole foods do. UPFs can also increase overall calorie intake. “Increased calorie intake and excess blood sugar spikes cause weight gain, high blood pressure, inflammation, diabetes, unhealthy blood lipids, generally poor metabolic health, and a variety of other effects which increase a person’s odds of the most common serious health conditions and diseases, reducing health span and lifespan,” Gilbert warns.

To illustrate, Hosmer points to what she calls a small but elegant 2019 National Institutes of Health (NIH) trial led by Kevin Hall, which she says has the strongest causal evidence. Twenty adults lived on a metabolic ward and ate either an ultra-processed or a minimally processed diet for two weeks each. The diets were matched in calories, sugar, fat, fiber, and sodium, and people could eat as much as they wanted. On the ultra-processed diet, participants ate about 500 more calories a day, ate faster, and gained weight—about two pounds; on the minimally processed diet, they lost about the same amount. “That points to something about the food’s form, not just its nutrients: it’s soft, energy-dense, quick to eat, and slow to trigger fullness,” says Hosmer.

Considering these results, she says there are multiple mechanisms present that likely work together:

Turn the package over and read the ingredient list. That tells you far more than the front of the box. Some signs:

Context matters too. A whole-grain bread with one dough conditioner is a very different food from a toaster pastry, even though both may technically count as ultra-processed. Ask two questions: how processed is it, and what is it actually giving me? Fiber, protein, whole grains, and added nutrients count for a lot.

This depends greatly on the specific foods in question. “That’s what makes this new study that differentiates between the different kinds of processed foods particularly important,” says Hosmer. “The clearest evidence is for processed meat. In 2015, the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified processed meat as a Group 1 carcinogen for colorectal cancer. That’s the category for strong evidence that something causes cancer, though it says nothing about how big the risk is,” Hosmer clarifies. More practically, she further explains that the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) estimated that eating 50 grams of processed meat every day—about one hot dog or a few slices of deli meat regularly—is associated with roughly an 18 percent increase in baseline colorectal cancer risk. “That’s a relative increase: for an average person, it moves a lifetime risk from approximately four to five percent to roughly five to six percent,” says Hosmer.

For ultra-processed foods as a whole category, Hosmer says the picture is less clear. The new NCI study is one of the largest ever done on this question. When the team looked by food group, whole grains and dairy were linked to lower risk and meat to higher risk. The researchers note possible opposing effects of some ultra-processed foods on colorectal cancer etiology—mainly that the helpful and harmful foods cancel each other out in the total. More specifically, the total consumption may matter more than the specific foods or food groups.

According to Hosmer, there’s also an indirect pathway. “Diets high in ultra-processed foods are linked to obesity, and excess body fat is an established risk factor for many cancers, including breast cancer after menopause, endometrial cancer, and colorectal cancer,” she notes. Hosmer warns, though, that this study’s findings shouldn’t be read as ultra-processed foods are fine. “Read it as a reminder that it’s hard to make a single recommendation about such a large and varied category of food.” When the researchers broke ultra-processed foods down by type, the results lined up with what we already know: whole grains, fiber, and dairy were linked to lower colorectal cancer risk, and processed meat to higher risk. Hosmer’s challenge is to check the new data against well-established research. “Headlines alone can be misleading, especially on topics as emotionally charged as what we eat.”

Turn the package over and read the ingredient list. That tells you far more than the front of the box. Here’s what to look for:

Context matters too. A whole-grain bread with one dough conditioner is a very different food from a toaster pastry, even though both may technically count as ultra-processed. Hosmer says to ask yourself two questions: “How processed is it, and what is it actually giving me?” Fiber, protein, whole grains, and added nutrients count for a lot.

Hosmer explains that the risks associated with ultra-processed foods include two things: how much of someone’s diet comes from these foods, and how much room their body has to absorb the negative effects.

One caveat from the new study that Hosmer points out is that participants were mostly older white Americans, so results may not generalize to younger or more diverse populations. “That matters because colorectal cancer is rising in adults under 50, the group that has grown up recently, and with the most ultra-processed food available,” she cautions.

Gilbert adds that knowing your family’s health history and getting various tests can offer some indications of individual risks, but predicting these risks is by no means foolproof. “Ultimately, those who have prediabetes, diabetes, high blood pressure, cardiovascular disease or cancer, or are living with overweight or obesity are the most at risk because these conditions can often be avoided or improved with better nutrition,” says Gilbert.

Both Gilbert and Hosmer agree here. “Some foods can be intentionally processed to increase and improve their nutritional profile rather than reduce it,” Gilbert explains. Frozen vegetables, canned beans, plain yogurt, canned salmon, and bagged salad are strong examples. They are processed and still very good for you. Processing often makes healthy food more affordable and accessible. Gilbert’s 1:1 Diet is designed to align with this. “The products we produce are processed, but instead of reducing the essential nutrient content of the products, we actually increase it, adding vitamins, minerals, essential fats, and quality protein,” Gilbert notes, adding that extensive research has shown his diet improves blood sugar, blood pressure, inflammation, metabolic health, cardiovascular health, and reverses diabetes in about half of dieters.

Myth: This new study proves ultra-processed food is safe.

Hosmer says explicitly that it doesn’t. “It looked at only one disease, colorectal cancer, in a mostly older population, and participants reported their diets just once, back in the mid-1990s. The authors themselves point out that ultra-processed foods became far more common and varied over the following two decades, so the study likely underestimated how much people were actually eating,” she clarifies. “The fairer reading is that which ultra-processed foods you eat matters more than the category itself: a whole-grain bread and a hot dog may both be “ultra-processed,” but they don’t affect the body the same way.”

Myth: It’s only about nutrients, and processing doesn’t matter.

Kevin Hall’s controlled feeding trial suggests otherwise. People ate significantly more on the ultra-processed diet even when nutrients were matched, so a food’s structure and how fast you eat it matter too.

Myth: Organic, plant-based, or “clean label” means it isn’t ultra-processed.

Myth: You have to completely eliminate ultra-processed foods.

Perfection isn’t the goal. Hosmer points out that in the NCI study, replacing 10 percent of the total weight of ultra-processed foods with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2 percent lower incidence of colorectal cancer. “We don’t yet know exactly what that looks like on an individual’s plate. The study measured diets statistically, not swap by swap. But the direction is clear, and it fits decades of nutrition research: incremental shifts away from ultra-processed foods appear to matter, even when they’re modest. Start with categories that matter most: processed meats and sweetened drinks,” she concludes.

#6710. The Governors Awards Marked the Official Start of the 'You Can See Everything' Oscars Campaign

This is an edition of the weekly newsletter Tap In, GQ senior associate editor Frazier Tharpe’s final word on the most heated online discourse about music, movies, and TV. Sign up here to get it free.

Start your engines: the 2027 Oscars race is officially underway. Awards Season always starts in earnest with the Governors Awards, a ceremony held in a smaller ballroom in the same Dolby Theater complex where the main event will take place early next spring. It’s where they give out honorary Academy Awards (and the esteemed Irving Thalberg Award) to the legends who, woefully, have yet have won a competitive Oscar—last year’s marquee honoree was Tom Cruise, this year’s were Glenn Close and Ridley Scott. But it’s also where Best Picture and the other awards narratives we will discuss endlessly for the next four months really begin to take shape.

Dune 3, Artificial, and Misty Green all had big presences in the room, which, duh. (Tim and Kylie in the cut, mostly sitting and not mingling, but it was interesting that he showed up this year but not last for the big Marty Supreme push.) But there were a few other films represented whose presence made their campaign intentions clear. Mahershala Ali presented the first award of the night to Floyd Norman (a 90-year-old trailblazing cartoonist who worked with Walt Disney and later Pete Docter) but the Your Mother 3x squad was deep, from director Bassam Tariq to John Cho. Jesse Eisenberg, Paul Giamatti and Julianne Moore put on for A24’s The Debut, Eisenberg's second directorial effort. (Watching Jesse and Andrew Garfield reconnect made for a beautiful Social Network reunion.) And Curry Barker and Inde Navarette being there would certainly imply a real push for Obsession. The duo with the most motion in the room, though, was unquestionably Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. The only time they didn’t seem like the big dogs that everyone was gassed to chat with was when they were talking to King Big Dog himself, Christopher Nolan, front and center receiving will-wishers at The Odyssey table. Nolan and Fielder is a crossover that needs to be cemented on wax, a drum I will continue to beat. But it was cool to see Zendaya talking intently with Oppenheim; her collaborator curation has been pretty elite—imagine her in whatever Oppenheim chooses to follow Primetime with?

When I asked Fielder about embarking on the campaign trail and how far the doc can actually go, he sighed and said “one day at a time,” in that Fielder monotone where you can’t quite tell if he’s being earnest or not. But he laughed off the idea of being too invested in any nominations either way.

But most importantly: the Governors Awards is just a really fun room in which to be an interloper or fly on the wall. I spotted Shawn Levy and my brain immediately started spamming the word “sublime.” Daniel Kaluuya started cracking up at the mention of his great airport interview with Tyriq Withers. Olivia Wilde, Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Ed Norton joined ranks for a brief Invite huddle. Everywhere I turned, there was either a person so famous or certified that it startled me to see them walk by (like Zendaya breezing in right as the show started, or turning around to find myself face-to-face with personal favorite Carla Gugino. (Karen Sisco mentioned!) Unlike some stuffier award ceremonies, the Governors Awards is kind of like the cocktail hour before the big sit-down dinner in March.

Ambling around the room with a stiff glass of Johnnie Walker in hand—“Did you just get carded”? an exec asked me incredulously; the bartender replied that he thought I was “like, 14"—I briefly caught up with David Corenswet, who, true to form, was unfazed by the forces beyond his control as ever. When I said “weird week huh?” he didn’t even realize I was referring to James Gunn’s DC exit, then laughed when it dawned on him and said “above my pay-grade” with a genuine shrug. We should all be so blissfully unbothered.

Later, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II told me he was excited for this week’s Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth red carpet premiere, noting that this film will be the first time he only read his scenes for a project and no other part of the story. Without wanting to give too much away, Yahya said Tarantino’s script is structured in a way where he could comfortably read his parts and get enough of the gist to stay in the dark about the rest, because the only thing better than starring in a new Tarantino joint is getting to still experience it like a fan.

Other notable sightings, interactions, and crossovers: Travis Scott doubled down on what he told me at our Men of the Year party: he wants that golden statue for his original Odyssey song, and he’s willing to play the campaign game for it, dutifully sitting through the whole night (and jetting off immediately after the ceremony ended to go catch Future’s 10 pm set at Camp Flog Gnaw up at Dodger Stadium.) Speaking of Odyssey collaborators, James Blake was also in attendance—I watched him meet H.E.R. and talk about potentially collaborating. Tom Cruise was the belle of the ball at last year’s ceremony but played it super lowkey this year, to the point where I didn’t actually realize he was there until I saw him sneak out of a secret side exit after briefly talking with Tessa Thompson. Digger’s divisive reviews and reactions have evidently not knocked Tom off of his Best Actor pivot.

As for the actual awards, after Floyd, John Malkovich charmed the room with a great toast to Glenn Close, and King Storyteller Matt Damon regaled everyone with a great impression of triple-OG crank Ridley Scott from their time together on The Martian. (Matt was hesitant to do another movie about a loner astronaut right after Interstellar, to which Ridley apparently replied “No one gives a shit.”) Both tributes and subsequent speeches were expectedly emotional; Damon pointedly said that "it’s about time we see Ridley Scott with an Oscar in his hand,” but Ridley’s remarks were all about how much the late great Tony Scott would’ve deserved one too, leading to misty eyes and standing ovations. Close addressed going 0 for 8 but said the work is the real reward as her daughter tearfully watched on. But there were great moments of levity, too, like Todd Haynes presenting Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler with an award by revealing that he and Christine both slept with the same guy back in college.

Either way, a narrative of being long overdue seems to be emerging. An Awards Season where the Tom Cruises and Glenn Closes of the game finally get theirs, while upsets like You Can See Everything shake the table. What more could you ask for?

Anne Hathaway is officially a mom of three, and her smile says she couldn’t be happier. After months of witnessing Hathaway’s incredible maternity style as she promoted her many projects of the year, we’re ready to be inspired by her mom fashion.

#6708. An Up-Close Look at The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power’s Twisted Love Triangle

Morfydd Clark, Jamie Campbell Bower, and Charlie Vickers unpack that tree nest scene.

This story contains spoilers for The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.

After sleeping alone, it takes some getting used to sharing a bed with someone. This is a challenging proposition in the third season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power for the recently reunited Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and her husband, Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower), when they use a tree nest as a makeshift bedchamber, as the Dark Lord Sauron (Charlie Vickers) hunts them down. But Elves are not mere mortals, and after centuries apart, they slip back into slumbering beside each other as if not a day has passed. On set, however, things were much more awkward: Galadriel’s sword gets in Clark’s way, she struggles to roll over in chainmail, and the couple’s moss pillow is too small.

It is mid-September 2025 at the legendary Shepperton Studios just outside London, and there has been another request for more real moss to elevate Bower’s head. (He likens this grassy pillow to the mattresses in The Princess and the Pea when we talk a year later.) The mood up in the tree nest, as Clark and Bower rehearse a scene from the fifth episode, is much lighter than what plays out on screen. Under the watchful eyes of director Sanaa Hamri, the actors figure out the logistics of spooning in this confined space, mimicking sleep so the camera can see their faces, and allowing Clark to shift to her side, then quickly back away when Galadriel imagines Sauron lying beside her. Later in the day, Vickers will switch in. The shock sends Galadriel falling backward out of the tree and straight into danger. This is not your run-of-the-mill love triangle or burgeoning throuple.

To put it mildly, Galadriel has been going through it in the adaptation of J.R.R. Tolkien’s history of Middle-earth. After she rejected Sauron’s offer to be his queen (again) at the end of season 2, he has since taken much of Middle-earth, and his quest to create the One Ring—and thereby rule over all—continues. In the previous episode, he attempted to locate an elf being held prisoner in Gundabad who knew the secrets of forging the One Ring. It turns out the last Elven-smith was already dead, but Galadriel’s long-lost husband, Celeborn, was locked up in a neighboring cell. Celeborn likely knows those same secrets that Sauron needs, making him invaluable. During their escape, Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova) is slain, and Sauron comes face-to-face with Galadriel for the first time this season. Well, other than popping into her subconscious.

When Sauron appears in Galadriel’s dreams again in the fifth episode, “The Lady of Lórien,” the safety of the tree canopy is immediately shattered as Galadriel’s sleeping mind pictures Sauron lying inches away where she expects to see Celeborn. When I catch up with Clark on Zoom a year later in September 2026, her face lights up when I mention this scene. “I loved being up there [in the tree nest],” she says. “It was so cozy.” While the episode ends with Celeborn being captured by Sauron—separating the couple once again—there is a brief respite from the horrors of this war-torn land. “There’s a real unabashed lean into the gorgeousness of fantasy,” Clark says of this season, including the foray into swoon-worthy romance in the cocooned foliage.

While the Elves have only just reunited, Clark and Bower had already established the foundation of Galadriel and Celeborn’s relationship during a dance sequence in the season 3 premiere episode, revealing a far lighter Galadriel than we have seen for some time. This also gave the actors an opportunity to get to know each other. “There is a magic about him,” Clark says of Bower. “We did get to rehearse that together, which also took away a certain type of magic in that learning a dance with someone is pretty vulnerable. We got to know each other doing that, which was really nice. He was so lovely, and he is elf-like.”

As we learned in season 1, Celeborn left to fight in the war during the First Age and never came home—Middle-earth is now in its Second Age. Galadriel and Celeborn share battle stories, but it is Sauron informing Celeborn that they have previously met (Celeborn claims he has no memory of this) that throws more fire onto this already sizzling dynamic. But before Sauron storms in like a jealous ex, Celeborn and Galadriel manage some K-I-S-S-I-N-G in the tree. “It was a tight space,” Bower laughs over the phone earlier this month. “Towards the end of that scene, there’s that beautiful moment of physical reconnection, and our intimacy coordinator [Sophie Cooch] was so helpful in finding a beauty and almost like a dance and a grace within that physical reconnection into the falling down [together], and being able to lie side by side,” Bower says.

Having just played Stranger Things’ big bad Vecna, Bower (who is a huge fan of Tolkien’s work) said he was looking for a character who represented love, and Celeborn radiates light even in the darkest circumstances. In the episode, Celeborn senses Galadriel is holding back, but doesn’t press too hard about what. “She definitely feels like she’s lost a sparkle, and he’s a mirror to her,” says Clark. “She can’t ignore the parts of it that have changed.” Clark recalls discussing with Bower that there should be zero “feeling of ownership between them.” When I mention this to Bower, he references the line from Breakfast at Tiffany’s to sum up this dynamic: “We belong to nobody, and nobody belongs to us. We don’t even belong to each other.”

Tolkien’s marriage and experience in World War I provided inspiration for this union, but it was The Magnetic Fields song “Abigail, Belle of Kilronan” that Clark says she became obsessed with while filming. “It’s about someone going off to war, and it’s like, ‘And when I come home, if I come home, you’ll be a grown woman. And when I come home, if I come home, don’t be alone, Abigail, Belle of Kilronan,’” Clark says. “That’s almost been her biggest betrayal of him that she allowed herself to be lonely for so long, which I found really beautiful.”

One person Galadriel was close to before knowing his real identity was Sauron. Although she vocalizes that she doesn’t want Sauron present in this moment—not even uttering his name—the image of him lying next to her is a jolt back to reality, even if he is a figment of her imagination. “Even though in many ways her dreams are coming true with being reunited with Celeborn,” Clark says, “they can’t live in a simple vacuum of happiness. The world is still out there, and she’s part of the world.” Unfortunately for Galadriel, as she quickly backs away, she falls from the tree, alerting the nearby orcs to their presence.

The vision seems to be Galadriel’s own doing; Sauron is living rent-free in her mind instead of intentionally popping into her dreams. Vickers discussed this approach with Clark. “The way I play it was determined by what she [Clark] had in her mind—because it’s Galadriel’s experience, it’s not Sauron’s experience—and that was to be the scariest I could be in Galadriel’s mind,” Vickers says.

When I met Vickers on set, he was in costume, grabbing a juice from craft services before joining Clark up in the tree nest. Having spent a lot of time on a nearby soundstage, where Sauron’s bleak Barad-dûr lair is located, the Australian actor was happy to experience this change of scenery. “Barad-dûr this season is incredibly intense. It was 35 degrees [95°F] on the days we were filming there,” Vickers says over Zoom. “There was a lot of sweat. It was wonderful to go into the forest on a soundstage.” Still, there were some logistical issues for Vickers up in the nest, first finding the same eyeline to match Bower’s sleeping position and then trying not to stab Clark with Sauron’s pointy gloves. “Lying down in all that stuff is incredibly challenging,” Vickers says.

Of course, you don’t see this human behavior in the final cut. “It’s a very particular thing to film something fantasy in this way because the look is so important,” Clark says. “It does matter that their hair looks absolutely lovely in that light, and they move like they’re artists with their bodies.” This includes scenes that might require a stunt double, like the one I observed. “Your stunt double is always a huge part of creating the character, but I think more so than ever with an elf, because she’s got to be excellent,” Clark says. “We do as much as we can with me being as excellent as I can be.” For everything else, Clark’s stunt double Hannah Grant (who has a ballet and martial arts background) steps in.

While the version of Sauron in this scene is a figment of Galadriel’s imagination, the real Dark Lord is traveling to the Eryn Galen woodland. Celeborn sacrifices himself to stop his wife (who is lying unconscious nearby) from being discovered. What comes next will likely be incredibly unpleasant, but Bower enjoyed going head-to-head with Vickers as the twisted trio enters its next phase.

“It’s where sparks can fly,” Bower says. “You need to build a rapport, have a friendship, a comfortability, and a trust in one another. Charlie made that so easy from day one.” However, Sauron won’t be as accommodating. “Celeborn has something that Sauron really needs,” Vickers says. “It’s the key to his whole existence up to this point, so you have all the emotional interplay, but then beneath that you have this real psychological drive, which is, ‘I will do anything. I will not stop. I will do all I can to get this secret out of you.’” It seems unlikely that Celeborn, Galadriel, or Sauron will get any sleep anytime soon.

#6707. Chanel’s Watches & Fine Jewelry Dinner Christened Daniel Humm’s New Hotspot

“Yes, it’s my first time here, too,” was the refrain repeatedly heard around the room at Humm on Hudson Street on Tuesday evening, as guests stole glances at their Première Galon watches to count down the minutes to dinner. After a candlelit cocktail hour, right on cue, at 8 p.m., the moment had come to experience Daniel Humm’s new restaurant, some two years in the making.

Chanel has been keeping New York’s best-dressed guests busy as of late: The last few weeks alone have seen outings for the Museum of Modern Art’s Film Benefit, the Dia Art Foundation, the Women’s Prize Trust, and Tribeca Through Her Lens. This time around, the annual Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner was as good an excuse as any for the group to get dolled up and enjoy a pause before the busiest season of all.

Sarah Pidgeon, who became an official ambassador for the house’s watches and fine jewelry last year, was among the earliest to arrive. For the occasion, the Love Story star donned a Coco Crush necklace and bracelets. The night was also a chance for the actress to reunite with fellow Ryan Murphy-universe newcomer Ella Beatty, fresh off her acclaimed turn as the notorious Lizzie Borden.

Though the restaurant has been open for just a month and change—Chanel’s get-together being the first brand event hosted there—word has traveled fast about its menu. Luckily, the evening’s sampling incorporated the soon-to-be-renowned caviar-topped miniature bagels, which, along with the disco-tiled bathroom, seem destined for Instagram Stories fame.

A crowd, including Ella Rubin, Jack Harlow, and Quen Blackwell, settled in, drinking up the oxblood and velvet interiors, co-designed by Pierre Yovanovitch and Humm’s longtime friend, Italian artist Francesco Clemente. Clemente—yes, the namesake of the bar at Humm’s Eleven Madison Park—covered the ceilings in hand-painted stars, bricks, tiles, and trains. Works by Louise Bourgeois, Rashid Johnson, and Roni Horn round out the feast for the eyes.

As chocolate mousses and endless trays of espresso martinis did the rounds and the clock struck 10 p.m., Pidgeon stood to introduce a surprise performance by breakthrough Canadian singer girlsweetvoiced to end the night. “I was listening to her earlier today while walking around New York, and she captures something that’s very tender and honest in her stories,” Pidgeon said. “Her music is both singular and expansive and entirely her own.”

After girlsweetvoiced serenaded the room with three songs—“Cranberry,” “Spearmint,” and “Tonight,” her Joni Mitchell–approved single that samples “California”—the night drew to a close. Guests slowly made their way toward the exit, taking engraved gold matchboxes home with them as a keepsake of a reliably good time with Chanel, no matter the theme.

#6705. Leighton Meester on the New Blair Waldorf Novel—and Whether She’d Play the Character Again

The former Gossip Girl star has already read part of the book.

In February, news broke that Gossip Girl author Cecily von Ziegesar was writing a new standalone novel about Blair Waldorf, aptly titled Blair, that would capture the iconic character’s life 20 years after the original novels took place. Leighton Meester, who famously played Blair in the 2007 show, is well aware of the project, which is tentatively set for a summer 2027 release. In fact, she told ELLE in a new interview that she has already read the first seven chapters.

When deputy editor and features director Kayla Webley Adler suggested that she could play the role again if the book was adapted into a show, she simply smiled.

She is open to revisiting the character, though. “I’ve been asked this exact question forever, but I never have a good answer because I just am always like, ‘I never say never because I don’t know,’” Meester said. “Obviously that character meant something to me. And I’m grateful that it meant something to other people. So you never know, but I really just don’t know.”

Of course, the actress didn’t share any details about Blair. Deadline wrote in February that its plot is “still under wraps, but it’s expected to follow the former NYC socialite as she returns to the Big Apple to climb her way back to the top of Upper East Side food chain.”

For her part, Meester is just happy to keep acting. “I’m sure that this is cliché at this point, but every time I finish a job, I don’t know what my next job is,” she said. “There’s nothing that’s guaranteed, so every time you get a role, you’re like, ‘I get to do this again. Here we go.’”

It’s a privilege to have a career in the industry, she said: “To be an actor is such a dream, and it’s never lost on me. I’m almost nostalgic about it because I can’t believe I still get to do this. Not to sound like a crazy person, but sometimes before I do a scene, I will tell myself, ‘This is my dream, and my life, in one way or another, has led to me being able to be there when they yell ‘action!’”

#6704. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6701. Willy Chavarria Debuts His Dream “Bitchy Little Bags”

Are you a woman chasing the Willy Chavarria look? You’ll want to channel a Hitchcock heroine—Tippi Hedren is his favorite. Elongating skirt? Check. Strong-shouldered blouse or jacket? Done. Swooping french twist? Looking up Youtube tutorials now. But what about the classic handbag hitched up in the crook of your arm? Now, that can be yours, too.

Launched this morning on willychavarria.com, two new styles—the Bronca and the W Slouch—mark the New York designer’s official debut in the handbag space. Despite the pretty regular appearance of bags at his runway shows (both the Bronca and the W Slouch were seen at his spring 2027 menswear outing), introducing the category was a long time coming for Chavarria. “I’ve just been really timid about launching bags because it’s such a big thing,” he tells Vogue. “I never wanted to have a bag that ends up at the back of the store, doesn’t get the attention it needs—we just kind of pulled back and we said, okay, we’re going to launch this very soft bag that feels good.” Hence, only two styles, and direct-to-consumer only.

The Bronca is “sassy,” “a bitchy little bag,” even, and that’s just how Chavarria likes it. Available in pink, blue, black, and chocolate brown, it features a rolled leather handle with a set of keys dangling from the clasp. His dream girl to sport it is his forever muse Bianca Jagger; he’s fantasized about her pairing it with the iconic Yves Saint Laurent white wedding suit she wore to marry Mick in 1971.

In contrast, Chavarria says the W Slouch, available in green, chocolate brown, and black, is geared more towards his menswear customers. It comes with a detachable padded long strap, making it ideal for trekking across town with half of your belongings. To style it, he suggests following the wrong shoe theory. “I think it’s really cool with a tough look for a guy to have a bag that throws it off,” he says. “I always love those looks that just make you do a double take.”

Prior to today’s release, the designer has produced a W-embossed leather tote, some clutches, and a few coin purses, but he doesn’t look at those offerings in the same light. “This is more of me looking at [the category] as a business opportunity and building a plan and thinking about how I can grow this business,” he says.

It helps that with every collection, he’s dabbling in womenswear more and more. For his women customers, he sees a handbag as the perfect way in. “The brand is still small enough that I’m very careful about adding new categories, but as I’ve seen my womenswear business grow, it makes sense from a strategic standpoint to add a bag to the collection that actually enhances the full collection. And maybe she just buys the bag, maybe that’s all she wants.”

Though Chavarria is personally partial to a razor-sharp evening clutch, he doesn’t have plans to expand into additional silhouettes anytime soon. “I want to sit with these for a while,” he says. “I want to get these in the market and have people wearing them and get comfortable with them, and then maybe add on some little offspring, some little babies that go inside.” A nesting doll of handbag options await.

#6700. Only Murders in the Building Season 6: Everything We Know So Far

Though Only Murders in the Building wrapped its fifth season in October 2025, the Hulu hit is hardly slowing down. The series is heading toward its next chapter with awards-season momentum after earning Golden Globe nominations for Best Television Series – Musical or Comedy, as well as best performance nods for stars Selena Gomez, Steve Martin, and Martin Short.

The final episode of season 5, which ended with the suspicious death of Cinda Canning, left fans on a major cliffhanger that begs for a deeper investigation. Here’s everything we know so far about the future of the show.

Yes! The news came shortly after the season 5 finale premiered. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the forthcoming season will officially switch locations and be filmed in London. The previous season’s finale ended with the trio listening to a new Cinda Canning podcast set across the pond. That, along with Canning’s mysterious death at the end of the episode, may hint at why the group could travel to the U.K.

Selena Gomez previously stated that she hopes Only Murders continues for many seasons to come. “I really hope that I can just keep evolving Mabel as I get older, because I want to do this for a long time,” she told USA Today in September 2025.

Steve Martin also felt optimistic about a sixth season. “We believe we’re doing another season,” he said. “We think so. But you have to live season by season. And even if it was canceled tomorrow, we would have to say, ‘We had a great, great run. We loved what we were doing. It was a great way to spend five, six years.’”

In May 2026, Gomez shared that filming had officially begun when she reposted a photo from the show’s Instagram account to her Instagram Story. The image, showing Gomez alongside some of the cast members together in London, was captioned, “Season 6 🇬🇧 Day 1!”

Just like previous seasons, season 6 is confirmed to have 10 episodes.

Only Murders in the Building season 6 is taking place in London, as well as a select few countryside locations in England. In an August 2026 interview with Vulture, showrunner Josh Hoffman teased, “one of the more signature episodes is called ‘The Country House,’ and that sits in a very specific vibe and look, and quite a collection of characters.” He added, “We got about an hour outside of London…and into some of the stately homes.”

Season 5 concluded with Cinda Canning (Tina Fey) dropping dead in front of the Arconia, the same night that her new U.K.-set podcast The Girl With the Curls aired. Given the proximity, Charles, Oliver, and Mabel set out to solve her murder. “It was technically a murder in the building because she did it with her last gasp,” Hoffman told Vulture. “But the question is, what was going on with her? That is what our trio is off to investigate.”

Specific plot points will remain under wraps until its premiere, but Hoffman revealed that Charles’s Brazzos television show is getting a reboot in the U.K. “Martin Freeman will go toe-to-toe at some point with Charles as to who’s the better Brazzos,” he shared.

The show will also be taking place during the holiday season. “With the show airing at the top of December, it was impossible to avoid,” Hoffman added. “Within the story, we are moving towards the end of the year. The end of last season was fall, so we had to carry through on that.” The sixth season was shot in an uncharacteristically hot summer, but the show did its best to capture an English winter “that feels a bit rainy and a bit cloudy. There will be a bit of a lean into the holiday season by the end of it all.”

Selena Gomez, Steve Martin, and Martin Short have returned for another season. Season 5 featured newcomers Renée Zellweger and Logan Lerman, while Keegan-Michael Key was elevated to a recurring role. It’s not yet clear whether these supporting characters, along with Meryl Streep and Da’Vine Joy Randolph, will return for season 6, but we’ll stay tuned.

Season 6 has also added several notable new faces. In June 2026, Deadline reported that David Tennant, Nicola Coughlan, Jodie Whittaker, Jim Broadbent, Richard Ayoade, Adrian Lukis, and Kathryn Hunter had joined the cast in recurring roles. By August 2026, Deadline reported that Doctor Who star Peter Capaldi will also be joining the upcoming season—Whittaker, Tennant, and Broadbent have all had roles within the Doctor Who universe.

Olivia Colman was added to the cast days later, with Gomez, Streep, and Short announcing the news via an Instagram video. “We have had so many amazing guest stars for Only Murders in the Building,” Gomez said in the short clip, with Streep adding, “We’re just missing one.”

Short jokingly pops into the frame before making way for Colman to appear alongside the trio.

Colman’s character will be a writer, Hoffman revealed in the Vulture interview. “The U.K. is the home of Agatha Christie. This is where Cinda Canning might have met her maker in some way,” he said. “And all of them are following along in the tradition of the cozy murder mystery. Olivia is in that line as well as a memoirist.”

Jennifer Saunders will also have a role in the sixth season, with Hoffman telling Vulture that her character takes significant inspiration from Vivienne Westwood. “I had an incredible time many years ago working on a screenplay with Brian Grazer and Ron Howard on the life of Vivienne Westwood,” he said. “So I spent a lot of time here in London developing that screenplay with her.” Though that movie never materialized, Hoffman used his research to inform Saunders’s character, which will “lean into the fashion design world in great British style, with a tip of the hat to the great Vivienne.”

Queen Camilla was extremely close to having a role in Only Murders in the Building season 6, with Hoffman telling Vulture, “We almost got Camilla...I know it’s insane, but yes, there was a moment.”

The Queen Camilla cameo never materialized because of logistics, but Hoffman “did pursue it a little bit, until I realized it’s going to be a whole thing.” Hoffman isn’t ruling out Prince Harry and Meghan Markle cameos, though—“When is she traveling? We’re leaving in three days.” He added, “I wouldn’t rule anything out.”

Season 6 of Only Murders in the Building will arrive on December 8. Gomez and the rest of her castmates revealed that filming wrapped in an August 28 video shared to the show’s social media platforms.

Yes. First look photos arrived on August 25, and feature Gomez, Martin, and Short back in costume as Mabel, Charles, and Oliver in winter-approved wardrobe staples.

The trailer for Only Murders in the Building season 6 arrived on November 17. In the trailer, Mabel, Oliver, and Charles try to find out the truth about Cinda’s death after seeing her leave her hand on the gates of The Arconia in her final moments. “Cinda died dropping a hand on our gate,” Mabel says, to which Oliver adds, “She clearly wants our help.” After discovering that Cinda was in London just before her death, the trio travels across the pond to London with the hopes of finding out who did it.

The trio struggles with getting used to how life works in England. Simple things like drinking tea prove to be a challenge when Mabel suggests that Cinda could have died from a poisonous pot of tea. The suspects—aside from Gemma Joyce, Coughlan’s character—aren’t immediately clear, but there are a host of individuals who could be guilty of the crime as the first glimpses of Streep, Ashley, Colman, and more characters are revealed in the trailer.

#6698. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6696. David Corenswet Wore a Cult-Favorite Seiko on the Red Carpet

Superman actor David Corenswet, who’s set to reprise his Man of Steel role in Man of Tomorrow next year, just wore a way-out-of-left-field watch with a tuxedo during the 17th Governors Awards last night. There was no mistaking the glint of its dial from across the step-and-repeat: a Seiko ref. 6139 "Pogue" automatic chronograph. The bulky sport watch looked totally out of place in the restrained, elegant atmosphere of the awards ceremony…and absolutely perfect.

The “Pogue,” as the yellow-dial variant is known, is a wildly cool and beloved watch, and Corenswet smartly took advantage of the way it pops against the black-and-white of a classic tux. Plus, it doesn’t hurt that among Seiko collectors, the Pogue is a cult classic, often ranking towards the top of best-Seiko-ever lists. Not only is it an aesthetic swerve on the red carpet, but it’s the type of relatively affordable oddball celebrities rarely reach for.

What’s so special about the 6139, and why is it called the “Pogue,” you might ask? The 6139 was among the very first batch of automatic chronographs. A group of brands—Seiko; a consortium of Hamilton-Büren, Heuer-Leonaids, Breitling, and Dubois Dépraz; and Zenith-Movado—raced to be the first to debut the mechanical innovation. Who won the race is still a matter of debate, but one thing is for certain: when the 6139 hit the Japanese market in 1969, it featured an integrated design, a column wheel, and a vertical clutch. Meshing hallmarks of classic chronograph construction with the convenience of automatic winding at a relatively affordable price, it was paired with a wide variety of colorful dials and funky cases and produced for roughly a decade.

One of these designs, the ref. 6139-6002, is particularly eye-catching thanks to its bright-yellow dial with a contrasting blue-and-red tachymeter bezel, a 30-minute chronograph register, and a day-date display. American astronaut Col. William R. famously wore the Pogue during the Skylab 4 mission from November 1973 to February 1974. Subsequently, the 6139-6002 took on Pogue’s name, and is now one of the most collectible vintage Seiko references.

The best part? Though there’s unfortunately no magic bullet to make you 6’4” and handsome as Superman, you can snag a pretty good “Pogue” for under $2,000. It may not take you into space, but as Corenswet has proven, it sure livens up your average black-tie outfit.

#6692. Aman Essentials Creative Director Kristina Romanova on Collaborating With Kim Jones

“I think the most successful collaborations are the ones that feel a little unexpected at first, but completely natural once you see the result,” the creative director told Bazaar

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Kim Jones is, in his own words, an “Aman junkie.” Over the years, the designer—known for his work as artistic director of Fendi (2020–2024) and Dior Mens (2018-2025) and who recently announced his own soon to be launched namesake label—has turned to the luxury hospitality group for its suite of exclusive resorts, hotels, and private residences, traveling the world and experiencing more than 30 of the company’s destinations. It was this, even more so than his longstanding career in fashion, that made creative director Kristina Romanova declare him the “perfect” choice for retail subsidiary Aman Essentials’s debut collaboration.

“He knows exactly what makes the brand special,” says Romanova, who first met Jones at a masked ball in Venice, where the two creatives bonded over a shared love of travel, fashion, and art—all pillars of the broader Aman ethos. “We didn’t need to explain the Aman philosophy to him; he already lived it. When the idea of a fashion collaboration came up, I had absolutely no doubt that it had to be Kim.”

“For me, I’m not interested in collaborations simply for the sake of creating something new or generating attention. There has to be a shared sensibility, mutual respect and something meaningful that both sides bring to the table. At the same time, I don’t want someone who simply repeats what Aman already does. The whole point of collaborating is to introduce a fresh perspective, perhaps even challenge us a little, while staying true to who we are.”

With this trust, Romanova and the Aman Essentials team gave Jones full creative reign, asking the designer to offer his own interpretation of the Aman world through a line of knitwear, silks, accessories, and more. The result was “Lines of Passage,” a capsule wardrobe that could take a traveler from airplane to adventure, with an emphasis on practicality, timelessness, and high-quality materials. In colorways that might blend into the blues of an ocean getaway or the greens of hiking retreat, Jones designed windbreakers and pullovers alongside silk pajamas and slippers, everyday polos and T-shirts, and swimwear. And to celebrate, travelled to one of the Aman’s most famed locations, Aman Tokyo for not only the campaign’s stirring visuals but a bespoke trip that included an itinerary that showcased the finest of Japanese craft and culture as well as a dinner that was attended by the likes of Claire Waight Keller and Yoon Ahn.

“Aman has always been more than a hotel brand. It represents a particular way of living, one rooted in a love of travel, nature, culture and the freedom to be completely at ease,” Romanova adds. “The collection is a natural extension of that philosophy.”

#6691. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

But rather than keeping everything box-fresh, Social Status has roughed up the leather so it arrives pre-scuffed, as though you’ve owned these shoes for years.

The big switch happens across the sidewalls. The usual white leather panels have been replaced with mismatched patches of indigo fabric covered in white sashiko-style stitching. Sashiko is a traditional Japanese embroidery technique used to reinforce, repair, and extend the life of clothing. It’s particularly associated with vintage workwear and denim, which is why these Jordans look like they’ve been mended using a very expensive pair of jeans.

There’s also an old-school nylon tongue, a slightly aged sole, and a custom shoebox wrapped in the same blue pattern.

Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’

While you might normally expect this sort of big Jordan release to land on the High, it’s nice to see the Low silhouette get some love. Some dudes prefer it, after all—it’s less bulky around the ankle and works better under wider trousers. You still get all the bits that make an Air Jordan 1 instantly recognizable, only without half the collar.

The Social Status x Air Jordan 1 Low OG ‘Sashiko’ is set to drop on December 18 for $155 through Social Status, with a wider release via Nike, the SNKRS app, and select stockists expected to arrive later on. Japanese denim guys, get your credit cards ready.

A version of this story originally appeared on British GQ.

#6689. The Vogue Business People Moves Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business People Moves Tracker, a running list highlighting the key executive appointments and exits across the fashion and beauty industries. From CEOs to creative directors to other key C-suite hires, we track the leadership shifts that are reshaping the industry.

Background: Alessandro Pungetti has been appointed head designer and creative director of Japanese brand White Mountaineering, starting with the FW27 season. Pungetti previously held roles as knitwear designer at Stone Island before joining CP Company as head designer across all collections. In 2009, he founded Ten C with Paul Harvey, who he previously collaborated with at Stone Island.

Company comments: “While inheriting the core values ​​of White Mountaineering, [Alessandro] will also pioneer new possibilities, leading to the brand’s further development,” the press release said.

Background: Justin Boxford has been appointed CEO of Capri Holdings, following John D Idol’s announcement that he will retire as chairman and CEO after two decades of leadership. Boxford joins from The Estée Lauder Companies, where he most recently served as global president, luxury beauty brands. He previously served as global brand president of Estée Lauder. To support the transition, Idol will serve as a senior advisor to Capri Holdings through March 31.

Company comments: “We are confident that Justin is the right leader to guide Capri in its next chapter of growth,” said Robin Freestone, incoming independent chairman of the board. “He brings an exceptional track record of revitalizing and growing global luxury and beauty brands, deep international experience and a people-centered leadership approach.”

“It has been an extraordinary privilege to lead Capri for the past 23 years,” said Idol. “I am immensely proud of what we have accomplished together. I have had the opportunity to work with Justin in the past while he helped build the Michael Kors fragrance business at The Estée Lauder Companies and have watched his successes over the years. I am confident he is the ideal person to lead Capri into the future.”

Background: Jonatan Janmark has stepped down as CEO of Circulose (formerly Renewcell), with CFO Amanda Geijer appointed to lead the business in the interim. In 2024, textile-to-textile recycler Renewcell filed for bankruptcy, having struggled to get the brand buy-in needed to keep its commercial-scale production facility in Sweden afloat. Former McKinsey partner Janmark was appointed CEO the same year, after renaming the company to Circulose under the ownership of private equity firm Altor. Now, Janmark has stepped down, having completed his mandate of securing enough brand partnerships to restart the production plant. Geijer will take over with the support of executive chair Helena Helmersson.

Company comments: “When Jonatan joined, Circulose had just been given a second chance. Since then, he has made Circulose a leading player in textile-to-textile recycling again. That has taken a lot of energy, creativity and teamwork. I have learnt a lot from working with Jonatan, and I want to thank him for everything he has built,” Helmersson said in a statement. “For the upcoming phase, I am very pleased that Amanda, who knows the company and our plans well, has agreed to lead Circulose as interim CEO until a permanent CEO is in place.”

Background: Caroline Deroche Pasquier joins Dior in a newly created role as director of press, VIP and cultural relations. She began her career at Saint Laurent before joining LVMH, where she worked at Louis Vuitton and Givenchy. During the last six years, Pasquier has led global communications for Bottega Veneta and then Versace. At Dior, she will work closely with the house’s creative director Jonathan Anderson, reporting to Olivier Bialobos, deputy managing director in charge of global communication and image.

Company comments: “[Deroche Pasquier’s] career spans communication, creative collaboration, international markets and cultural relationships, giving her a broad perspective on the development and expression of luxury brands,” the company said in a statement.

Background: Oliver Timm has voluntarily stepped down from Hugo Boss, where he’s been both chief sales officer and deputy CEO since 2024, as well as the company board. In the meantime, CEO Daniel Grieder, alongside CFO and COO Ivica Maric, will split Timm’s previous duties. Timm was initially appointed as chief sales officer in 2021, to oversee Hugo Boss’s two brands (Boss and Hugo), including wholesale, e-commerce, visual merchandizing, retail operations, and customer relations.

The announcement follows Hugo Boss’s 5% sales drop in Q3 — attributed to an ongoing turnaround at the company — and Frasers Group’s de-facto takeover of the company on October 23.

Company comments: “Oliver Timm and I have been working side by side throughout our careers for almost 30 years, and it is a great honor for me to look back on this time and the many moments we have shared. I will miss working alongside him,” said Grieder in a statement. “During his time at Hugo Boss, he has repositioned sales with a future-oriented omnichannel approach and a strong customer-centric mindset, making a significant contribution to our growth and digitalization. As I look back at these achievements, I wish him, also on behalf of the entire managing board, the very best for the future.”

Michael Murray, Hugo Boss chair and Frasers Group CEO, also shared his appreciation: “On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to thank Oliver Timm for his contribution to Hugo Boss over the past years. We appreciate his commitment and wish him all the best for his professional and personal future.”

Background: Ben Hallam, most recently SVP of marketing at Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts, has been appointed as Lululemon’s chief brand officer. At the sportswear brand, Hallam will lead global brand marketing, brand creative, store experience, and community. He will join the company’s senior leadership team and report to CEO Heidi O’Neill who joined in April 2026.

The announcement comes after the appointments of Maggie Gauger as president and chief product officer and Joseph Godsey as chief operating officer. On Friday, the company also announced the appointment of Emily Sunderland as chief strategy officer, effective November 23. Sunderland joins from Boston Consulting Group and will report to chief financial officer Meghan Frank. Searches remain underway for a chief technology officer and a chief communications officer.

Company comments: “Ben brings an exceptional combination of creative vision, commercial discipline, and experience transforming iconic, premium brands at scale,” O’Neill said in a statement. “His proven ability to translate brand strategy into distinctive and compelling guest experiences will be critical as we strengthen how our brand comes to life across every touchpoint. Ben will play a central role in building a stronger and more competitive Lululemon.”

Background: Daisy Shaw-Ellis has been appointed CMO of Malone Souliers, where she will oversee the brand’s global marketing and communications, with an emphasis on expansion in North America. Shaw-Ellis joins from Condé Nast, where she was most recently accessories and jewelry director for Vogue and Vanity Fair.

Company comments: “We are delighted to welcome Daisy to Malone Souliers as global chief marketing officer,” CEO Andrew Wright said in a statement. “Her experience in executive positions at some of the industry’s most established and influential titles, alongside her exceptional eye and proven track record in luxury brand-building, will both enhance and amplify our voice globally. This is a pivotal moment for Malone Souliers as we embark on a new and exciting trajectory, and we look forward to presenting the brand in new and exciting ways in the coming seasons.”

Background: Clarisse Godbillon, who was CFO and COO of Lemaire from 2020 to 2025, is returning to the brand as managing director. She left Lemaire in 2025 to become COO of Jacquemus, and made the move back to the French label after Laetitia Mergui stepped down from the head job earlier this year.

Company comments: “Clarisse possesses an in-depth understanding of the company’s various activities and a profound knowledge of its identity,” the house said in a statement. “As managing director, she will oversee the development of the brand and lead its strategic and operational direction, working closely with [the house’s artistic directors and majority shareholders] Christophe Lemaire and Sarah-linh Tran.”

Background: Lady Gaga has moved into the CEO role at Haus Labs, the clean beauty company she founded in 2019. This comes after co-founder and former CEO Ben Jones exited the brand in early October. Gaga will now lead all commercial aspects of Haus Labs, alongside her prior responsibilities of creative direction and product development.

Background: Ryan Lally has been promoted to chief brand communications officer at Ralph Lauren Corp. Formerly SVP of global public relations and brand communications, Lally will continue to build on the company’s global comms strategy in this newly created role, while overseeing talent partnerships, events and more. Lally has been with the company for more than two decades, and will continue to report to David Lauren, chief branding and innovation officer.

Background: Alexis Hoopes, formerly global fashion VP at Ebay, has joined The RealReal as chief merchandising officer. At Ebay, she led the company’s $10 billion global fashion business for two-plus years, including the expansion of its Authenticity Guarantee program to new categories, price points and markets, strengthening trust among buyers and sellers. Hoopes will now lead The RealReal’s merchandising strategy, focusing on its luxury assortment and personalized product discovery — as the platform further advances its AI capabilities and unlocks growth opportunities.

Company comments: “Alexis is a proven leader who brings a rare combination of luxury merchandising expertise, global marketplace experience and operational discipline,” Rati Sahi Levesque, president and CEO of The RealReal, said in a statement. “As we build on our leadership in luxury resale, her ability to connect exceptional merchandise with evolving consumer demand will be instrumental in accelerating growth.”

Background: Hector Muelas joined LVMH in 2015 as global VP of content and creative, after working for Apple. Between 2017 and 2019, he was chief brand officer of LVMH-owned luggage brand Rimowa under chief executive Alexandre Arnault. Muelas then returned to Apple as global group creative director in 2019, a role he held until 2021. He returned to LVMH in 2023 as Tiffany & Co.’s global chief brand and creative officer, reuniting with Alexandre Arnault.

He has now been named Louis Vuitton chief brand creative officer, a newly created position reporting to Louis Vuitton deputy CEO Damien Bertrand.

Company comments: “Hector will define and steer our creative storytelling across all touchpoints, thereby ensuring strong overall image consistency. Leading creative and content execution, he will oversee all brand campaigns, with the art buying team led by Magena Chansarel and the content factory team led by Carole Fuchs joining his organization. In close collaboration with our business units, regions, and creative talents, Hector will further elevate our brand desirability, ensuring the house continues to set the benchmark in cultural resonance, creative boldness, and emotional connection with our clients worldwide,” Bertrand said in an internal announcement.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky, who most recently exited the board at Chanel, but remains president of Chanel SAS and fashion, is now co-chair of The Fashion Pact. A non-profit organization, The Fashion Pact is a coalition of CEOs from more than 150 companies representing a third of the global fashion industry by volume. Pavlovsky will work alongside Inditex CEO Óscar García Maceiras and climate campaigner Paul Polman to build on the work of the pact in creating a net-zero fashion industry. (Chanel is among the coalition’s founding signatories back in 2019.)

Company comments: “As we look ahead to 2027, our focus is increasingly on translating collective ambition into implementation, and scaling solutions across the industry. Bruno’s appointment marks an important step in this journey, bringing valuable leadership and perspective as we work to strengthen collaboration across regions, business models and supply chains,” The Fashion Pact wrote on LinkedIn.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky joined Chanel in 1990 and became a board member in 2018, a duty he will now step down from. Since 2022, he has also been president of the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode. Pavlovsky remains president of Chanel SAS and of the house’s fashion activities.

Company comments: “This latest move marks the completion of the board’s evolution toward a composition of independent directors, bringing diverse external expertise and perspectives, while retaining executive representation through the global executive chair and global CEO. Bruno Pavlovsky remains fully committed to his role as president of Chanel’s fashion activities and president of Chanel SAS,” Chanel said in a statement.

Background: Zankov has appointed Jack Tobin, founder of luxury brand development consultancy Jack Tobin Agency, as CEO and business partner of Zankov, formalizing a partnership that has developed since Tobin began consulting for the brand two years ago. Since beginning its partnership with Jack Tobin Agency, Zankov has increased its international business more than tenfold and doubled its global stockist network.

Company comments: “Zankov is at an incredibly exciting stage in its growth. I have always envisioned having a partner who could join me in shaping the next chapter of the brand — someone who shares my ambition to build an enduring business while staying true to the creative vision that has always defined Zankov. Jack is the ideal partner to take this next step with, and I’m excited about what we can build together,” says Henry Zankov, founder and creative director.

Background: Net-a-Porter (NAP) has appointed Devina Foley as Americas president to oversee the retailer’s US and Canada strategy. With more than 20 years of experience across retail, merchandising and e-commerce, Foley will help strengthen NAP’s market positioning as it settles into a new era under LuxExperience Group. She has held senior leadership roles at Bandier, Rockets of Awesome and Gilt, following earlier positions at Loft and Gap Inc. Based in New York, Foley will report to NAP CEO Heather Kaminetsky.

Company comments: “Devina brings an impressive breadth of experience and a proven track record of driving growth and leading businesses through transformation,” Kaminetsky said in a statement. “Her leadership and expertise will be invaluable as we continue to grow Net-a-Porter’s US business.”

Background: LVMH has promoted Clara Boissonnas, formerly women’s leather goods product director at Louis Vuitton, to CEO of Pucci. Boissonnas joined Louis Vuitton in 2002 as a product manager, before exiting four years later. After a decade working across Lanvin and Byredo, she returned to LV where she helped shape the maison’s coveted leather goods business. At Pucci, Boissonnas will strengthen the brand’s distinctive creative identity, desirability, and international reach, while reporting to Pietro Beccari, chair and CEO of the LVMH Fashion Group. As for Saar Debrouwere, who has led Pucci since 2022, her future role will be announced in due course, according to the group.

Company comments: “Clara has made a significant contribution to Louis Vuitton through her deep product expertise, strong creative sensibility, and unwavering commitment to excellence. Her ability to combine creative ambition with a clear understanding of the business makes her ideally suited to lead Pucci into its next chapter,” Beccari said in a statement.

Background: Yanina Novitskaya, who has spent the last 19 years at Cartier, most recently as CEO of South East Asia and Oceania, is the next chief executive of Richemont-owned Delvaux. Delvaux, the world’s oldest fine leather goods house, was founded in Brussels in 1829. In its next chapter, Novitskaya succeeds Jean-Marc Loubier, who returned to lead the brand after its acquisition in 2021, and will report to Richemont fashion and accessories CEO Philippe Fortunado.

Company comments: “Yanina’s strong knowledge of the luxury industry will be instrumental in leading Delvaux into its next chapter, strengthening its distinctive positioning and continuing to drive product desirability and international growth,” Fortunato said in a statement.

Background: Marc Jacobs has appointed John Wattiker as CMO to lead the brand’s global marketing strategy. Wattiker joins the brand after almost 15 years at Hearst Magazines working in the company’s advertising business, where he most recently held the role of VP of fashion and luxury. Prior to Hearst, he worked in the banking sector. At Marc Jacobs, Wattiker will oversee efforts to strengthen brand positioning, deepen consumer engagement and further expand the recently acquired brand’s global reach and relevance under new owner WHP Global.

Company comments: “John brings deep experience across luxury, fashion and media, with a clear understanding of how to build brands and engage consumers,” Marc Jacobs CEO Eric Marechalle said in a statement. “He pairs creative instinct with strategic and commercial discipline and brings an extensive network of relationships built over the course of his career. I am confident he will be a great addition to our leadership team as we grow Marc Jacobs globally.”

Background: Chanel has appointed a creative makeup director, Lucia Pieroni. Previously, Pieroni was creative director of makeup at Shiseido-owned Clé de Peau Beauté (2006-2019), which led to a series of partnerships with photographers and designers where Pieroni helped shape beauty direction for fashion shows, editorials, and campaigns. At Chanel, she will work alongside the makeup creation studio reporting to Simona Cattaneo, president of fragrance and beauty.

Company comments: “Lucia possesses an extraordinary instinct for beauty. She perceives the individuality in every face and understands with precision how to reveal it, creating makeup that feels intuitive and expressive, while always celebrating singularity. Her artistic vision and unique savoir-faire will make this collaboration a decisive new chapter for Chanel Makeup,” Cattaneo said in a statement.

Background: Alistair McCallum, formerly global communications VP at Burberry, has been appointed chief marketing officer of Givenchy. McCallum arrives with international comms experience at fellow LVMH house Fendi, and before that, at Alexander McQueen, where he worked with now-Givenchy creative director Sarah Burton.
